formulation.evidence: Clauses (i)-(viii) state the setting (model data, time window, inertial frame, C^2 motion with body angular velocity and body inertia matrix), the declared continuous external torque datum tau with dimension mu l^2 tau^-2 and its reading as the total external torque about the centre of mass, the adopted balance L_c'=tau, the torque-free case, the relation to the particle balance, the absence of any momentum or energy balance, the transformation law of a datum under a change of inertial frame, and the scope and exclusions.

scope.evidence: physical_scope states that no force law producing tau, no momentum balance for the centre of mass, no conservation law and no measured torque is asserted; it excludes deformable bodies, variable mass, impacts and contact or sliding laws, requires friction, contact and drive torques to be declared inside tau with their own models, and carries AC_omega only for the finiteness of the defining integrals of the model's angular momentum.

sources.evidence: Tong, Classical Dynamics, Section 3.3 (printed pages 53-55, PDF pages 59-61) presents the angular-momentum rate and Euler's equations with an applied torque; Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics CM, Chapter 4 Section 4.4, Eq. (4.66) (chapter page 15, PDF page 69) states Euler's equations with torque components; Sussman-Wisdom, SICM 2nd ed., Section 2.9, Eqs. (2.80)-(2.83) treats angular-momentum evolution under an applied torque. All three treat the torque as an input datum, not as derived from the mass distribution.

non_derivation.evidence: No Proof section; provenance.proof is not-applicable; clause (v) states explicitly that no claim that the balance follows from the particle balance or any other item is made or proved on the page, and clauses (iv) and (viii) record that no measured value and no concrete body is asserted.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed clauses (i)-(viii) and every formulation supplier: bounded centred positive-mass measure, open nondegenerate time window, C^2 placement, C^1 body angular velocity and finite L_c=RIomega under AC_omega. Torque is a declared continuous spatial vector with torque dimension; L_c prime=tau is adopted, not inferred from the finite-particle supplier. Degenerate inertia remains allowed until an inverse is used; Galilean boosts cancel in relative velocity. Citation locator correction is sound; no empirical premise.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only to make the integrals below finite.
Adopt the model and notation of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: a reference
mass distribution $\nu$ with total mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates,
a fixed inertial frame, and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^{2}$ on
the time window $I_0$, body angular velocity $\omega$
([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]]) and body inertia matrix $I$
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]). Define the **total momentum**, **kinetic
energy** and **angular momentum about the centre of mass** of the model along
the motion by the componentwise integrals
$$P(t):=\int\partial_tx(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho),\qquad K(t):=\frac12\int\lVert\partial_tx(t,\rho)\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),$$
$$L_c(t):=\int\bigl(x(t,\rho)-c(t)\bigr)\times\bigl(\partial_tx(t,\rho)-c'(t)\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho),$$
with dimensions $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$, $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ and
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). Then for every $t\in I_0$:

1. the three integrands are $\nu$-integrable, so $P(t)$, $K(t)$ and
   $L_c(t)$ are a well-defined finite vector and finite real numbers;
2. $P(t)=m\,c'(t)$;
3. $K(t)=\dfrac12m\lVert c'(t)\rVert_2^{2}+\dfrac12\omega(t)^{\mathsf T}I\omega(t)$;
4. $L_c(t)=R(t)\,I\,\omega(t)$.

The identities hold for every $C^{2}$ configuration path; no equation of
motion, force law or conservation statement is used or asserted.

Adopt the model, inertial frame and notation of
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] and [[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]], and
let a motion $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ have configuration path $(c,R)$ of
class $C^2$ on the time window $I_0$ ([[def-interval]]).

**(a) Body angular velocity.** By
[[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]], the matrix
$R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)$ is skew-symmetric at every $t\in I_0$
([[lem-cm-matrix-curve-derivative-rules]] clause 3), and by
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]] clause 2 there is exactly
one vector $\omega(t)\in\mathbb R^3$ with
$$R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)=[\omega(t)]_\times .$$
The map $\omega:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ is the **body angular velocity** of the
motion. Since $R$ is of class $C^2$, the entries of $R^{\mathsf T}R'$ are
differentiable and hence $\omega$ is of class $C^1$; its derivative is the
**body angular acceleration**. The dimension is $[\omega]=\tau^{-1}$
([[def-cm01-units]]), read in radians per second under the radian convention,
in which angles are dimensionless.

**(b) Spatial angular velocity.** The **spatial angular velocity** of the
motion is
$$\omega_{\mathrm s}(t):=R(t)\omega(t)\in\mathbb R^3,$$
of the same dimension $\tau^{-1}$. By the conjugation clause of
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]],
$R'(t)R(t)^{\mathsf T}=[\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)]_\times$; this is the
space-frame rate matrix of the motion.

**(c) Material velocity field.** For every material label $\rho$,
$$\partial_tx(t,\rho)=c'(t)+R(t)\bigl(\omega(t)\times\rho\bigr),$$
because $R'(t)=R(t)[\omega(t)]_\times$ and
$[\omega]_\times\rho=\omega\times\rho$
([[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]],
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]] clause 1). Writing
$p=x(t,\rho)$ for the spatial position of the label and using
$R(\omega\times\rho)=(R\omega)\times(R\rho)$, the same identity reads
$$\partial_tx(t,\rho)=c'(t)+\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\times\bigl(p-c(t)\bigr):$$
the material velocity field is that of a translation $c'(t)$ composed with a
rotation of angular velocity $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ about the centre of mass
$c(t)$. The motion is a **pure translation** at time $t$ exactly when
$\omega(t)=0$, equivalently $R'(t)=0$; then every material velocity equals
$c'(t)$.

**(d) Uniqueness of the velocity data.** The velocity field determines
$c'(t)$ and $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ uniquely: if a motion has material
velocity field $p\mapsto v(t,p)=c'(t)+\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\times(p-c(t))$,
then evaluating at $p=c(t)$ gives $c'(t)=v(t,c(t))$, and for $u\in\mathbb R^3$
the difference $v(t,c(t)+u)-v(t,c(t))=\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\times u$ is a
linear map of $u$; testing it on two linearly independent vectors determines
$\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ by the injectivity clause of
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]], and then
$\omega(t)=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$. The pair
$\bigl(c'(t),\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\bigr)$ is therefore an intrinsic
description of the velocity field; the body angular velocity is its
description in the body-fixed frame, and the choice of reference coordinates
is part of the model data fixed in [[post-cm10-rigid-material]].

**(e) Instantaneous rotation axis.** If $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\neq0$, the line
$$\bigl\{c(t)+s\,\omega_{\mathrm s}(t):s\in\mathbb R\bigr\}$$
is the **instantaneous rotation axis** of the motion at time $t$: it is the
set of spatial points whose material velocity equals $c'(t)$, as follows from
$\omega_{\mathrm s}\times(\omega_{\mathrm s}s)=0$. Conversely, write
$w=\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ and $z=p-c(t)$. If $w\times z=0$, choose a
coordinate $i$ with $w_i\neq0$; the cross-product coordinate equations
([[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]] clause 1) give
$w_i z_j=w_j z_i$ for every $j$, hence $z=(z_i/w_i)w$.
This proves that the zero relative-velocity set is exactly the displayed
line. The velocity field is
constant on lines parallel to $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ and rotates about this
axis; if also $c'(t)=0$ at that instant, every point of the axis is
instantaneously at rest and the motion is an instantaneous rotation about it.
No claim is made that the axis is fixed in time or in space.

**(f) Conventions and scope.** The convention fixed here is the body-fixed
one of the cited mathematical definition: $\Omega=R^{\mathsf T}R'=[\omega]_\times$
and $R'=R\Omega$. A consumer using the space-fixed convention must state the
change, which is the rotation by $R$ recorded in (b); the two vectors agree
only when $R(t)$ fixes $\omega(t)$. Both vectors are kinematic quantities of
the motion: no torque, no angular momentum and no equation of motion for
$\omega$ is asserted, and no measured angular velocity is recorded. The
behaviour of $\omega$ under a change of inertial frame is proved in the
frame-covariance theorem of this page.

Adopt the model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: the reference mass
distribution $\nu$, its total mass $m=\nu(\mathbb R^3)$ and its centred
reference coordinates $\int\rho\,d\nu(\rho)=0$. Assume the Axiom of Countable
Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, used only through
[[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]] to make the polynomial moments of $\nu$ of
degree at most two finite real numbers. Fix an inertial frame and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^2$
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]).

**(a) Body inertia matrix.** The **body inertia matrix** of the model is the
inertia matrix of the reference mass distribution,
$$I:=I(\nu)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}I_3-\rho\rho^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
with entries $I_{jk}=\int(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}\delta_{jk}-\rho_j\rho_k)\,d\nu$
as in [[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]; the matrix is expressed
in the standard basis of the reference coordinates. Its entries are finite
real numbers, it is symmetric, and for every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)\ \ge 0$$
by [[lem-cm-inertia-matrix-properties]] clauses 1-2; hence $I$ is symmetric
and its quadratic form is positive semidefinite. The dimension is
$[I]=\mu\ell^{2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]), read in kilogram metres squared. The
model is **nondegenerate** when no line through the origin carries the whole
mass, that is $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega\bigr)>0$ for every
$\omega\neq0$, and **degenerate** otherwise; the connection between this
criterion and the strict positivity and invertibility of $I$ is proved in the
principal-axes theorem of this page.

**(b) Spatial inertia tensor at the centre of mass.** The **spatial inertia
tensor** of the model at time $t$ is
$$I(t):=R(t)\,I\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
the matrix of the same quadratic form in the frame's spatial coordinates: for
every $n\in\mathbb R^3$,
$n^{\mathsf T}I(t)n=(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)^{\mathsf T}I(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)$. Its
entries are $C^2$ functions of $t$, since $R$ is of class $C^2$ and $I$ is
constant; the matrix rotates with the body and returns to $I$ in the
body-fixed frame, where $R=I_3$.

**(c) Inertia tensor about a spatial point.** For a spatial point
$p\in\mathbb R^3$ let
$$a(t,p):=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\bigl(p-c(t)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^3$$
be the **reference coordinate of $p$**, that is the label of the material
point of the reference placement that is placed at $p$ at time $t$. The
**inertia tensor of the model about $p$** at time $t$ is
$$I(t,p):=R(t)\,I_\nu\bigl(a(t,p)\bigr)\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
where
$$I_\nu(a)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho-a\rVert_2^{2}I_3-(\rho-a)(\rho-a)^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)$$
is the inertia tensor of the mass distribution about the point $a$ of the
reference coordinates ([[def-cm-inertia-tensor-about-a-point]]). Since the
label of a spatial point is uniquely determined by the placement, this is
well defined; for the centre of mass, $a(t,c(t))=0$ and
$I(t,c(t))=I(t)$. The dimension is again $\mu\ell^{2}$, read in kilogram
metres squared.

**(d) Moment of inertia about an axis.** Let $\ell$ be a spatial line at time
$t$, given by a point $p\in\mathbb R^3$ and a unit direction $n\in\mathbb R^3$
($\lVert n\rVert_2=1$). The **moment of inertia of the model about $\ell$** is
$$\Theta_\ell(t):=n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n .$$
Its invariance under the choices entering the description of the line and
its identification with the integral defining the physical moment of inertia
about the line are statements, not conventions; they are proved in clause
(c) of the principal-axes theorem of this page. For a **body-fixed
axis**, that is a line through the centre of mass whose direction in
reference coordinates is a constant unit vector $n_0$, the moment is
$$n_0^{\mathsf T}I n_0=\int\lVert n_0\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),$$
by clause (a), and is independent of time, because $I$ and $n_0$ are model
data.

**(e) What is constant and what moves.** The body inertia matrix $I$ is
determined by the model's reference mass distribution alone and does not
depend on the time, the frame or the motion; the spatial inertia tensor
$I(t)$ depends on the motion through the orientation $R(t)$; the inertia
tensor $I(t,p)$ about a spatial point depends on the motion through both the
orientation and the position of $p$. Principal axes and principal moments of
$I$ are the subject of the principal-axes theorem of this page.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), used only in [L1], through [[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]], to make the entries of $I$ finite real numbers. Let $

u(\mathbb R^3)$ and inertia matrix $I=I(
u)$ ([[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]). Write $\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega:=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\omega_jI_{jk}\omega_k$ for the quadratic form of $I$ on $\mathbb R^3$ and $\lVert\cdotVert_2$ for the Euclidean norm ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then:

1. $I$ is symmetric: $I_{jk}=I_{kj}$ for all $j,k$.
2. For every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$, $$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\int\lVert\omega	imeshoVert_2^2\,d
u(ho)\ \ge 0,$$ the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].
3. The symmetric bilinear form $(u,v)\mapsto u^{\mathsf T}Iv$ on $\mathbb R^3$ is therefore positive semidefinite ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]); for each $\omega
e0$, writing $\mathbb R\omega=\{t\omega:t\in\mathbb R\}$, one has $\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=0$ if and only if $
u(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega)=0$. Thus it is positive definite if and only if $

e0$, that is, no line through the origin carries the entire mass ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).
4. If the form is positive definite, then $I$ is invertible.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following
**external-torque branch** of the rigid-material model, in the setting of
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]].

**(i) Setting.** A model of the branch carries the data of
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: a reference mass distribution $\nu$ with total
mass $m>0$ and centred reference coordinates, a time window $I_0$, an
inertial frame with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]), and a
motion $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class
$C^{2}$ ([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]). Assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), used only
through [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]] to make the defining integrals of the
model's inertial quantities finite. Along the motion the body angular
velocity $\omega$ and the body inertia matrix $I$ are those of
[[def-cm10-angular-velocity]] and [[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]], and the
**angular momentum about the centre of mass** is
$$L_c(t):=\int\bigl(x(t,\rho)-c(t)\bigr)\times\bigl(\partial_tx(t,\rho)-c'(t)\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho),$$
the finite vector of clause 1 of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]], which by
clause 4 of that item satisfies the identity
$$L_c(t)=R(t)\,I\,\omega(t)\qquad(t\in I_0).$$

**(ii) External torque datum.** An **external torque datum** of the branch on
the time window $I_0$ is a continuous map
$$\tau:I_0\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,\qquad [\tau]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2},$$
the dimension being read in newton metres ([[def-cm01-units]]). Its intended
physical reading is: $\tau(t)$ is the **total external torque about the
centre of mass** at time $t$, the resultant moment about $c(t)$ of the forces
external to the model that act on the body at time $t$: weight in a declared
gravitational field, forces exerted by supports, pivots, axles or contacts,
thrusts and drives, applied couples, and frictional torques. Which external
agencies occur and which datum they jointly produce is model data fixed by
the model's further assumptions; this postulate does not derive $\tau$ from
any force system, and the statements of the pair use $\tau$ only through the
balance below.

**(iii) The adopted balance.** Along every motion of a model of the branch
with external torque datum $\tau$, adopt the **external-torque balance**
$$L_c'(t)=\tau(t)\qquad(t\in I_0).$$
This is an adopted dynamical law of the model. Through the identity
$L_c=RI\omega$ of clause (i) it is one vector equation relating the
configuration path, its first two time derivatives and the datum; it does
not by itself determine $(c,R)$, and it is not a consequence of the kinematic
definitions of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]].

**(iv) Torque-free motions.** A model of the branch whose datum vanishes,
$\tau\equiv0$ on $I_0$, is called **torque-free**; for such a model the
balance reads $L_c'\equiv0$ on $I_0$. Torque-free is a property of the
declared datum, not of the mass distribution: every model of
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] may be used with the zero datum, and the
statements of this page about torque-free motions are conditional on that
use.

**(v) Relation to the particle branch.** The framework's angular-momentum
balance for finitely many particle labels is
[[pthm-cm03-angular-momentum-balance]]: for a model that declares the
external-plus-pair presentation with antisymmetric pair forces, the angular
momentum about a fixed reference point has derivative equal to the total
torque about that point, the internal torque sum cancelling when the
evaluated pair forces are central. The rigid-material model has no particle
labels; its mass data are the measure $\nu$, and all its physical statements
weight material points by $\nu$. That balance is therefore not available
verbatim for the model of clause (i), and clause (iii) is adopted here as the
rigid-material analogue. No claim that clause (iii) follows from
[[pthm-cm03-angular-momentum-balance]], or from any other item of the
framework, is made by this postulate or proved anywhere on this page.

**(vi) No other balances.** This postulate asserts no balance for the total
momentum $mc'$ and no equation of motion for the centre of mass: an external
force datum is not part of the branch, the curve $c$ remains free except as
restricted by further model assumptions (for instance a pivot constraint
adopted on this page), and the theorems of the pair use only the balance
(iii). In particular the branch neither asserts nor denies that the centre of
masses moves uniformly, and it asserts no conservation of the rotational
kinetic energy; the power identity for the rotational term is a theorem of
this page, not an assumption.

**(vii) Frame consistency.** Let a second inertial frame be related to the
chosen one by the transformation $t'=t+b$, $x'=Qx+ut+a$ of
[[post-cm01-frames]] clause (iv), with $b\in\mathbb R$, $a,u\in\mathbb R^{3}$
and $Q\in SO(3)$, and let $\tilde x(t',\rho):=Q\,x(t'-b,\rho)+u\,(t'-b)+a$ be
the description of the same motion in the second frame
([[pthm-cm10-frame-covariance]] clause 1). Adopt: this description is again a
motion of the same model of the branch, and an external torque datum of the
model transforms between the two descriptions by
$$\tilde\tau(t'):=Q\,\tau(t'-b),$$
the transformation of a spatial vector under the rotation $Q$ alone, with no
contribution from the boost $u$, the translation $a$ or the time shift $b$.
The consistency of the balance (iii) with this transformation law — namely
that the description in the second frame satisfies the balance with datum
$\tilde\tau$, because
$\tilde L_c(t')=QL_c(t'-b)$ by clause 5 of
[[pthm-cm10-frame-covariance]] and differentiation commutes with the
constant rotation $Q$ and the time shift — is recorded and proved as a clause
of the frame-covariance theorem of this page; it is not an assumption of
the present postulate.

**(viii) Scope and exclusions.** The branch excludes deformable bodies,
internal degrees of freedom, variable mass, ablation, impact and contact
events, and every constitutive law for friction, rolling or slipping; any
such effect that is present must be declared as part of the datum $\tau$ of
clause (ii) with its own model, and a datum is a model object, not a
measurement. The branch also excludes relativistic and quantum descriptions.
Wherever a statement of the pair needs the inverse $I^{-1}$ it assumes the
model is nondegenerate in the sense of [[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] clause
(a), and that hypothesis is stated explicitly in the theorem that uses it.
The postulate asserts no measured torque, no numerical value, and no claim
that any concrete body or apparatus is described by the branch; whether a
given datum is adequate for a given apparatus is decided by comparing the
model's conditional predictions with reported observations under the
apparatus's stated regime.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points, let $t_0\in I$ and let $A,B:I\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be **differentiable at $t_0$**, meaning ([[def-matrix-space]]) that every entry function $t\mapsto A(t)_{ij}$ and $t\mapsto B(t)_{ij}$ is differentiable at $t_0$ in the sense of [[def-derivative]]; write $A'(t_0)$ for the matrix with entries $A'(t_0)_{ij}:=(t\mapsto A(t)_{ij})'(t_0)$, and similarly for $B$.

1. $A+B$ and $A^{\mathsf T}$ are differentiable at $t_0$, with $(A+B)'(t_0)=A'(t_0)+B'(t_0)$ and $(A^{\mathsf T})'(t_0)=(A'(t_0))^{\mathsf T}$.
2. $AB$ is differentiable at $t_0$, with $(AB)'(t_0)=A'(t_0)B(t_0)+A(t_0)B'(t_0)$.
3. If $A(t)\in SO(3)$ for every $t\in I$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]), then the matrix $A(t_0)^{\mathsf T}A'(t_0)$ is skew-symmetric, i.e. $(A^{\mathsf T}A')^{\mathsf T}=-A^{\mathsf T}A'$ at $t_0$, and likewise $A'(t_0)A(t_0)^{\mathsf T}$ is skew-symmetric. In particular the trace of each of these two matrices vanishes.

Use the standard basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ and coordinates $\omega=\omega_1e_1+\omega_2e_2+\omega_3e_3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], [[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Define the map $[\cdot]_\times:\mathbb R^3\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ by
$$[\omega]_\times:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\omega_3&\omega_2\\ \omega_3&0&-\omega_1\\ -\omega_2&\omega_1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then:

1. $[\omega]_\times z=\omega\times z$ for all $\omega,z\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].
2. $[\omega]_\times^{\mathsf T}=-[\omega]_\times$ for every $\omega$; the map $\omega\mapsto[\omega]_\times$ is linear and injective, and its image is exactly the set of skew-symmetric matrices of $M_3(\mathbb R)$. Consequently every skew-symmetric $\Omega\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ equals $[\omega]_\times$ for exactly one $\omega$, namely $\omega=(\Omega_{32},\Omega_{13},\Omega_{21})$.
3. For every $R\in SO(3)$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]) and every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$, $$R[\omega]_\times R^{\mathsf T}=[R\omega]_\times.$$

Let $M_3(\mathbb R)$ be the set of $3\times3$ matrices over $\mathbb R$ ([[def-matrix-space]]), with identity $I_3$ and product as in [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], transpose $R^{\mathsf T}$ as in [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]], and determinant $\det R$ as in [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]].

The **orthogonal group** and the **special orthogonal group** are the subsets

$$O(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\},\qquad SO(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\ \text{and}\ \det R=1\}.$$

Equivalently $SO(3)=O(3)\cap\{R:\det R=1\}$. Elements of $SO(3)$ are called **rotations**. The identification of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ with the function space $\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ and hence with $\mathbb R^9$ is the one of [[def-matrix-space]]; when $M_3(\mathbb R)$ is regarded as a metric or topological space, this is always the Euclidean metric of that identification.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only to make the integrals finite. Adopt the
model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] and its inertia data
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]): the reference mass distribution $\nu$ with
total mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates, the body inertia matrix $I$,
the spatial inertia tensor $I(t)=R(t)IR(t)^{\mathsf T}$ of a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$, and the inertia tensor $I(t,p)$ about a spatial
point $p$ ([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]). Then:

**(a) Principal basis.** There is an orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of
$\mathbb R^3$ and real numbers $I_1,I_2,I_3$, the **principal axes** and
**principal moments** of the model, with
$$Ie_j=I_je_j\qquad(j=1,2,3).$$

**(b) Quadratic form and rotational term.** For every
$\omega=\sum_j\omega_je_j\in\mathbb R^3$ one has
$I\omega=\sum_jI_j\omega_je_j$ and
$$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\sum_jI_j\omega_j^{2}=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)\ \ge 0,$$
and each principal moment is
$I_j=e_j^{\mathsf T}Ie_j=\int\lVert e_j\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)$.

**(c) Axis moments.** For every unit vector $n\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$n^{\mathsf T}In=\int\lVert n\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho);$$
for every spatial point $p$ and unit vector $n$, with $x=x(t,\cdot)$ the
placement at time $t$,
$$n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n=\int\lVert n\times\bigl(x(t,\rho)-p\bigr)\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho).$$
Consequently the number $\Theta_\ell(t)=n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n$ of
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] depends only on the spatial line $\ell$
$\{p+sn:s\in\mathbb R\}$ and not on the choice of the point $p$ on it nor on
the sign of the unit direction $n$.

**(d) Vanishing and positivity.** Each principal moment satisfies $I_j\ge0$,
and $I_j=0$ exactly when $\nu$ is supported on the line $\mathbb Re_j$ of the
principal axis, that is $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Re_j\bigr)=0$.
If the model is nondegenerate, that is if
$\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega\bigr)>0$ for every
$\omega\neq0$, then every $I_j>0$ and $I$ is invertible. If $\nu$ is
supported on some line through the origin (such a line exists whenever the
support of a centred $\nu$ is contained in a line, because the mean of $\nu$
is the origin), then $I$ is not invertible.

**(e) Extremal moments.** For every unit vector
$n=\sum_jc_je_j$ one has $n^{\mathsf T}In=\sum_jI_jc_j^{2}$ and therefore
$$\min_jI_j\ \le\ n^{\mathsf T}In\ \le\ \max_jI_j,$$
with the value $\max_jI_j$ attained at a unit eigenvector for a maximal
principal moment and the value $\min_jI_j$ attained at a unit eigenvector for
a minimal principal moment. Hence the largest and smallest principal moments
are the maximum and minimum of the rotational-inertia quadratic form over the
unit sphere.

The identities are conditional on the model data and the stated choice
assumption; no equation of motion and no conservation statement is used or
asserted.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Adopt the model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] and notation of
[[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]], [[def-cm10-angular-velocity]] and
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]: a reference mass distribution $\nu$ with total
mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates, a body inertia matrix $I$, a
motion $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ in one inertial frame with configuration path
$(c,R)$ of class $C^2$ and body angular velocity $\omega$, and the quantities
of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]],
$$P(t)=\int\partial_tx(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho),\qquad K(t)=\frac12\int\lVert\partial_tx(t,\rho)\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),\qquad L_c(t)=\int\bigl(x(t,\rho)-c(t)\bigr)\times\bigl(\partial_tx(t,\rho)-c'(t)\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho).$$
Let a second inertial frame be related to the first by the transformation
$t'=t+b$, $x'=Qx+ut+a$ of [[post-cm01-frames]] clause (iv), with
$b\in\mathbb R$, $a,u\in\mathbb R^3$ and $Q\in SO(3)$; the rotation $Q$ and
the boost velocity $u$ are the parameters written $R$ and $v$ in
[[post-cm01-frames]], renamed here to avoid clashes with the orientation path
$R(t)$ and the material velocity field $v(t,p)$ of
[[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]. Let
$\tilde x(t',\rho):=Q\,x(t'-b,\rho)+u\,(t'-b)+a$ be the description of the
same motion in the second frame. Then:

1. $\tilde x(t',\rho)=\tilde c(t')+\tilde R(t')\rho$ with
   $\tilde c(t')=Qc(t'-b)+u\,(t'-b)+a$ and
   $\tilde R(t')=Q\,R(t'-b)$; the maps $\tilde c$ and $\tilde R$ are of class
   $C^2$, $\tilde R$ takes values in $SO(3)$, and $\tilde x$ is a motion of
   the same model with the same reference mass distribution;
2. the body angular velocities satisfy
   $\tilde\omega(t')=\omega(t'-b)$, and the spatial angular velocities satisfy
   $\tilde\omega_{\mathrm s}(t')=Q\omega_{\mathrm s}(t'-b)$;
3. the material velocity fields satisfy
   $\partial_{t'}\tilde x(t',\rho)=Q\,\partial_tx(t'-b,\rho)+u$;
   equivalently, for a spatial point $p$ of the first frame with image
   $p'=Qp+ut+a$, $\tilde v(t',p')=Q\,v(t,p)+u$;
4. the body inertia matrix computed from $\nu$ is the same matrix $I$ in
   either frame, and the spatial inertia tensors satisfy
   $\tilde I(t')=Q\,I(t'-b)\,Q^{\mathsf T}$; consequently
   $\tilde\omega(t')^{\mathsf T}I\tilde\omega(t')=\omega(t'-b)^{\mathsf T}I\omega(t'-b)$
   and
   $\tilde\omega_{\mathrm s}(t')^{\mathsf T}\tilde I(t')\tilde\omega_{\mathrm s}(t')=\omega_{\mathrm s}(t'-b)^{\mathsf T}I(t'-b)\omega_{\mathrm s}(t'-b)$;
5. the inertial quantities satisfy
   $$\tilde P(t')=Q\,P(t'-b)+mu,\qquad \tilde L_c(t')=Q\,L_c(t'-b),$$
   $$\tilde K(t')=\frac12m\lVert Qc'(t'-b)+u\rVert_2^{2}+\frac12\omega(t'-b)^{\mathsf T}I\omega(t'-b).$$

The statements are kinematic and inertial identities for the model; no
equation of motion, no conservation law and no measured value is asserted.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

A matrix $A\in M_n(F)$ is **invertible** when there is a matrix $B\in M_n(F)$
such that

$$AB=I_n=BA.$$

Such a $B$ is unique and is denoted $A^{-1}$. The **general linear set** is

$$\operatorname{GL}_n(F):=\{A\in M_n(F):A\text{ is invertible}\}.$$

It is the set of units of the ring $M_n(F)$. The fact that it is a group under
matrix multiplication is [[cor-general-linear-group-is-a-group]]. For $n=0$,
the unique empty matrix is $I_0$ and is its own inverse.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

derivations.claim: By [L1] and [L3] the product $Rl$ is differentiable on $I_0$ with $(Rl)'=R'l+Rl'=R\bigl([\omega]_\times l+l'\bigr)=R\bigl(\omega\times l+l'\bigr)$, and by [L2] this equals $\tau$. Multiplying by $R^{\mathsf T}$ and using $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_{3}$ gives $\omega\times l+l'=R^{\mathsf T}\tau$.

Let $t'=t+b$ and use [L7]: $\tilde\omega(t')=\omega(t'-b)$ and $\tilde L_c(t')=QL_c(t'-b)$; differentiating the second identity in $t'$ by the chain rule [L7] gives $\tilde L_c'(t')=Q L_c'(t'-b)=Q\tau(t'-b)=\tilde\tau(t')$, so the adopted balance holds in the second frame.

Since $l=I\omega$ and $I$ is a constant matrix, $l'=I\omega'$; substituting $l=I\omega$ into step 1.1 gives $I\omega'+\omega\times I\omega=R^{\mathsf T}\tau$, which is clause 1 (and the alternative form $l'=R^{\mathsf T}\tau-\omega\times I\omega$).

Assume $\tau\equiv0$ and nondegeneracy. From step 1.1, $l'=-\omega\times l=(I\omega)\times\omega=l\times(I^{-1}l)$, the middle equality by antisymmetry [L4] and the last by $I^{-1}l=\omega$ from [L8]; similarly $\omega'=I^{-1}(-\omega\times I\omega)=F(\omega)$, which is clause 4.

In the positively oriented principal basis of [L5], the basis matrix $Q$ belongs to $SO(3)$ and the skew/cross correspondence [L3] gives $Q(u\times v)=(Qu)\times(Qv)$, so the usual cross-product coordinates apply. Any orthonormal principal basis can be given this orientation by negating one eigenvector, without changing eigenvalues or the motion. $I\omega=\sum_{j}I_{j}\omega_{j}e_{j}$ and the first component of $\omega\times I\omega$ is $\omega_{2}I_{3}\omega_{3}-\omega_{3}I_{2}\omega_{2}=(I_{3}-I_{2})\omega_{2}\omega_{3}$, with the cyclic analogues; writing $R^{\mathsf T}\tau=\sum_{j}\tau_{j}e_{j}$, clause 1 reads $I_{1}\omega_{1}'=(I_{2}-I_{3})\omega_{2}\omega_{3}+\tau_{1}$ and cyclically, which is clause 2.

Differentiating $K_{\mathrm{rot}}=\tfrac12\langle\omega,I\omega\rangle$ with [L6] and using the symmetry of $I$ from [L1] gives $K_{\mathrm{rot}}'=\langle\omega',I\omega\rangle=\langle\omega,I\omega'\rangle$; substituting $I\omega'=R^{\mathsf T}\tau-\omega\times I\omega$ from step 2.1 and using $\langle\omega,\omega\times I\omega\rangle=0$ by [L4] gives $K_{\mathrm{rot}}'=\langle\omega,R^{\mathsf T}\tau\rangle$, which is clause 3; when $\tau\equiv0$ this derivative vanishes identically and [L6] makes $K_{\mathrm{rot}}$ constant on $I_0$. The identification with the kinetic splitting is clause 3 of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]].

Applying step 2.1 in the second frame (whose configuration path is $(\tilde c,\tilde R)$ of class $C^{2}$ by [L7]) gives $I\tilde\omega'+\tilde\omega\times I\tilde\omega=\tilde R^{\mathsf T}\tilde\tau$ on $I_0+b$; and $\tilde R(t')^{\mathsf T}\tilde\tau(t')=R(t'-b)^{\mathsf T}Q^{\mathsf T}Q\tau(t'-b)=R(t'-b)^{\mathsf T}\tau(t'-b)$ because $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_{3}$ [L3], so the body-frame torque is unchanged; this is clause 5.

Degenerate models are allowed in clauses 1-3 and 5: only step 2.2 assumes nondegeneracy, and the remark 'Where the nondegeneracy is used' records that clause 4 alone requires invertibility of I.

citations.quote:
Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following **rigid-material
model** branch, in the spacetime and frames of [[post-cm01-spacetime]] and
[[post-cm01-frames]].

**(i) Reference mass distribution.** A rigid-material model carries, besides
the framework's time and frame structure, a **reference mass distribution**: a
measure $\nu$ on the Borel space $(\mathbb R^3,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3))$ that
is a mass distribution in the sense of
[[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]] — finite and bounded, with
$\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline B_R(0)\bigr)=0$ for some real $R>0$,
and of total mass $m:=\nu(\mathbb R^3)\in(0,+\infty)$ — whose reference
coordinates are **centred**,
$$\int\rho\,d\nu(\rho)=0\in\mathbb R^3 .$$
The label variable $\rho$ is a coordinate of the model's reference placement
and has dimension $\ell$, each component read in metres; the total mass $m$
has dimension $\mu$, read in kilograms, and $R$ has dimension $\ell$ and is
the model's **reference size**
([[def-cm01-units]]). Under the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$,
used only through [[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]] to make the polynomial
moments of $\nu$ of degree at most two finite, the first and second moments
of $\nu$ are finite real numbers. The measure $\nu$ and the number $m$ are
model data: no distribution of mass of any concrete body and no measured mass
is asserted.

**(ii) Time window and motions.** A model carries a **time window**
$I_0\subseteq\mathbb R$, a nondegenerate open interval $(a,b)$ with
$-\infty\le a<b\le+\infty$ and at least two points, read in seconds. Fix an
**inertial frame** of the model, that is the adapted chart
$(o,u,(e_1,e_2,e_3))$ with coordinates $(t,x)$ of [[post-cm01-frames]]. A
**motion** of the model in this frame is a map
$x:I_0\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ for which there exist a map
$c:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ and a map $R:I_0\to SO(3)$, both of class $C^2$
(componentwise derivatives, [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] for the coordinates
and [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]] for the target), such that
$$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho\qquad(t\in I_0,\ \rho\in\mathbb R^3).$$
Adopt: the motions of the model are the maps of this form, and the pair
$(c,R)$ is the **configuration path** of the motion. The map
$x(t,\cdot):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is the **placement** at time $t$ and is
the rigid placement of [[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]]
with translation $c$ and rotation $R$; its material velocity is
$\partial_tx(t,\rho)=c'(t)+R'(t)\rho$, defined by differentiability of $c$ and
of the entries of $R$. The time window $I_0$ is the interval on which the
model's configuration path is considered; the model's time coordinate is
the frame time $t$.

**(iii) Rigidity idealization.** The idealization adopted is that the model
describes a body that does not deform, and its content is the representation
(ii): a placement of the form $x=c+R\rho$ with $R\in SO(3)$ preserves every
mutual distance, since $R(t)$ preserves the Euclidean norm
([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]), so for all $\rho,\rho'\in\mathbb R^3$
the number $\lVert x(t,\rho)-x(t,\rho')\rVert_2=\lVert\rho-\rho'\rVert_2$ is
independent of $t$. The model class (ii) is *adopted* as the definition of a
rigid-material placement; a motion of material points that preserves all
mutual distances but whose label set fails to determine a rotation is not
claimed to be of this form, and the general characterization of
distance-preserving placements is neither asserted nor used on this page.
For a **nondegenerate labeling** — a label set containing the origin and two
linearly independent material vectors — distinct configurations $(c,R)$ and
$(\bar c,\bar R)$ give distinct placements, by [[lem-cm-rigid-labeling-stabilizer]];
the configuration data of (ii) therefore do not overcount for such a body.
Degenerate labelings and degenerate mass distributions are not excluded by
this postulate; the later items of the pair state where invertibility of the
inertial data must be assumed.

**(iv) Centre of mass and orientation.** Because the reference coordinates are
centred, the identity
$$\int x(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho)=mc(t)$$
holds for every motion, by linearity of the integral and
$\int\rho\,d\nu=0$; the physical reading is that $c(t)$ is the position of the
centre of mass of the model in the placement at time $t$. The rotation
$R(t)$ is the model's **orientation**: it carries reference coordinates into
the frame's spatial coordinates, and the **body-fixed frame** at time $t$ is
the ordered orthonormal basis $(R(t)e_1,R(t)e_2,R(t)e_3)$ of the spatial
space. The reading of $R(t)$ as the orientation of the placement uses the
nondegeneracy of (iii): for a nondegenerate labeling the material points
determine $R(t)$ uniquely, so the orientation is an attribute of the body's
placement and not of the choice of label coordinates.

**(v) Frame changes.** The description of a motion in a second inertial frame
is obtained by the change of coordinates $t'=t+b$, $x'=Qx+ut+a$ of
[[post-cm01-frames]] clause (iv), applied to every event of the motion; here
$Q\in SO(3)$ and $u\in\mathbb R^3$ are the rotation and the boost velocity of
that clause, written $R$ and $v$ there and renamed here to avoid a clash with
the orientation path $R(t)$ of clause (ii) and with the material velocity
field of the pair's definition. With the same $\rho$ labelling a material
point, the description in the second frame is
$$\tilde x(t',\rho):=Q\,x(t'-b,\rho)+u\,(t'-b)+a .$$
This description is again a motion of the model, with configuration path
$$\tilde c(t')=Qc(t'-b)+u\,(t'-b)+a,\qquad \tilde R(t')=Q\,R(t'-b),$$
because $SO(3)$ is closed under multiplication
([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]); this is a consistency requirement of
the model's frame language, exactly as for the particle worldlines of
[[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (ii). The derived transformation laws of the
angular velocity, of the inertia data and of the kinetic splitting are
theorems of this pair's page, not part of this postulate.

**(vi) No dynamics.** This postulate fixes the kinematic class of the model
and its mass data only. It asserts no force law, no torque law, no equation of
motion for the pair $(c,R)$, and no balance or conservation law; in
particular the model does not by itself constrain the configuration path,
and the effect of forces and torques on a body is a separate model
assumption. It also asserts no measured value of any mass, length, duration
or orientation.

**(vii) Scope and exclusions.** The branch excludes deformation, internal
degrees of freedom such as temperature, chemical state or an independent spin
variable, variable mass, ablation and impact events, contact, friction and
dissipative constitutive laws, and any relativistic or quantum description.
It excludes bodies whose mass distribution is not a bounded finite Borel
measure of the stated kind. A rigid-material model is not a system of
finitely many particle labels: the continuum measure $\nu$ carries the mass
data of the model, and the situations of point masses are the special cases
of measures supported on finitely many points. All physical statements about
the model weight material points by $\nu$; properties of $\nu$-null sets of
labels are not physical properties of the body.

Let $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3)$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) and let $
u$ be a measure on the measurable space $(\mathbb R^3,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3))$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-measure-space]]) that is **finite**, $
u(\mathbb R^3)<+\infty$, and **bounded**, meaning that there is a real $R>0$ with
$$
u igl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline B_R(0) igr)=0,$$
the closed ball being that of [[def-metric-ball]]. Throughout, integrals are Lebesgue integrals against $
u$ in the sense of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] and [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], and for a measurable vector- or matrix-valued function the integral is defined **componentwise**: $\int F\,d
u:= igl(\int F_1\,d
u,\int F_2\,d
u,\int F_3\,d
u igr)$ and $ igl(\int M\,d
u igr)_{jk}:=\int M_{jk}\,d
u$, whenever every displayed scalar integral is finite.

A **mass distribution on $\mathbb R^3$** is a bounded finite Borel measure $
u$ with $m:=
u(\mathbb R^3)\in(0,+\infty)$; the number $m$ is its **total mass**. Writing points of $\mathbb R^3$ as $ho$ and using the Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdotangle$ and norm $\lVerthoVert_2=\sqrt{\langleho,hoangle}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], define:

1. the **first moment** $\mu(
u):=\intho\,d
u\in\mathbb R^3$, read componentwise as $\mu(
u)_j=\intho_j\,d
u$;
2. the **inertia matrix** $I(
u)\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]) by its entries $I(
u)_{jk}:=\int igl(\lVerthoVert_2^2\,\delta_{jk}-ho_jho_k igr)\,d
u$, where $\delta_{jk}=1$ if $j=k$ and $\delta_{jk}=0$ otherwise; equivalently $I(
u)=\int igl(\lVerthoVert_2^2 I_3-hoho^{\mathsf T} igr)\,d
u$ with $I_3$ the identity matrix and $hoho^{\mathsf T}$ the matrix product of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]].

The mass distribution is **centred** when $\mu(
u)=0$. Under the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), each of the integrals above is a finite real number: on $\overline B_R(0)$ one has $|ho_j|\le R$ and $|ho_jho_k|\le R^2$, and $
u(\mathbb R^3)<+\infty$; the precise statement and proof are [[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]], which depends on this definition only for its notation. The assumption is used there exactly once, to obtain the Borel measurability of the polynomial integrands from the published continuity criterion; every later item that invokes this finiteness carries the assumption explicitly.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $
u$ be a measure on $(\mathbb R^3,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3))$ ([[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]) that is finite and bounded: $
u(\mathbb R^3)<+\infty$ and $
u(\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline B_R(0))=0$ for some $R>0$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). Then:

1. for all $j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$ the functions $ho\mapstoho_j$ and $ho\mapstoho_jho_k$ are Borel measurable and $
u$-integrable, with $\int\lvertho_jvert\,d
u\le R\,
u(\mathbb R^3)$ and $\int\lvertho_jho_kvert\,d
u\le R^2\,
u(\mathbb R^3)$;
2. consequently $m:=
u(\mathbb R^3)$ and the scalar integrals $\intho_j\,d
u$ and $\int(\lVerthoVert_2^2\delta_{jk}-ho_jho_k)\,d
u$ are finite, with $\lvert\intho_j\,d
uvert\le Rm$ and $\lvert\int(\lVerthoVert_2^2\delta_{jk}-ho_jho_k)\,d
uvert\le 2R^2m$. When $m>0$, these integrals are precisely the components of the first moment $\mu(
u)$ and inertia matrix $I(
u)$ of [[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]. When $m=0$, all these integrals vanish; the zero measure is not called a mass distribution.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only to make the integrals below finite.
Adopt the model and notation of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: a reference
mass distribution $\nu$ with total mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates,
a fixed inertial frame, and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^{2}$ on
the time window $I_0$, body angular velocity $\omega$
([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]]) and body inertia matrix $I$
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]). Define the **total momentum**, **kinetic
energy** and **angular momentum about the centre of mass** of the model along
the motion by the componentwise integrals
$$P(t):=\int\partial_tx(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho),\qquad K(t):=\frac12\int\lVert\partial_tx(t,\rho)\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),$$
$$L_c(t):=\int\bigl(x(t,\rho)-c(t)\bigr)\times\bigl(\partial_tx(t,\rho)-c'(t)\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho),$$
with dimensions $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$, $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ and
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). Then for every $t\in I_0$:

1. the three integrands are $\nu$-integrable, so $P(t)$, $K(t)$ and
   $L_c(t)$ are a well-defined finite vector and finite real numbers;
2. $P(t)=m\,c'(t)$;
3. $K(t)=\dfrac12m\lVert c'(t)\rVert_2^{2}+\dfrac12\omega(t)^{\mathsf T}I\omega(t)$;
4. $L_c(t)=R(t)\,I\,\omega(t)$.

The identities hold for every $C^{2}$ configuration path; no equation of
motion, force law or conservation statement is used or asserted.

Adopt the model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: the reference mass
distribution $\nu$, its total mass $m=\nu(\mathbb R^3)$ and its centred
reference coordinates $\int\rho\,d\nu(\rho)=0$. Assume the Axiom of Countable
Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, used only through
[[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]] to make the polynomial moments of $\nu$ of
degree at most two finite real numbers. Fix an inertial frame and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^2$
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]).

**(a) Body inertia matrix.** The **body inertia matrix** of the model is the
inertia matrix of the reference mass distribution,
$$I:=I(\nu)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}I_3-\rho\rho^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
with entries $I_{jk}=\int(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}\delta_{jk}-\rho_j\rho_k)\,d\nu$
as in [[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]; the matrix is expressed
in the standard basis of the reference coordinates. Its entries are finite
real numbers, it is symmetric, and for every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)\ \ge 0$$
by [[lem-cm-inertia-matrix-properties]] clauses 1-2; hence $I$ is symmetric
and its quadratic form is positive semidefinite. The dimension is
$[I]=\mu\ell^{2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]), read in kilogram metres squared. The
model is **nondegenerate** when no line through the origin carries the whole
mass, that is $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega\bigr)>0$ for every
$\omega\neq0$, and **degenerate** otherwise; the connection between this
criterion and the strict positivity and invertibility of $I$ is proved in the
principal-axes theorem of this page.

**(b) Spatial inertia tensor at the centre of mass.** The **spatial inertia
tensor** of the model at time $t$ is
$$I(t):=R(t)\,I\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
the matrix of the same quadratic form in the frame's spatial coordinates: for
every $n\in\mathbb R^3$,
$n^{\mathsf T}I(t)n=(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)^{\mathsf T}I(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)$. Its
entries are $C^2$ functions of $t$, since $R$ is of class $C^2$ and $I$ is
constant; the matrix rotates with the body and returns to $I$ in the
body-fixed frame, where $R=I_3$.

**(c) Inertia tensor about a spatial point.** For a spatial point
$p\in\mathbb R^3$ let
$$a(t,p):=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\bigl(p-c(t)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^3$$
be the **reference coordinate of $p$**, that is the label of the material
point of the reference placement that is placed at $p$ at time $t$. The
**inertia tensor of the model about $p$** at time $t$ is
$$I(t,p):=R(t)\,I_\nu\bigl(a(t,p)\bigr)\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
where
$$I_\nu(a)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho-a\rVert_2^{2}I_3-(\rho-a)(\rho-a)^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)$$
is the inertia tensor of the mass distribution about the point $a$ of the
reference coordinates ([[def-cm-inertia-tensor-about-a-point]]). Since the
label of a spatial point is uniquely determined by the placement, this is
well defined; for the centre of mass, $a(t,c(t))=0$ and
$I(t,c(t))=I(t)$. The dimension is again $\mu\ell^{2}$, read in kilogram
metres squared.

**(d) Moment of inertia about an axis.** Let $\ell$ be a spatial line at time
$t$, given by a point $p\in\mathbb R^3$ and a unit direction $n\in\mathbb R^3$
($\lVert n\rVert_2=1$). The **moment of inertia of the model about $\ell$** is
$$\Theta_\ell(t):=n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n .$$
Its invariance under the choices entering the description of the line and
its identification with the integral defining the physical moment of inertia
about the line are statements, not conventions; they are proved in clause
(c) of the principal-axes theorem of this page. For a **body-fixed
axis**, that is a line through the centre of mass whose direction in
reference coordinates is a constant unit vector $n_0$, the moment is
$$n_0^{\mathsf T}I n_0=\int\lVert n_0\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),$$
by clause (a), and is independent of time, because $I$ and $n_0$ are model
data.

**(e) What is constant and what moves.** The body inertia matrix $I$ is
determined by the model's reference mass distribution alone and does not
depend on the time, the frame or the motion; the spatial inertia tensor
$I(t)$ depends on the motion through the orientation $R(t)$; the inertia
tensor $I(t,p)$ about a spatial point depends on the motion through both the
orientation and the position of $p$. Principal axes and principal moments of
$I$ are the subject of the principal-axes theorem of this page.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), used through the inertia suppliers to ensure finiteness of the integrals. Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), let $\nu$ be a centred mass distribution on $\mathbb R^3$ that is not supported on any line through the origin, with inertia matrix $I$ ([[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]), let $c:J\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable and let $R:J\to SO(3)$ be twice differentiable, and let $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ be the rigid placement with body angular velocity $\omega$ ([[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]]). Write $l:=I\omega:J\to\mathbb R^3$; by [[cor-cm-principal-axes-of-the-inertia-matrix]] the inertia form is positive definite and $I$ is invertible.

Adopt the **balance hypothesis** (B): there is a map $\tau:J\to\mathbb R^3$ such that the curve $t\mapsto R(t)l(t)$ is differentiable and
$$(Rl)'(t)=\tau(t)\qquad(t\in J).$$
Then:

1. $l$ is differentiable and **Euler's equations with torque** hold: $$I\omega'+\omega\times I\omega=R^{\mathsf T}\tau\qquad\text{on }J;$$
2. if $\tau=0$ on $J$, then $l$ satisfies the **torque-free Euler equations** $l'=l\times(I^{-1}l)$, and the functions $t\mapsto\langle l(t),l(t)\rangle$ and $t\mapsto\tfrac12\langle l(t),I^{-1}l(t)\rangle=\tfrac12\omega(t)^{\mathsf T}I\omega(t)$ are constant on $J$;
3. if $\tau=0$ on $J$ and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is a positively oriented orthonormal eigenbasis of $I$ with $Ie_j=I_je_j$ and $l=\sum_jl_je_j$, then $\langle l,l\rangle=\sum_jl_j^2$ and $\tfrac12\langle l,I^{-1}l\rangle=\sum_jl_j^2/(2I_j)$ are constant on $J$, and the torque-free equations read $$l_1'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_3}-\frac1{I_2}\Bigr)l_2l_3,\qquad l_2'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_1}-\frac1{I_3}\Bigr)l_1l_3,\qquad l_3'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_2}-\frac1{I_1}\Bigr)l_1l_2.$$

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following
**external-torque branch** of the rigid-material model, in the setting of
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]].

**(i) Setting.** A model of the branch carries the data of
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: a reference mass distribution $\nu$ with total
mass $m>0$ and centred reference coordinates, a time window $I_0$, an
inertial frame with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]), and a
motion $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class
$C^{2}$ ([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]). Assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), used only
through [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]] to make the defining integrals of the
model's inertial quantities finite. Along the motion the body angular
velocity $\omega$ and the body inertia matrix $I$ are those of
[[def-cm10-angular-velocity]] and [[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]], and the
**angular momentum about the centre of mass** is
$$L_c(t):=\int\bigl(x(t,\rho)-c(t)\bigr)\times\bigl(\partial_tx(t,\rho)-c'(t)\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho),$$
the finite vector of clause 1 of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]], which by
clause 4 of that item satisfies the identity
$$L_c(t)=R(t)\,I\,\omega(t)\qquad(t\in I_0).$$

**(ii) External torque datum.** An **external torque datum** of the branch on
the time window $I_0$ is a continuous map
$$\tau:I_0\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,\qquad [\tau]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2},$$
the dimension being read in newton metres ([[def-cm01-units]]). Its intended
physical reading is: $\tau(t)$ is the **total external torque about the
centre of mass** at time $t$, the resultant moment about $c(t)$ of the forces
external to the model that act on the body at time $t$: weight in a declared
gravitational field, forces exerted by supports, pivots, axles or contacts,
thrusts and drives, applied couples, and frictional torques. Which external
agencies occur and which datum they jointly produce is model data fixed by
the model's further assumptions; this postulate does not derive $\tau$ from
any force system, and the statements of the pair use $\tau$ only through the
balance below.

**(iii) The adopted balance.** Along every motion of a model of the branch
with external torque datum $\tau$, adopt the **external-torque balance**
$$L_c'(t)=\tau(t)\qquad(t\in I_0).$$
This is an adopted dynamical law of the model. Through the identity
$L_c=RI\omega$ of clause (i) it is one vector equation relating the
configuration path, its first two time derivatives and the datum; it does
not by itself determine $(c,R)$, and it is not a consequence of the kinematic
definitions of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]].

**(iv) Torque-free motions.** A model of the branch whose datum vanishes,
$\tau\equiv0$ on $I_0$, is called **torque-free**; for such a model the
balance reads $L_c'\equiv0$ on $I_0$. Torque-free is a property of the
declared datum, not of the mass distribution: every model of
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] may be used with the zero datum, and the
statements of this page about torque-free motions are conditional on that
use.

**(v) Relation to the particle branch.** The framework's angular-momentum
balance for finitely many particle labels is
[[pthm-cm03-angular-momentum-balance]]: for a model that declares the
external-plus-pair presentation with antisymmetric pair forces, the angular
momentum about a fixed reference point has derivative equal to the total
torque about that point, the internal torque sum cancelling when the
evaluated pair forces are central. The rigid-material model has no particle
labels; its mass data are the measure $\nu$, and all its physical statements
weight material points by $\nu$. That balance is therefore not available
verbatim for the model of clause (i), and clause (iii) is adopted here as the
rigid-material analogue. No claim that clause (iii) follows from
[[pthm-cm03-angular-momentum-balance]], or from any other item of the
framework, is made by this postulate or proved anywhere on this page.

**(vi) No other balances.** This postulate asserts no balance for the total
momentum $mc'$ and no equation of motion for the centre of mass: an external
force datum is not part of the branch, the curve $c$ remains free except as
restricted by further model assumptions (for instance a pivot constraint
adopted on this page), and the theorems of the pair use only the balance
(iii). In particular the branch neither asserts nor denies that the centre of
masses moves uniformly, and it asserts no conservation of the rotational
kinetic energy; the power identity for the rotational term is a theorem of
this page, not an assumption.

**(vii) Frame consistency.** Let a second inertial frame be related to the
chosen one by the transformation $t'=t+b$, $x'=Qx+ut+a$ of
[[post-cm01-frames]] clause (iv), with $b\in\mathbb R$, $a,u\in\mathbb R^{3}$
and $Q\in SO(3)$, and let $\tilde x(t',\rho):=Q\,x(t'-b,\rho)+u\,(t'-b)+a$ be
the description of the same motion in the second frame
([[pthm-cm10-frame-covariance]] clause 1). Adopt: this description is again a
motion of the same model of the branch, and an external torque datum of the
model transforms between the two descriptions by
$$\tilde\tau(t'):=Q\,\tau(t'-b),$$
the transformation of a spatial vector under the rotation $Q$ alone, with no
contribution from the boost $u$, the translation $a$ or the time shift $b$.
The consistency of the balance (iii) with this transformation law — namely
that the description in the second frame satisfies the balance with datum
$\tilde\tau$, because
$\tilde L_c(t')=QL_c(t'-b)$ by clause 5 of
[[pthm-cm10-frame-covariance]] and differentiation commutes with the
constant rotation $Q$ and the time shift — is recorded and proved as a clause
of the frame-covariance theorem of this page; it is not an assumption of
the present postulate.

**(viii) Scope and exclusions.** The branch excludes deformable bodies,
internal degrees of freedom, variable mass, ablation, impact and contact
events, and every constitutive law for friction, rolling or slipping; any
such effect that is present must be declared as part of the datum $\tau$ of
clause (ii) with its own model, and a datum is a model object, not a
measurement. The branch also excludes relativistic and quantum descriptions.
Wherever a statement of the pair needs the inverse $I^{-1}$ it assumes the
model is nondegenerate in the sense of [[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] clause
(a), and that hypothesis is stated explicitly in the theorem that uses it.
The postulate asserts no measured torque, no numerical value, and no claim
that any concrete body or apparatus is described by the branch; whether a
given datum is adequate for a given apparatus is decided by comparing the
model's conditional predictions with reported observations under the
apparatus's stated regime.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only to make the integrals finite. Adopt the
model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] and its inertia data
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]): the reference mass distribution $\nu$ with
total mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates, the body inertia matrix $I$,
the spatial inertia tensor $I(t)=R(t)IR(t)^{\mathsf T}$ of a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$, and the inertia tensor $I(t,p)$ about a spatial
point $p$ ([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]). Then:

**(a) Principal basis.** There is an orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of
$\mathbb R^3$ and real numbers $I_1,I_2,I_3$, the **principal axes** and
**principal moments** of the model, with
$$Ie_j=I_je_j\qquad(j=1,2,3).$$

**(b) Quadratic form and rotational term.** For every
$\omega=\sum_j\omega_je_j\in\mathbb R^3$ one has
$I\omega=\sum_jI_j\omega_je_j$ and
$$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\sum_jI_j\omega_j^{2}=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)\ \ge 0,$$
and each principal moment is
$I_j=e_j^{\mathsf T}Ie_j=\int\lVert e_j\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)$.

**(c) Axis moments.** For every unit vector $n\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$n^{\mathsf T}In=\int\lVert n\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho);$$
for every spatial point $p$ and unit vector $n$, with $x=x(t,\cdot)$ the
placement at time $t$,
$$n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n=\int\lVert n\times\bigl(x(t,\rho)-p\bigr)\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho).$$
Consequently the number $\Theta_\ell(t)=n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n$ of
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] depends only on the spatial line $\ell$
$\{p+sn:s\in\mathbb R\}$ and not on the choice of the point $p$ on it nor on
the sign of the unit direction $n$.

**(d) Vanishing and positivity.** Each principal moment satisfies $I_j\ge0$,
and $I_j=0$ exactly when $\nu$ is supported on the line $\mathbb Re_j$ of the
principal axis, that is $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Re_j\bigr)=0$.
If the model is nondegenerate, that is if
$\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega\bigr)>0$ for every
$\omega\neq0$, then every $I_j>0$ and $I$ is invertible. If $\nu$ is
supported on some line through the origin (such a line exists whenever the
support of a centred $\nu$ is contained in a line, because the mean of $\nu$
is the origin), then $I$ is not invertible.

**(e) Extremal moments.** For every unit vector
$n=\sum_jc_je_j$ one has $n^{\mathsf T}In=\sum_jI_jc_j^{2}$ and therefore
$$\min_jI_j\ \le\ n^{\mathsf T}In\ \le\ \max_jI_j,$$
with the value $\max_jI_j$ attained at a unit eigenvector for a maximal
principal moment and the value $\min_jI_j$ attained at a unit eigenvector for
a minimal principal moment. Hence the largest and smallest principal moments
are the maximum and minimum of the rotational-inertia quadratic form over the
unit sphere.

The identities are conditional on the model data and the stated choice
assumption; no equation of motion and no conservation statement is used or
asserted.

Adopt the model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: the reference mass
distribution $\nu$, its total mass $m=\nu(\mathbb R^3)$ and its centred
reference coordinates $\int\rho\,d\nu(\rho)=0$. Assume the Axiom of Countable
Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, used only through
[[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]] to make the polynomial moments of $\nu$ of
degree at most two finite real numbers. Fix an inertial frame and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^2$
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]).

**(a) Body inertia matrix.** The **body inertia matrix** of the model is the
inertia matrix of the reference mass distribution,
$$I:=I(\nu)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}I_3-\rho\rho^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
with entries $I_{jk}=\int(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}\delta_{jk}-\rho_j\rho_k)\,d\nu$
as in [[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]; the matrix is expressed
in the standard basis of the reference coordinates. Its entries are finite
real numbers, it is symmetric, and for every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)\ \ge 0$$
by [[lem-cm-inertia-matrix-properties]] clauses 1-2; hence $I$ is symmetric
and its quadratic form is positive semidefinite. The dimension is
$[I]=\mu\ell^{2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]), read in kilogram metres squared. The
model is **nondegenerate** when no line through the origin carries the whole
mass, that is $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega\bigr)>0$ for every
$\omega\neq0$, and **degenerate** otherwise; the connection between this
criterion and the strict positivity and invertibility of $I$ is proved in the
principal-axes theorem of this page.

**(b) Spatial inertia tensor at the centre of mass.** The **spatial inertia
tensor** of the model at time $t$ is
$$I(t):=R(t)\,I\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
the matrix of the same quadratic form in the frame's spatial coordinates: for
every $n\in\mathbb R^3$,
$n^{\mathsf T}I(t)n=(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)^{\mathsf T}I(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)$. Its
entries are $C^2$ functions of $t$, since $R$ is of class $C^2$ and $I$ is
constant; the matrix rotates with the body and returns to $I$ in the
body-fixed frame, where $R=I_3$.

**(c) Inertia tensor about a spatial point.** For a spatial point
$p\in\mathbb R^3$ let
$$a(t,p):=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\bigl(p-c(t)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^3$$
be the **reference coordinate of $p$**, that is the label of the material
point of the reference placement that is placed at $p$ at time $t$. The
**inertia tensor of the model about $p$** at time $t$ is
$$I(t,p):=R(t)\,I_\nu\bigl(a(t,p)\bigr)\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
where
$$I_\nu(a)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho-a\rVert_2^{2}I_3-(\rho-a)(\rho-a)^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)$$
is the inertia tensor of the mass distribution about the point $a$ of the
reference coordinates ([[def-cm-inertia-tensor-about-a-point]]). Since the
label of a spatial point is uniquely determined by the placement, this is
well defined; for the centre of mass, $a(t,c(t))=0$ and
$I(t,c(t))=I(t)$. The dimension is again $\mu\ell^{2}$, read in kilogram
metres squared.

**(d) Moment of inertia about an axis.** Let $\ell$ be a spatial line at time
$t$, given by a point $p\in\mathbb R^3$ and a unit direction $n\in\mathbb R^3$
($\lVert n\rVert_2=1$). The **moment of inertia of the model about $\ell$** is
$$\Theta_\ell(t):=n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n .$$
Its invariance under the choices entering the description of the line and
its identification with the integral defining the physical moment of inertia
about the line are statements, not conventions; they are proved in clause
(c) of the principal-axes theorem of this page. For a **body-fixed
axis**, that is a line through the centre of mass whose direction in
reference coordinates is a constant unit vector $n_0$, the moment is
$$n_0^{\mathsf T}I n_0=\int\lVert n_0\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),$$
by clause (a), and is independent of time, because $I$ and $n_0$ are model
data.

**(e) What is constant and what moves.** The body inertia matrix $I$ is
determined by the model's reference mass distribution alone and does not
depend on the time, the frame or the motion; the spatial inertia tensor
$I(t)$ depends on the motion through the orientation $R(t)$; the inertia
tensor $I(t,p)$ about a spatial point depends on the motion through both the
orientation and the position of $p$. Principal axes and principal moments of
$I$ are the subject of the principal-axes theorem of this page.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$

Adopt the model and notation of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: a reference
mass distribution $\nu$ with total mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates,
a fixed inertial frame, and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^{2}$ on
