([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]]) and body inertia matrix $I$
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]). Define the **total momentum**, **kinetic

the motion by the componentwise integrals
$$P(t):=\int\partial_tx(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho),\qquad K(t):=\frac12\int\lVert\partial_tx(t,\rho)\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),$$
$$L_c(t):=\int\bigl(x(t,\rho)-c(t)\bigr)\times\bigl(\partial_tx(t,\rho)-c'(t)\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho),$$

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

For $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, $\|u\times v\|_2^2=\det G(u,v)$, and this value is positive exactly when $u$ and $v$ are linearly independent.

Equivalently,
$$\|u\times v\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2.$$

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $F$ is **locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniformly in time**, if every compact time-state cylinder $C\subseteq D$ has a finite $L\ge0$ such that

$$\|F(t,x)-F(t,y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$$

whenever $(t,x),(t,y)\in C$ have the same time coordinate.

On every compact time-state cylinder the state-variable inequality holds with one finite constant $L$. More generally, let $p\ge1$, let $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, let $D_\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\times\Lambda$ be open in its relative Euclidean topology, and let $F:D_\Lambda\to\mathbb R^n$. The parameter family is **locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniform in time and parameters** when every compact time-state-parameter cylinder $C\subseteq D_\Lambda$ has one finite $L\ge0$ such that

$$\|F(t,x,\lambda)-F(t,y,\lambda)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$$

whenever $(t,x,\lambda),(t,y,\lambda)\in C$ have the same time and parameter coordinates.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ and $y:J\to\mathbb R^n$ solve the same IVP. The solution $y$ is an **extension** of $x$ when $I\subseteq J$ and $y|_I=x$. It is a proper extension when $I\subsetneq J$.

A solution is **maximal** when it has no proper extension. Its domain is its **maximal interval of existence**. A solution is **global** when its domain is the entire time projection allowed by the ODE domain; for a vector field on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$, this means domain $\mathbb R$.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Hence clause 2 of [L2] gives $l'=l\times(I^{-1}l)$ and the constancy of $C$ and $E$, and clause 3 of [L2] gives their principal-basis expressions and the component equations.

By [L3] the continuous function $L_c$ has zero derivative on $I_0$, so it is constant on $I_0$; hence $\lVert L_c\rVert_2$ is constant, and $\lVert L_c(t)\rVert_2^{2}=\langle l(t),l(t)\rangle=C$ by [L1]. This is clause 1.

The field $F(l)=l\times(I^{-1}l)$ is locally Lipschitz in the state variable: by bilinearity and additivity of the cross product [L6], for all $x,y\in\mathbb R^{3}$ one has $F(x)-F(y)=(x-y)\times(I^{-1}x)+y\times(I^{-1}(x-y))$, so with the bound $\lVert I^{-1}z\rVert_2\le\lVert z\rVert_2/I_{\min}$ valid in the principal basis [L4] and the norm bound of [L6], $\lVert F(x)-F(y)\rVert_2\le\lVert x-y\rVert_2\lVert I^{-1}x\rVert_2+\lVert y\rVert_2\lVert I^{-1}(x-y)\rVert_2\le\bigl(\lVert x\rVert_2+\lVert y\rVert_2\bigr)\lVert x-y\rVert_2/I_{\min}$; on the ball $\lVert z\rVert_2\le r$ this is at most $2r\lVert x-y\rVert_2/I_{\min}$, a finite state-Lipschitz constant on every compact cylinder.

Writing $\omega=\sum_{j}\omega_{j}e_{j}$ in the principal basis of [L4], one has $\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\sum_{j}I_{j}\omega_{j}^{2}\ge I_{\min}\sum_{j}\omega_{j}^{2}=I_{\min}\lVert\omega\rVert_2^{2}$, so $\lVert\omega(t)\rVert_2^{2}\le2E/I_{\min}$ with $E=\tfrac12\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega$ constant by step 1.1 and $I_{\min}>0$ by [L4]; together with $l=I\omega$ this bounds $\lVert l\rVert_2^{2}=C$ on $I_0$. The identification of $E$ with the rotational term of the kinetic energy is clause 3 of [L5]. This is clause 3.

Every solution of $l'=F(l)$ has a unique maximal extension defined on all of $\mathbb R$: by [L7] and step 1.3 a unique maximal solution exists through every datum, with open domain $(a,b)$; along it $\frac{d}{dt}\lVert l(t)\rVert_2^{2}=2\langle l'(t),l(t)\rangle=2\langle l(t)\times(I^{-1}l(t)),l(t)\rangle=0$ because the cross product is orthogonal to each factor [L6], so by [L3], applied to this continuous differentiable scalar on $(a,b)$, $\lVert l(t)\rVert_2^{2}\equiv\lVert l(t_0)\rVert_2^{2}$ for any datum time $t_0\in(a,b)$ and its values over $(a,b)$ lie in the sphere $\{z:\lVert z\rVert_2=\lVert l(t_0)\rVert_2\}\subseteq\mathbb R^{3}$, which is closed and bounded and therefore compact by [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]. If $b<+\infty$, then near $b$ the solution stays in that compact subset of the state domain, and clause 2 of [L7] extends it past $b$, contradicting maximality; hence $b=+\infty$. If $a>-\infty$, put $z(s):=l(-s)$ on $(-b,-a)$. By the chain rule [L8], $z\prime(s)=-F(z(s))$. The field $-F$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz with the same constants as $F$, and $z$ stays in the same compact sphere near its finite right endpoint $-a$. Applying the autonomous compact continuation of [L7] to $-F$ extends $z$ past $-a$; reflecting this extension back extends $l$ past $a$, contradicting maximality. Hence $a=-\infty$. Every original solution is a restriction of this unique global maximal solution by the uniqueness assertion of [L7].

The $l$-path of a torque-free motion is a solution of $l'=F(l)$ on $I_0$ by step 1.1, hence by step 2.2 it is the restriction of a solution defined on all of $\mathbb R$ (uniqueness), its maximal extension satisfies $\lVert l(t)\rVert_2=\lVert l(t_0)\rVert_2$ for any datum time $t_0$ and every $t$, and it takes values in $\Lambda(C,E)$, which is compact as the intersection of the closed sphere and the closed level set $\{z:\langle z,I^{-1}z\rangle=2E\}$ and nonempty because it contains $l(t_0)$. This is clause 4.

boundaries.reason: The nondegenerate reference mass distribution has positive total mass. The principal-coordinate sum in step 2.1 runs over the three eigenvalues of the body inertia matrix, all positive by the nondegeneracy hypothesis.

boundaries.reason: A single motion or a single time is enough: steps 1.1-1.3 and 2.1-2.2 give identities valid at every t in I_0, and step 3.1 concerns the single l-path of the motion.
Degeneracy is excluded by hypothesis: the statement assumes the model nondegenerate so that I^{-1} exists, and step 2.1 uses the bound ||I^{-1}z|| <= ||z||/I_min which requires I_min>0.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.2 excludes each finite endpoint of the maximal l-solution using its conserved norm and the compact closed ball of that radius. Thus the supplied torque-free solution extends through every finite time, including the zero-radius equilibrium.

boundaries.reason: AC_omega is declared and used only through the finiteness of the defining integrals in [L1]-[L2]; the global-existence argument of steps 2.1-2.2 is choice-free.

The forward direction is the constancy and global-existence conclusion, proved in steps 1.1-3.1; the statement also contains the converse-type clause 'the l-path is the restriction of a global solution', which is discharged by uniqueness in step 3.1.

The reverse reading (from constancy to the equations) is not claimed: the statement never asserts that prescribed constant values of C and E determine a solution, and the remark records that no periodicity or elliptic-function computation is claimed.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only to make the integrals below finite.
Adopt the model and notation of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: a reference
mass distribution $\nu$ with total mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates,
a fixed inertial frame, and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^{2}$ on
the time window $I_0$, body angular velocity $\omega$
([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]]) and body inertia matrix $I$
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]). Define the **total momentum**, **kinetic
energy** and **angular momentum about the centre of mass** of the model along
the motion by the componentwise integrals
$$P(t):=\int\partial_tx(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho),\qquad K(t):=\frac12\int\lVert\partial_tx(t,\rho)\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),$$
$$L_c(t):=\int\bigl(x(t,\rho)-c(t)\bigr)\times\bigl(\partial_tx(t,\rho)-c'(t)\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho),$$
with dimensions $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$, $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ and
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). Then for every $t\in I_0$:

1. the three integrands are $\nu$-integrable, so $P(t)$, $K(t)$ and
   $L_c(t)$ are a well-defined finite vector and finite real numbers;
2. $P(t)=m\,c'(t)$;
3. $K(t)=\dfrac12m\lVert c'(t)\rVert_2^{2}+\dfrac12\omega(t)^{\mathsf T}I\omega(t)$;
4. $L_c(t)=R(t)\,I\,\omega(t)$.

The identities hold for every $C^{2}$ configuration path; no equation of
motion, force law or conservation statement is used or asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only through the integrals of
[[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]]. Adopt a model of the rigid-material branch
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] that is **nondegenerate** in the sense of
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] clause (a) (no line through the origin carries
the whole mass), and use it in the **torque-free** external-torque branch of
[[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iv): the datum vanishes, so along every
motion of the resulting model the adopted balance reads $L_c'=0$ on the time
window $I_0$. Let $\omega$ be the body angular velocity, $I$ the body inertia
matrix and $l:=I\omega$ ([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]],
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]). Then:

1. **Conservation of angular momentum.** The angular momentum about the
   centre of mass $L_c(t)=R(t)l(t)$ of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]] clause
   4 is constant on $I_0$; in particular $\lVert L_c\rVert_2$ is constant.
2. **Energy-momentum invariants and principal components.** The scalars
   $$C:=\langle l,l\rangle=\lVert L_c\rVert_2^{2},\qquad E:=\tfrac12\,\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\tfrac12\,\langle l,I^{-1}l\rangle$$
   are constant on $I_0$, and $l$ satisfies the torque-free equation
   $$l'=l\times(I^{-1}l).$$
   If $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ is a positively oriented orthonormal eigenbasis of $I$ with
   $Ie_{j}=I_{j}e_{j}$ and $l=\sum_{j}l_{j}e_{j}$
   ([[pthm-cm10-principal-axes]] clauses (a)-(b)), then
   $$C=\sum_{j}l_{j}^{2},\qquad E=\sum_{j}\frac{l_{j}^{2}}{2I_{j}},$$
   and the component equations are
   $$l_{1}'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_{3}}-\frac1{I_{2}}\Bigr)l_{2}l_{3},\qquad l_{2}'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_{1}}-\frac1{I_{3}}\Bigr)l_{1}l_{3},\qquad l_{3}'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_{2}}-\frac1{I_{1}}\Bigr)l_{1}l_{2}.$$
3. **The energy invariant is the rotational kinetic energy.** $E$ equals the
   rotational term $\tfrac12\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega$ of the model's kinetic
   energy in clause 3 of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]]; and with
   $I_{\min}:=\min_{j}I_{j}>0$ one has
   $$\lVert\omega(t)\rVert_2^{2}\le\frac{2E}{I_{\min}}\qquad(t\in I_0).$$
   In particular both $l$ and $\omega$ are bounded on $I_0$.
4. **The spin field is globally solvable.** The autonomous field
   $F(l)=l\times(I^{-1}l)$ on $\mathbb R^{3}$ is locally Lipschitz in the
   state variable ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]), and
   every solution of $l'=F(l)$ has a unique maximal extension defined
   on all of $\mathbb R$, and that extension satisfies $\lVert l(t)\rVert_2=\lVert l(0)\rVert_2$
   for every $t$. Consequently the $l$-path of a torque-free motion is the
   restriction to $I_0$ of a solution defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and its
   path is contained in the compact level set
   $$\Lambda(C,E):=\bigl\{z\in\mathbb R^{3}:\langle z,z\rangle=C,\ \tfrac12\langle z,I^{-1}z\rangle=E\bigr\},$$
   which is nonempty because it contains the datum at any chosen time of the motion.

The statement is conditional on the adopted model, its nondegeneracy and the
zero-torque balance; it asserts no orientation of the body in space, no
measured value and no empirical law.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate open interval, let $\omega:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous, and consider on the open time-state domain $D:=I\times\mathbb H\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb H$ the initial value problem

$$q'(t)=\tfrac12\,q(t)\,\varphi\bigl(\omega(t)\bigr),\qquad q(t_0)=q_0,$$

read as the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] with time-state domain $D$, state space $\mathbb H$, and right-hand side $F:D\to\mathbb H$, $F(t,q)=\tfrac12q\,\varphi(\omega(t))$, where $\varphi$, $S^3$ and $\rho$ are those of [[def-cm-quaternion-rotation-map-and-cover]].

1. If $q:I\to\mathbb H$ is a $C^1$ solution of $q'=\tfrac12q\,\varphi(\omega(t))$, then $N\circ q$ is constant on $I$; if $q(t_0)\in S^3$ for one $t_0\in I$, then $q(I)\subseteq S^3$ and the curve

$$R:=\rho\circ q:I\longrightarrow SO(3),\qquad R(t):=\rho(q(t)),$$

is of class $C^1$ with $R'(t)=R(t)\,\Omega_{\omega(t)}$ for every $t\in I$; consequently $\omega$ is the body angular velocity of $R$ in the sense of [[lem-cm-body-angular-velocity-of-a-rotation-path]].
2. For every $t_0\in I$ and $q_0\in S^3$ the problem has exactly one maximal solution, and its domain is all of $I$; that is, there is exactly one $C^1$ curve $q:I\to S^3$ with $q(t_0)=q_0$ and $q'=\tfrac12q\,\varphi(\omega(t))$ on $I$, and clause 1 applies to it.

Let $\mathbb H$ be the quaternion algebra with its product, conjugation $x\mapsto\bar x$, real-valued norm $N:\mathbb H\to\mathbb R$, and real embedding $r\mapsto\hat r=(r,0,0,0)$, in the notation of [[def-quaternions]]. Thus $x=x_0+x_1i+x_2j+x_3k$ with the multiplication formula of [[def-quaternions]], and

$$N(x)=x_0^2+x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2,\qquad \widehat{N(x)}=x\bar x=\bar x x.$$

In particular, $N(x)>0$ for $x\ne0$, and the imported division-ring theorem gives the typed inverse formula $x^{-1}=\widehat{N(x)^{-1}}\,\bar x$ ([[thm-quaternions-form-a-division-ring]]). Under the identification of $\mathbb H$ with $\mathbb R^4$ by the coordinates $x_0,\dots,x_3$ one has $N(x)=\|x\|_2^2$ for the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

**Imaginary quaternions and the vector identification.** Put

$$\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H:=\{x\in\mathbb H:\bar x=-x\}=\mathbb Ri\oplus\mathbb Rj\oplus\mathbb Rk,\qquad \varphi:\mathbb R^3\to\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H,\quad \varphi(v_1,v_2,v_3):=v_1i+v_2j+v_3k .$$

Then $\varphi$ is a linear isomorphism with $N(\varphi(v))=\|v\|_2^2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^3$. Throughout the collection, $\varphi$ translates between vectors of $\mathbb R^3$ (their inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$, norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ and cross product) and imaginary quaternions inside quaternion products.

**The unit sphere.** Define

$$S^3:=\{q\in\mathbb H:N(q)=1\},$$

the unit sphere of $\mathbb H\cong\mathbb R^4$. The identification of $S^3$ with $SU(2)$ is the one of the published covering example `ex-su-two-to-so-three-as-a-covering-homomorphism`, which is also the source of the covering statement recorded in the second remark below; that example is linked from the page summary of this pair.

**Conjugation and the rotation map.** For $q\in\mathbb H$ with $q\ne0$ let $c_q:\mathbb H\to\mathbb H$ be

$$c_q(x):=qxq^{-1}=qx\,\widehat{N(q)^{-1}}\,\bar q,$$

where the real scalar is embedded by $r\mapsto\hat r$, and define

$$\rho(q):=c_q|_{\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H}:\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H\longrightarrow\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H .$$

Both the $\mathbb R$-linear map $\rho(q)$ and its matrix in the ordered basis $(i,j,k)$ of $\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H$ are written $\rho(q)$; the equality $\rho(q)\in SO(3)$ for $q\in S^3$ is part of the cited covering statement, and the matrix is the one meant whenever $\rho(q)$ is composed with the identifications above. The map $\rho$ itself is never linear in $q$ and no such structure is used.

**Quaternion lifts.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let $R:I\to SO(3)$ be a map, with $SO(3)$ as in [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]. A **quaternion lift** of $R$ is a map $q:I\to S^3$ with $\rho(q(t))=R(t)$ for every $t\in I$.

Use the standard basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ and coordinates $\omega=\omega_1e_1+\omega_2e_2+\omega_3e_3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], [[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Define the map $[\cdot]_\times:\mathbb R^3\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ by
$$[\omega]_\times:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\omega_3&\omega_2\\ \omega_3&0&-\omega_1\\ -\omega_2&\omega_1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then:

1. $[\omega]_\times z=\omega\times z$ for all $\omega,z\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].
2. $[\omega]_\times^{\mathsf T}=-[\omega]_\times$ for every $\omega$; the map $\omega\mapsto[\omega]_\times$ is linear and injective, and its image is exactly the set of skew-symmetric matrices of $M_3(\mathbb R)$. Consequently every skew-symmetric $\Omega\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ equals $[\omega]_\times$ for exactly one $\omega$, namely $\omega=(\Omega_{32},\Omega_{13},\Omega_{21})$.
3. For every $R\in SO(3)$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]) and every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$, $$R[\omega]_\times R^{\mathsf T}=[R\omega]_\times.$$

Adopt the model, inertial frame and notation of
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] and [[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]], and
let a motion $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ have configuration path $(c,R)$ of
class $C^2$ on the time window $I_0$ ([[def-interval]]).

**(a) Body angular velocity.** By
[[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]], the matrix
$R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)$ is skew-symmetric at every $t\in I_0$
([[lem-cm-matrix-curve-derivative-rules]] clause 3), and by
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]] clause 2 there is exactly
one vector $\omega(t)\in\mathbb R^3$ with
$$R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)=[\omega(t)]_\times .$$
The map $\omega:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ is the **body angular velocity** of the
motion. Since $R$ is of class $C^2$, the entries of $R^{\mathsf T}R'$ are
differentiable and hence $\omega$ is of class $C^1$; its derivative is the
**body angular acceleration**. The dimension is $[\omega]=\tau^{-1}$
([[def-cm01-units]]), read in radians per second under the radian convention,
in which angles are dimensionless.

**(b) Spatial angular velocity.** The **spatial angular velocity** of the
motion is
$$\omega_{\mathrm s}(t):=R(t)\omega(t)\in\mathbb R^3,$$
of the same dimension $\tau^{-1}$. By the conjugation clause of
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]],
$R'(t)R(t)^{\mathsf T}=[\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)]_\times$; this is the
space-frame rate matrix of the motion.

**(c) Material velocity field.** For every material label $\rho$,
$$\partial_tx(t,\rho)=c'(t)+R(t)\bigl(\omega(t)\times\rho\bigr),$$
because $R'(t)=R(t)[\omega(t)]_\times$ and
$[\omega]_\times\rho=\omega\times\rho$
([[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]],
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]] clause 1). Writing
$p=x(t,\rho)$ for the spatial position of the label and using
$R(\omega\times\rho)=(R\omega)\times(R\rho)$, the same identity reads
$$\partial_tx(t,\rho)=c'(t)+\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\times\bigl(p-c(t)\bigr):$$
the material velocity field is that of a translation $c'(t)$ composed with a
rotation of angular velocity $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ about the centre of mass
$c(t)$. The motion is a **pure translation** at time $t$ exactly when
$\omega(t)=0$, equivalently $R'(t)=0$; then every material velocity equals
$c'(t)$.

**(d) Uniqueness of the velocity data.** The velocity field determines
$c'(t)$ and $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ uniquely: if a motion has material
velocity field $p\mapsto v(t,p)=c'(t)+\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\times(p-c(t))$,
then evaluating at $p=c(t)$ gives $c'(t)=v(t,c(t))$, and for $u\in\mathbb R^3$
the difference $v(t,c(t)+u)-v(t,c(t))=\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\times u$ is a
linear map of $u$; testing it on two linearly independent vectors determines
$\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ by the injectivity clause of
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]], and then
$\omega(t)=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$. The pair
$\bigl(c'(t),\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\bigr)$ is therefore an intrinsic
description of the velocity field; the body angular velocity is its
description in the body-fixed frame, and the choice of reference coordinates
is part of the model data fixed in [[post-cm10-rigid-material]].

**(e) Instantaneous rotation axis.** If $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\neq0$, the line
$$\bigl\{c(t)+s\,\omega_{\mathrm s}(t):s\in\mathbb R\bigr\}$$
is the **instantaneous rotation axis** of the motion at time $t$: it is the
set of spatial points whose material velocity equals $c'(t)$, as follows from
$\omega_{\mathrm s}\times(\omega_{\mathrm s}s)=0$. Conversely, write
$w=\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ and $z=p-c(t)$. If $w\times z=0$, choose a
coordinate $i$ with $w_i\neq0$; the cross-product coordinate equations
([[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]] clause 1) give
$w_i z_j=w_j z_i$ for every $j$, hence $z=(z_i/w_i)w$.
This proves that the zero relative-velocity set is exactly the displayed
line. The velocity field is
constant on lines parallel to $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ and rotates about this
axis; if also $c'(t)=0$ at that instant, every point of the axis is
instantaneously at rest and the motion is an instantaneous rotation about it.
No claim is made that the axis is fixed in time or in space.

**(f) Conventions and scope.** The convention fixed here is the body-fixed
one of the cited mathematical definition: $\Omega=R^{\mathsf T}R'=[\omega]_\times$
and $R'=R\Omega$. A consumer using the space-fixed convention must state the
change, which is the rotation by $R$ recorded in (b); the two vectors agree
only when $R(t)$ fixes $\omega(t)$. Both vectors are kinematic quantities of
the motion: no torque, no angular momentum and no equation of motion for
$\omega$ is asserted, and no measured angular velocity is recorded. The
behaviour of $\omega$ under a change of inertial frame is proved in the
frame-covariance theorem of this page.

Let $M_3(\mathbb R)$ be the set of $3\times3$ matrices over $\mathbb R$ ([[def-matrix-space]]), with identity $I_3$ and product as in [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], transpose $R^{\mathsf T}$ as in [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]], and determinant $\det R$ as in [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]].

The **orthogonal group** and the **special orthogonal group** are the subsets

$$O(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\},\qquad SO(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\ \text{and}\ \det R=1\}.$$

Equivalently $SO(3)=O(3)\cap\{R:\det R=1\}$. Elements of $SO(3)$ are called **rotations**. The identification of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ with the function space $\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ and hence with $\mathbb R^9$ is the one of [[def-matrix-space]]; when $M_3(\mathbb R)$ is regarded as a metric or topological space, this is always the Euclidean metric of that identification.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points, let $t_0\in I$ and let $A,B:I\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be **differentiable at $t_0$**, meaning ([[def-matrix-space]]) that every entry function $t\mapsto A(t)_{ij}$ and $t\mapsto B(t)_{ij}$ is differentiable at $t_0$ in the sense of [[def-derivative]]; write $A'(t_0)$ for the matrix with entries $A'(t_0)_{ij}:=(t\mapsto A(t)_{ij})'(t_0)$, and similarly for $B$.

1. $A+B$ and $A^{\mathsf T}$ are differentiable at $t_0$, with $(A+B)'(t_0)=A'(t_0)+B'(t_0)$ and $(A^{\mathsf T})'(t_0)=(A'(t_0))^{\mathsf T}$.
2. $AB$ is differentiable at $t_0$, with $(AB)'(t_0)=A'(t_0)B(t_0)+A(t_0)B'(t_0)$.
3. If $A(t)\in SO(3)$ for every $t\in I$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]), then the matrix $A(t_0)^{\mathsf T}A'(t_0)$ is skew-symmetric, i.e. $(A^{\mathsf T}A')^{\mathsf T}=-A^{\mathsf T}A'$ at $t_0$, and likewise $A'(t_0)A(t_0)^{\mathsf T}$ is skew-symmetric. In particular the trace of each of these two matrices vanishes.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only through the integrals of
[[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]]; the theorems below neither use nor imply any
other choice principle. Adopt a model of the rigid-material branch
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] with the external-torque branch
[[post-cm11-torque-balance]]: a reference mass distribution $\nu$ with total
mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates, a time window $I_0$
([[def-interval]]), an inertial frame, a motion $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with
configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^{2}$
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]), body angular velocity $\omega$
([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]]) and body inertia matrix $I$
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]), and a continuous external torque datum
$\tau:I_0\to\mathbb R^{3}$ with respect to which the adopted balance of
[[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iii) holds along the motion. Then:

1. **Euler's equations with torque.** Writing $l:=I\omega$, one has
   $l'=R^{\mathsf T}\tau-\omega\times I\omega$ and
   $$I\omega'(t)+\omega(t)\times I\omega(t)=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\tau(t)\qquad(t\in I_0).$$
2. **Principal-axis components.** If $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ is a positively oriented orthonormal
   eigenbasis of $I$ with $Ie_{j}=I_{j}e_{j}$ ([[pthm-cm10-principal-axes]]
   clause (a)) and $\omega=\sum_{j}\omega_{j}e_{j}$,
   $R^{\mathsf T}\tau=\sum_{j}\tau_{j}e_{j}$, then the equations are
   componentwise
   $$I_{1}\omega_{1}'=(I_{2}-I_{3})\omega_{2}\omega_{3}+\tau_{1},\qquad I_{2}\omega_{2}'=(I_{3}-I_{1})\omega_{3}\omega_{1}+\tau_{2},\qquad I_{3}\omega_{3}'=(I_{1}-I_{2})\omega_{1}\omega_{2}+\tau_{3}.$$
3. **Rotational power identity.** The rotational kinetic energy
   $K_{\mathrm{rot}}(t):=\tfrac12\omega(t)^{\mathsf T}I\omega(t)$ is
   differentiable on $I_0$ with
   $$\frac{d}{dt}K_{\mathrm{rot}}(t)=\omega(t)\cdot R(t)^{\mathsf T}\tau(t)\qquad(t\in I_0);$$
   in particular, if $\tau\equiv0$, then $K_{\mathrm{rot}}$ is constant on
   $I_0$, and $K_{\mathrm{rot}}$ coincides with the rotational term
   $\tfrac12\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega$ of the model's kinetic energy in
   clause 3 of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]].
4. **Torque-free reduction and nondegeneracy.** Suppose $\tau\equiv0$ and the
   model is nondegenerate in the sense of [[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] clause
   (a), so that $I$ is invertible with $I^{-1}l=\omega$. Then, writing
   $\omega$ as a function of $l$,
   $$l'=l\times(I^{-1}l),\qquad \omega'=F(\omega):=-I^{-1}\bigl(\omega\times I\omega\bigr);$$
   the second form exhibits the torque-free body angular velocity as a
   solution of the autonomous field $F$ on $\mathbb R^{3}$.
5. **Frame covariance.** Let a second inertial frame be related to the first
   by $t'=t+b$, $x'=Qx+ut+a$ with $b\in\mathbb R$, $a,u\in\mathbb R^{3}$,
   $Q\in SO(3)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]] clause (iv)), and let
   $\tilde x(t',\rho):=Qx(t'-b,\rho)+u(t'-b)+a$, $\tilde\tau(t'):=Q\tau(t'-b)$
   be the transformed motion and datum of [[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause
   (vii). Then the balance holds in the second frame, and
   $$I\tilde\omega'(t')+\tilde\omega(t')\times I\tilde\omega(t')=\tilde R(t')^{\mathsf T}\tilde\tau(t')\qquad(t'\in I_0+b),$$
   where $\tilde\omega(t')=\omega(t'-b)$ and
   $\tilde R(t')=QR(t'-b)$; the body-frame torque is unchanged:
   $\tilde R(t')^{\mathsf T}\tilde\tau(t')=R(t'-b)^{\mathsf T}\tau(t'-b)$.

The statement is conditional on the adopted model and torque balance; it
asserts no force law for $\tau$, no conservation of $L_c$ and no measured
value.

derivations.claim: By [L2] the covering map $\rho$ is surjective; choose $q_{0}\in S^{3}$ with $\rho(q_{0})=R_{0}$, and let $\omega:I_0\to\mathbb R^{3}$ be the constant curve $\omega(t):=\Omega e_{j}$, which is continuous. Clause 2 of [L2] supplies a $C^{1}$ curve $q:I_0\to S^{3}$ with $q(t_{0})=q_{0}$ and $q'=\tfrac12q\varphi(\omega)$, and clause 1 of [L2] shows that $R:=\rho\circ q:I_0\to SO(3)$ is $C^{1}$ with $R(t_{0})=R_{0}$ and $R'(t)=R(t)\Omega_{\omega(t)}$; by [L3] this is $R^{\mathsf T}R'=[\Omega e_{j}]_\times$, so the body angular velocity of $R$ is the constant map $\Omega e_{j}$ by the uniqueness in [L3]. This is clause 1.

Let $R$ be a path as in clause 1 and let $c:I_0\to\mathbb R^{3}$ be of class $C^{2}$. Its body angular velocity is the constant $\omega\equiv\Omega e_{j}$ by step 1.1, so $l=I\omega=\Omega I_{j}e_{j}$ is constant, and by [L1] $L_c=Rl$; with [L4], $(Rl)'=R'l+Rl'=R[\omega]_\times l+0=R(\omega\times l)=R(\Omega^{2}I_{j}\,e_{j}\times e_{j})=0$ by [L5]. Moreover $R'=R[\omega]_\times$ is of class $C^{1}$ because $R$ is and $[\omega]_\times$ is constant, so $R$ is of class $C^{2}$ by definition of second differentiability and $(c,R)$ is a configuration path of class $C^{2}$; hence, on the model's time window $I_0$, $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ is a motion of the model by [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] clause (ii). Since $L_c$ is constant, the zero-torque balance $L_c'=0$ holds and the motion belongs to the torque-free branch; this is clause 2.

In the motions of step 2.1, $l=\Omega I_{j}e_{j}$ and by [L1] and [L5] $C=\langle l,l\rangle=\Omega^{2}I_{j}^{2}$ and $E=\tfrac12\langle l,I^{-1}l\rangle=\tfrac12\Omega^{2}I_{j}$. If $\Omega\neq0$, then $\Omega I_{j}\neq0$ and the identity $L_c=\Omega I_{j}R(t)e_{j}$ of step 2.1 gives $R(t)e_{j}=L_c/(\Omega I_{j})$ with $L_c$ constant, so the material axis $R(t)e_{j}$ is fixed in the inertial frame and the motion is the uniform rotation about that direction; if $\Omega=0$, then $R'=R[\omega]_\times=R[0]=0$, so $R$ is constant by [L4]. This is clause 3.

For the converse, let a torque-free motion have constant body angular velocity $\omega\equiv\omega_{0}$. By [L6] its body angular velocity satisfies $I\omega'+\omega	imes I\omega=0$; with $\omega'=0$ this reads $\omega_{0}	imes I\omega_{0}=0$. If $\omega_0
eq0$, in the positively oriented principal coordinates, the coordinate formula for the cross product in [L5] makes this the vanishing of all $2	imes2$ minors $u_i v_k-u_k v_i$ for $u=\omega_0$ and $v=I\omega_0$. Since $\omega_0
eq0$, choose $k$ with $(\omega_0)_k
eq0$; then $v_i=(v_k/(\omega_0)_k)(\omega_0)_i$ for every $i$, so $I\omega_0=\lambda\omega_0$ for $\lambda=v_k/(\omega_0)_k\in\mathbb R$ and $\omega_0$ is an eigenvector of $I$. Within its eigenspace choose the unit vector $e_j=\omega_0/\|\omega_0\|_2$. Starting with the original principal vectors in that eigenspace, subtract their projection onto $e_j$, and normalize a nonzero remainder if the eigenspace has dimension greater than one; subtract the projections onto both selected vectors and normalize a nonzero remainder if its dimension is three. Such remainders exist because the original vectors span the eigenspace; linear combinations remain eigenvectors for the same eigenvalue, and the projection subtractions give orthonormality by [L5]. Retain the original orthonormal vectors in the other eigenspaces. This supplies an adapted orthonormal principal basis directly in dimension three. Negating one of the other two basis vectors if necessary makes it positively oriented. In this adapted basis $\omega_0=\Omega e_j$, $\Omega=\|\omega_0\|_2

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only through the integrals of
[[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]]; the theorems below neither use nor imply any
other choice principle. Adopt a model of the rigid-material branch
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] with the external-torque branch
[[post-cm11-torque-balance]]: a reference mass distribution $\nu$ with total
mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates, a time window $I_0$
([[def-interval]]), an inertial frame, a motion $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with
configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^{2}$
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]), body angular velocity $\omega$
([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]]) and body inertia matrix $I$
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]), and a continuous external torque datum
$\tau:I_0\to\mathbb R^{3}$ with respect to which the adopted balance of
[[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iii) holds along the motion. Then:

1. **Euler's equations with torque.** Writing $l:=I\omega$, one has
   $l'=R^{\mathsf T}\tau-\omega\times I\omega$ and
   $$I\omega'(t)+\omega(t)\times I\omega(t)=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\tau(t)\qquad(t\in I_0).$$
2. **Principal-axis components.** If $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ is a positively oriented orthonormal
   eigenbasis of $I$ with $Ie_{j}=I_{j}e_{j}$ ([[pthm-cm10-principal-axes]]
   clause (a)) and $\omega=\sum_{j}\omega_{j}e_{j}$,
   $R^{\mathsf T}\tau=\sum_{j}\tau_{j}e_{j}$, then the equations are
   componentwise
   $$I_{1}\omega_{1}'=(I_{2}-I_{3})\omega_{2}\omega_{3}+\tau_{1},\qquad I_{2}\omega_{2}'=(I_{3}-I_{1})\omega_{3}\omega_{1}+\tau_{2},\qquad I_{3}\omega_{3}'=(I_{1}-I_{2})\omega_{1}\omega_{2}+\tau_{3}.$$
3. **Rotational power identity.** The rotational kinetic energy
   $K_{\mathrm{rot}}(t):=\tfrac12\omega(t)^{\mathsf T}I\omega(t)$ is
   differentiable on $I_0$ with
   $$\frac{d}{dt}K_{\mathrm{rot}}(t)=\omega(t)\cdot R(t)^{\mathsf T}\tau(t)\qquad(t\in I_0);$$
   in particular, if $\tau\equiv0$, then $K_{\mathrm{rot}}$ is constant on
   $I_0$, and $K_{\mathrm{rot}}$ coincides with the rotational term
   $\tfrac12\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega$ of the model's kinetic energy in
   clause 3 of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]].
4. **Torque-free reduction and nondegeneracy.** Suppose $\tau\equiv0$ and the
   model is nondegenerate in the sense of [[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] clause
   (a), so that $I$ is invertible with $I^{-1}l=\omega$. Then, writing
   $\omega$ as a function of $l$,
   $$l'=l\times(I^{-1}l),\qquad \omega'=F(\omega):=-I^{-1}\bigl(\omega\times I\omega\bigr);$$
   the second form exhibits the torque-free body angular velocity as a
   solution of the autonomous field $F$ on $\mathbb R^{3}$.
5. **Frame covariance.** Let a second inertial frame be related to the first
   by $t'=t+b$, $x'=Qx+ut+a$ with $b\in\mathbb R$, $a,u\in\mathbb R^{3}$,
   $Q\in SO(3)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]] clause (iv)), and let
   $\tilde x(t',\rho):=Qx(t'-b,\rho)+u(t'-b)+a$, $\tilde\tau(t'):=Q\tau(t'-b)$
   be the transformed motion and datum of [[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause
   (vii). Then the balance holds in the second frame, and
   $$I\tilde\omega'(t')+\tilde\omega(t')\times I\tilde\omega(t')=\tilde R(t')^{\mathsf T}\tilde\tau(t')\qquad(t'\in I_0+b),$$
   where $\tilde\omega(t')=\omega(t'-b)$ and
   $\tilde R(t')=QR(t'-b)$; the body-frame torque is unchanged:
   $\tilde R(t')^{\mathsf T}\tilde\tau(t')=R(t'-b)^{\mathsf T}\tau(t'-b)$.

The statement is conditional on the adopted model and torque balance; it
asserts no force law for $\tau$, no conservation of $L_c$ and no measured
value.

Adopt the model, inertial frame and notation of
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] and [[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]], and
let a motion $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ have configuration path $(c,R)$ of
class $C^2$ on the time window $I_0$ ([[def-interval]]).

**(a) Body angular velocity.** By
[[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]], the matrix
$R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)$ is skew-symmetric at every $t\in I_0$
([[lem-cm-matrix-curve-derivative-rules]] clause 3), and by
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]] clause 2 there is exactly
one vector $\omega(t)\in\mathbb R^3$ with
$$R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)=[\omega(t)]_\times .$$
The map $\omega:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ is the **body angular velocity** of the
motion. Since $R$ is of class $C^2$, the entries of $R^{\mathsf T}R'$ are
differentiable and hence $\omega$ is of class $C^1$; its derivative is the
**body angular acceleration**. The dimension is $[\omega]=\tau^{-1}$
([[def-cm01-units]]), read in radians per second under the radian convention,
in which angles are dimensionless.

**(b) Spatial angular velocity.** The **spatial angular velocity** of the
motion is
$$\omega_{\mathrm s}(t):=R(t)\omega(t)\in\mathbb R^3,$$
of the same dimension $\tau^{-1}$. By the conjugation clause of
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]],
$R'(t)R(t)^{\mathsf T}=[\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)]_\times$; this is the
space-frame rate matrix of the motion.

**(c) Material velocity field.** For every material label $\rho$,
$$\partial_tx(t,\rho)=c'(t)+R(t)\bigl(\omega(t)\times\rho\bigr),$$
because $R'(t)=R(t)[\omega(t)]_\times$ and
$[\omega]_\times\rho=\omega\times\rho$
([[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]],
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]] clause 1). Writing
$p=x(t,\rho)$ for the spatial position of the label and using
$R(\omega\times\rho)=(R\omega)\times(R\rho)$, the same identity reads
$$\partial_tx(t,\rho)=c'(t)+\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\times\bigl(p-c(t)\bigr):$$
the material velocity field is that of a translation $c'(t)$ composed with a
rotation of angular velocity $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ about the centre of mass
$c(t)$. The motion is a **pure translation** at time $t$ exactly when
$\omega(t)=0$, equivalently $R'(t)=0$; then every material velocity equals
$c'(t)$.

**(d) Uniqueness of the velocity data.** The velocity field determines
$c'(t)$ and $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ uniquely: if a motion has material
velocity field $p\mapsto v(t,p)=c'(t)+\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\times(p-c(t))$,
then evaluating at $p=c(t)$ gives $c'(t)=v(t,c(t))$, and for $u\in\mathbb R^3$
the difference $v(t,c(t)+u)-v(t,c(t))=\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\times u$ is a
linear map of $u$; testing it on two linearly independent vectors determines
$\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ by the injectivity clause of
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]], and then
$\omega(t)=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$. The pair
$\bigl(c'(t),\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\bigr)$ is therefore an intrinsic
description of the velocity field; the body angular velocity is its
description in the body-fixed frame, and the choice of reference coordinates
is part of the model data fixed in [[post-cm10-rigid-material]].

**(e) Instantaneous rotation axis.** If $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\neq0$, the line
$$\bigl\{c(t)+s\,\omega_{\mathrm s}(t):s\in\mathbb R\bigr\}$$
is the **instantaneous rotation axis** of the motion at time $t$: it is the
set of spatial points whose material velocity equals $c'(t)$, as follows from
$\omega_{\mathrm s}\times(\omega_{\mathrm s}s)=0$. Conversely, write
$w=\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ and $z=p-c(t)$. If $w\times z=0$, choose a
coordinate $i$ with $w_i\neq0$; the cross-product coordinate equations
([[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]] clause 1) give
$w_i z_j=w_j z_i$ for every $j$, hence $z=(z_i/w_i)w$.
This proves that the zero relative-velocity set is exactly the displayed
line. The velocity field is
constant on lines parallel to $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ and rotates about this
axis; if also $c'(t)=0$ at that instant, every point of the axis is
instantaneously at rest and the motion is an instantaneous rotation about it.
No claim is made that the axis is fixed in time or in space.

**(f) Conventions and scope.** The convention fixed here is the body-fixed
one of the cited mathematical definition: $\Omega=R^{\mathsf T}R'=[\omega]_\times$
and $R'=R\Omega$. A consumer using the space-fixed convention must state the
change, which is the rotation by $R$ recorded in (b); the two vectors agree
only when $R(t)$ fixes $\omega(t)$. Both vectors are kinematic quantities of
the motion: no torque, no angular momentum and no equation of motion for
$\omega$ is asserted, and no measured angular velocity is recorded. The
behaviour of $\omega$ under a change of inertial frame is proved in the
frame-covariance theorem of this page.

Let $I_1,I_2,I_3>0$ be pairwise distinct, let $I:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be the linear map with $Ie_j=I_je_j$ on the standard orthonormal basis, and let $I^{-1}$ denote its inverse, given by $I^{-1}e_j=I_j^{-1}e_j$. Define the formal torque-free Euler vector field
$$F(\omega):=-I^{-1}\bigl(\omega\times I\omega\bigr),\qquad \omega\in\mathbb R^3.$$
When $I$ is an actual rigid-body inertia map written in a principal basis, this is the angular-velocity vector field obtained from [[thm-cm-euler-equations-and-torque-free-invariants]]. Here the positive diagonal entries are otherwise arbitrary; no realization by a mass distribution is assumed. Let $\Omega\ne0$. Then:

1. $F(\Omega e_3)=0$, and for every $\delta\in\mathbb R^3$ $$F(\Omega e_3+\delta)=A\delta+R(\delta),\qquad (A\delta)_1=\frac{\Omega(I_2-I_3)}{I_1}\delta_2,\quad (A\delta)_2=\frac{\Omega(I_3-I_1)}{I_2}\delta_1,\quad (A\delta)_3=0,$$ where $\lVert R(\delta)\rVert_2\le C\lVert\delta\rVert_2^2$ for the explicit constant $C:=\lVert I^{-1}\rVert_F\lVert I\rVert_F$ and $\lVert M\rVert_F:=\bigl(\sum_{j,k}M_{jk}^2\bigr)^{1/2}$; consequently $A$ is the total derivative of $F$ at $\Omega e_3$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]).
2. Every solution of the linear system $\delta'=A\delta$ on $\mathbb R$ has $\delta_3$ constant, and with $$\lambda:=\frac{\Omega^2(I_2-I_3)(I_3-I_1)}{I_1I_2}\ne0$$ the pair $(\delta_1,\delta_2)$ is determined by its initial value as follows:
   - if $\lambda<0$, then with $\kappa:=\sqrt{-\lambda}>0$, $$\delta_1(t)=\delta_1(0)\cos(\kappa t)+\frac{\Omega(I_2-I_3)}{I_1\kappa}\delta_2(0)\sin(\kappa t),\qquad \delta_2(t)=\delta_2(0)\cos(\kappa t)+\frac{\Omega(I_3-I_1)}{I_2\kappa}\delta_1(0)\sin(\kappa t),$$ and every solution is bounded on $[0,\infty)$;
   - if $\lambda>0$, then the same two formulas hold with $\cosh$ and $\sinh$ in place of $\cos$ and $\sin$ and $\kappa:=\sqrt\lambda$, the system has unbounded solutions (for instance $\delta_2(0)=0$, $\delta_1(0)\ne0$), and if $\delta_1(0)+\frac{\Omega(I_2-I_3)}{I_1\kappa}\delta_2(0)\ne0$ then $\lVert\delta(t)\rVert_2\to+\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$.
3. Hence the linearization at the spin $\Omega e_3$ is oscillatory exactly when $(I_2-I_3)(I_3-I_1)<0$, i.e. when the third principal moment is a largest or a smallest moment, and it has exponentially growing solutions exactly when $\lambda>0$, i.e. when $I_3$ lies strictly between $I_1$ and $I_2$; in the latter case the zero solution of the linear system is not stable.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is **totally differentiable at $a$** when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) such that

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

where the quotient is considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$. The map $L$, when it exists, is denoted $Df(a)$ and called the **total derivative**. Equivalently, $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with $\|r(h)\|_2/\|h\|_2\to0$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a map; retain the convention of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]] that a solution means a solution of $z'(t)=F(z(t))$, read as a system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], and that it is defined for all $t\ge0$ when its interval contains $[0,\infty)$. A maximal solution means one with no proper extension, as defined there; the invariance and stability predicates below quantify over maximal solutions through time $0$, not their arbitrary local restrictions. No existence or uniqueness is asserted for an arbitrary $F$.

**Invariant sets.** A set $S\subseteq U$ is **forward invariant** (for this system) when every maximal solution $z$ with $z(0)\in S$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $z(t)\in S$ for all $t\ge0$.

**Distance to a set.** For a nonempty $S\subseteq U$ define

$$\operatorname{dist}(z,S):=\inf\{\,\|z-s\|_2:s\in S\,\}\qquad(z\in\mathbb R^n),$$

the infimum of a nonempty set of nonnegative reals that is bounded below, computed for the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Define the Euclidean closure of $S$ by

$$\overline S:=\{z\in\mathbb R^n:\text{for every }\varepsilon>0\text{ there is }s\in S\text{ with }\|z-s\|_2<\varepsilon\}.$$

The map $z\mapsto\operatorname{dist}(z,S)$ is nonnegative and vanishes exactly on $\overline S$: by the defining property of the infimum, $\operatorname{dist}(z,S)=0$ exactly when every positive-radius Euclidean ball about $z$ meets $S$. When $S=\{z_*\}$ is a singleton, $\operatorname{dist}(z,S)=\|z-z_*\|_2$.

**Orbital stability.** Let $S\subseteq U$ be nonempty and forward invariant. Then $S$ is **orbitally stable** when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that every maximal solution $z$ with $\operatorname{dist}(z(0),S)<\delta$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies

$$\operatorname{dist}(z(t),S)<\varepsilon\qquad(t\ge0).$$

It is **asymptotically orbitally stable** when it is orbitally stable and there is $\delta_0>0$ such that every maximal solution with $\operatorname{dist}(z(0),S)<\delta_0$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $\operatorname{dist}(z(t),S)\to0$ as $t\to\infty$.

**Linear stability.** Let $z_*\in U$ be an equilibrium of $F$ and suppose $F$ is totally differentiable at $z_*$ in the sense of [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], with total derivative $DF(z_*):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$; write $L:=DF(z_*)$. The **linearized system** at $z_*$ is the autonomous linear system

$$y'(t)=L\,y(t).$$

The equilibrium $z_*$ is **linearly stable** when every maximal solution $y$ of the linearized system ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]) is defined for all $t\ge0$ and is bounded on $[0,\infty)$, that is, there is a real constant $C\ge0$ with $\|y(t)\|_2\le C$ for every $t\ge0$. It is **linearly asymptotically stable** when every maximal solution of the linearized system is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $\|y(t)\|_2\to0$ as $t\to\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), carried through [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]
clause (i) and [[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] for finite mass moments, through
[[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]] and [[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (i)
for the finite inertial integrals, and through the double-cover supplier of
[[def-cm-quaternion-rotation-map-and-cover]] (its second remark) for the
surjectivity used to choose an initial unit quaternion. Adopt a **nondegenerate** model of the
rigid-material branch [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: a reference mass
distribution $\nu$ with total mass $m$, centred reference coordinates and no
line through the origin carrying the whole mass
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] clause (a)). Fix an orthonormal principal basis
$(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ with $Ie_{j}=I_{j}e_{j}$ and $I_{j}>0$
([[pthm-cm10-principal-axes]] clauses (a) and (d)), use the model in the
**torque-free** branch of [[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iv), and fix
an index $j\in\{1,2,3\}$ and a rate $\Omega\in\mathbb R$. Use the model's nondegenerate open
time window $I_0$ ([[def-interval]] and
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] clause (ii)), and fix a time $t_{0}\in I_0$ and an orientation
$R_{0}\in SO(3)$. Then:

1. **Existence of the uniform rotation.** There is a path
   $R:I_0\to SO(3)$ of class $C^{1}$ with $R(t_{0})=R_{0}$ and
   $$R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)=[\Omega e_{j}]_\times\qquad(t\in I_0),$$
   that is, with constant body angular velocity $\omega\equiv\Omega e_{j}$
   ([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]] clause (a)).
2. **It is a torque-free motion.** For every such path $R$ and every curve
   $c:I_0\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{2}$, the map
   $x(t,\rho):=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ is a motion of the torque-free model of the
   branch: its angular momentum about the centre of mass is
   $$L_c(t)=\Omega I_{j}\,R(t)e_{j},$$
   it is constant on $I_0$, and the adopted balance $L_c'=0$ holds. (Here $R$
   is automatically of class $C^{2}$, because $R'=R[\Omega e_{j}]_\times$ is
   the product of the $C^{1}$ curve $R$ with a constant matrix, so the
   configuration path $(c,R)$ has the regularity required of a motion.)
3. **Geometry and invariants.** In the motions of clause 2 one has
   $l=I\omega=\Omega I_{j}e_{j}$ constant,
   $$C=\lVert L_c\rVert_2^{2}=\Omega^{2}I_{j}^{2},\qquad E=\tfrac12\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\tfrac12\Omega^{2}I_{j};$$
   if $\Omega\neq0$, define the spatial line of the body-fixed axis by
   $\ell_j(t):=\{c(t)+sR(t)e_j:s\in\mathbb R\}$ and its unit direction by
   $n_j(t):=R(t)e_j$. Then $n_j(t)=L_c/(\Omega I_j)$ for every $t$, so this
   direction is **fixed in the inertial frame** and the spatial angular
   velocity $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t):=R(t)\omega(t)=\Omega n_j$ of
   [[def-cm10-angular-velocity]] clause (b) is constant; the line
   $\ell_j(t)$ need not be fixed because $c$ is arbitrary. If $\Omega=0$,
   then $R$ is constant on $I_0$.
4. **Converse classification.** Conversely, let a motion of a nondegenerate
   torque-free model have **constant** body angular velocity
   $\omega\equiv\omega_{0}$ on its time window. Then
   $I\omega_{0}=\lambda\omega_{0}$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb R$: either
   $\omega_{0}=0$ and the orientation path is constant, or $\omega_{0}\neq0$
   and $\omega_{0}$ lies along a principal axis; in the latter case an orthonormal principal basis can be chosen with one vector $e_j=\omega_0/\|\omega_0\|_2$ and $\Omega=\|\omega_0\|_2\ne0$, and the conclusions of clauses 2 and 3 hold in that adapted basis. It can be made positively oriented by negating a different basis vector. No alignment with the initially fixed basis is asserted when eigenvalues repeat.

The statement is conditional on the adopted model and zero-torque balance; it
asserts no force, no measurement and no empirical law, and the existence
clause is a statement about the model's kinematic class, not about nature.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only to make the integrals finite. Adopt the
model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] and its inertia data
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]): the reference mass distribution $\nu$ with
total mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates, the body inertia matrix $I$,
the spatial inertia tensor $I(t)=R(t)IR(t)^{\mathsf T}$ of a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$, and the inertia tensor $I(t,p)$ about a spatial
point $p$ ([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]). Then:

**(a) Principal basis.** There is an orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of
$\mathbb R^3$ and real numbers $I_1,I_2,I_3$, the **principal axes** and
**principal moments** of the model, with
$$Ie_j=I_je_j\qquad(j=1,2,3).$$

**(b) Quadratic form and rotational term.** For every
$\omega=\sum_j\omega_je_j\in\mathbb R^3$ one has
$I\omega=\sum_jI_j\omega_je_j$ and
$$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\sum_jI_j\omega_j^{2}=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)\ \ge 0,$$
and each principal moment is
$I_j=e_j^{\mathsf T}Ie_j=\int\lVert e_j\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)$.

**(c) Axis moments.** For every unit vector $n\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$n^{\mathsf T}In=\int\lVert n\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho);$$
for every spatial point $p$ and unit vector $n$, with $x=x(t,\cdot)$ the
placement at time $t$,
$$n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n=\int\lVert n\times\bigl(x(t,\rho)-p\bigr)\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho).$$
Consequently the number $\Theta_\ell(t)=n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n$ of
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] depends only on the spatial line $\ell$
$\{p+sn:s\in\mathbb R\}$ and not on the choice of the point $p$ on it nor on
the sign of the unit direction $n$.

**(d) Vanishing and positivity.** Each principal moment satisfies $I_j\ge0$,
and $I_j=0$ exactly when $\nu$ is supported on the line $\mathbb Re_j$ of the
principal axis, that is $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Re_j\bigr)=0$.
If the model is nondegenerate, that is if
$\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega\bigr)>0$ for every
$\omega\neq0$, then every $I_j>0$ and $I$ is invertible. If $\nu$ is
supported on some line through the origin (such a line exists whenever the
support of a centred $\nu$ is contained in a line, because the mean of $\nu$
is the origin), then $I$ is not invertible.

**(e) Extremal moments.** For every unit vector
$n=\sum_jc_je_j$ one has $n^{\mathsf T}In=\sum_jI_jc_j^{2}$ and therefore
$$\min_jI_j\ \le\ n^{\mathsf T}In\ \le\ \max_jI_j,$$
with the value $\max_jI_j$ attained at a unit eigenvector for a maximal
principal moment and the value $\min_jI_j$ attained at a unit eigenvector for
a minimal principal moment. Hence the largest and smallest principal moments
are the maximum and minimum of the rotational-inertia quadratic form over the
unit sphere.

The identities are conditional on the model data and the stated choice
assumption; no equation of motion and no conservation statement is used or
asserted.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Use the standard basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ and coordinates $\omega=\omega_1e_1+\omega_2e_2+\omega_3e_3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], [[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Define the map $[\cdot]_\times:\mathbb R^3\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ by
$$[\omega]_\times:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\omega_3&\omega_2\\ \omega_3&0&-\omega_1\\ -\omega_2&\omega_1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then:

1. $[\omega]_\times z=\omega\times z$ for all $\omega,z\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].
2. $[\omega]_\times^{\mathsf T}=-[\omega]_\times$ for every $\omega$; the map $\omega\mapsto[\omega]_\times$ is linear and injective, and its image is exactly the set of skew-symmetric matrices of $M_3(\mathbb R)$. Consequently every skew-symmetric $\Omega\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ equals $[\omega]_\times$ for exactly one $\omega$, namely $\omega=(\Omega_{32},\Omega_{13},\Omega_{21})$.
3. For every $R\in SO(3)$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]) and every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$, $$R[\omega]_\times R^{\mathsf T}=[R\omega]_\times.$$

derivations.claim: The spin $\Omega e_{j}$ is a solution of $\omega'=F(\omega)$ on every interval with at least two points, because it is the constant body angular velocity of the torque-free motion of [L4] and [L1] is the same equation; with $l=I\omega=\Omega I_{j}e_{j}$ and $I^{-1}l=\Omega e_{j}$ the right-hand side $F(\Omega e_{j})=-I^{-1}(\Omega e_{j}\times\Omega I_{j}e_{j})=0$ vanishes.

Identify $\mathbb R^{3}$ with the supplier's $\mathbb R^{3}$ of [L2] by the map $Q$ carrying its standard basis to the cyclic basis $(e_{a},e_{b},e_{j})$. By the positive orientation stipulated in [L5], $Q\in SO(3)$, so $Q(u\times v)=(Qu)\times(Qv)$ ([L6]); then the supplier's diagonal map with entries $(I_{a},I_{b},I_{j})$ is the model's inertia operator $I$ expressed in the principal basis [L5], and the fields $F(\omega)=-I^{-1}(\omega\times I\omega)$ correspond. Clause 1 of [L2] applied at the spin about the third basis vector gives the total differentiability of $F$ at $\Omega e_{j}$ and the derivative $A_{j}$ of clause 1: the components are $(A_j\delta)_a=\Omega(I_b-I_j)\delta_b/I_a$, $(A_j\delta)_b=\Omega(I_j-I_a)\delta_a/I_b$, $(A_j\delta)_j=0$, so evaluating at $e_a$ and $e_b$ gives exactly the stated basis images. The supplier also gives the remainder bound and explicit constant, and clauses 2-3 of [L2] give the transverse formulas, the criterion for the sign of $\lambda_{j}=\Omega^{2}(I_{a}-I_{j})(I_{j}-I_{b})/(I_{a}I_{b})$ and the bounded/unbounded alternatives. The displayed sine/cosine and hyperbolic formulas are defined on all of $\mathbb R$, satisfy the linear system, and have the prescribed initial data; the uniqueness assertion in the supplier proof makes every local solution their restriction. This is clause 1 and the case analysis of clause 2 up to the sign criterion.

The product $(I_{a}-I_{j})(I_{j}-I_{b})$ is positive exactly when $I_{j}$ lies strictly between $I_{a}$ and $I_{b}$ and negative exactly when $I_{j}$ is larger than both or smaller than both; since $\Omega^{2}/(I_{a}I_{b})>0$, the criterion of clause 3 of [L2] reads: $\lambda_{j}<0$ (oscillatory, bounded, the displayed $\cos,\sin$ formulas with $\kappa_{j}=\sqrt{-\lambda_{j}}$) exactly for the extreme axes, and $\lambda_{j}>0$ (the $\cosh,\sinh$ formulas with $\kappa_{j}=\sqrt{\lambda_{j}}$, unbounded solutions, the stated growth criterion) exactly for the intermediate axis. This completes clause 2.

By [L3] the boundedness of every global maximal solution of the linearized system on $[0,\infty)$ in the extreme case is exactly linear stability of the spin, and the existence of an unbounded solution in the intermediate case is the failure of linear stability, since a solution that is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$ is not bounded there.

boundaries.reason: The hypotheses are satisfiable: any nondegenerate model with three distinct positive principal moments and any Omega != 0 gives the data of the statement; step 1.1 exhibits the spin solution explicitly.

The zero case of the perturbation is included: delta=0 gives the spin itself, and the remainder bound of step 1.2 is trivial there; the statement also covers the zero solutions of the linearized system in the boundedness claims.
One axis at a time: steps 1.1-2.1 fix a single j and Omega, and the statement quantifies over them; the case analysis uses the two other axes only through the product (I_a - I_j)(I_j - I_b).

Repeated principal moments are excluded by the pairwise-distinctness hypothesis, which the supplier requires and which step 2.1 uses in forming the nonzero lambda_j; the remark records that the case of repeated moments is not covered.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.2 supplies explicit global formulas and identifies every local solution as their restriction by uniqueness; step 3.1 applies boundedness to maximal global solutions. No finite linearized endpoint occurs.

boundaries.reason: No choice principle is used or needed in this item; AC_omega appears nowhere in its hypotheses.

The forward direction is the dichotomy as stated: extreme axis gives bounded oscillatory solutions (step 2.1) and intermediate axis gives exponential growth (step 2.1), with linear stability read off in step 3.1.
The reverse direction is the 'only if' reading of the same criterion: lambda_j < 0 occurs exactly for extreme axes, proved in step 2.1 by the sign of the product of the two differences.

risk_review.notes: Four proof steps checked and full mathematical linearization supplier read. Cyclic oriented basis (e_a,e_b,e_j) preserves cross product. Quadratic remainder -I^-1(delta cross I delta) bounded by product Frobenius norms; derivative coefficients and lambda product match basis images. Pairwise distinct positive moments and Omega nonzero exclude lambda=0. Explicit trig/hyperbolic solutions are global; linear uniqueness ensures all maximal solutions are these. Extreme sign negative, intermediate positive; no inference of nonlinear stability. Principal-rotation direction repair does not affect use. No measured input.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only through the integrals of
[[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]]. Adopt a model of the rigid-material branch
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] that is **nondegenerate** in the sense of
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] clause (a) (no line through the origin carries
the whole mass), and use it in the **torque-free** external-torque branch of
[[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iv): the datum vanishes, so along every
motion of the resulting model the adopted balance reads $L_c'=0$ on the time
window $I_0$. Let $\omega$ be the body angular velocity, $I$ the body inertia
matrix and $l:=I\omega$ ([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]],
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]). Then:

1. **Conservation of angular momentum.** The angular momentum about the
   centre of mass $L_c(t)=R(t)l(t)$ of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]] clause
   4 is constant on $I_0$; in particular $\lVert L_c\rVert_2$ is constant.
2. **Energy-momentum invariants and principal components.** The scalars
   $$C:=\langle l,l\rangle=\lVert L_c\rVert_2^{2},\qquad E:=\tfrac12\,\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\tfrac12\,\langle l,I^{-1}l\rangle$$
   are constant on $I_0$, and $l$ satisfies the torque-free equation
   $$l'=l\times(I^{-1}l).$$
   If $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ is a positively oriented orthonormal eigenbasis of $I$ with
   $Ie_{j}=I_{j}e_{j}$ and $l=\sum_{j}l_{j}e_{j}$
   ([[pthm-cm10-principal-axes]] clauses (a)-(b)), then
   $$C=\sum_{j}l_{j}^{2},\qquad E=\sum_{j}\frac{l_{j}^{2}}{2I_{j}},$$
   and the component equations are
   $$l_{1}'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_{3}}-\frac1{I_{2}}\Bigr)l_{2}l_{3},\qquad l_{2}'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_{1}}-\frac1{I_{3}}\Bigr)l_{1}l_{3},\qquad l_{3}'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_{2}}-\frac1{I_{1}}\Bigr)l_{1}l_{2}.$$
3. **The energy invariant is the rotational kinetic energy.** $E$ equals the
   rotational term $\tfrac12\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega$ of the model's kinetic
   energy in clause 3 of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]]; and with
   $I_{\min}:=\min_{j}I_{j}>0$ one has
   $$\lVert\omega(t)\rVert_2^{2}\le\frac{2E}{I_{\min}}\qquad(t\in I_0).$$
   In particular both $l$ and $\omega$ are bounded on $I_0$.
4. **The spin field is globally solvable.** The autonomous field
   $F(l)=l\times(I^{-1}l)$ on $\mathbb R^{3}$ is locally Lipschitz in the
   state variable ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]), and
   every solution of $l'=F(l)$ has a unique maximal extension defined
   on all of $\mathbb R$, and that extension satisfies $\lVert l(t)\rVert_2=\lVert l(0)\rVert_2$
