   for every $t$. Consequently the $l$-path of a torque-free motion is the
   restriction to $I_0$ of a solution defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and its
   path is contained in the compact level set
   $$\Lambda(C,E):=\bigl\{z\in\mathbb R^{3}:\langle z,z\rangle=C,\ \tfrac12\langle z,I^{-1}z\rangle=E\bigr\},$$
   which is nonempty because it contains the datum at any chosen time of the motion.

The statement is conditional on the adopted model, its nondegeneracy and the
zero-torque balance; it asserts no orientation of the body in space, no
measured value and no empirical law.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only through the integrals of
[[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]]; the theorems below neither use nor imply any
other choice principle. Adopt a model of the rigid-material branch
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] with the external-torque branch
[[post-cm11-torque-balance]]: a reference mass distribution $\nu$ with total
mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates, a time window $I_0$
([[def-interval]]), an inertial frame, a motion $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with
configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^{2}$
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]), body angular velocity $\omega$
([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]]) and body inertia matrix $I$
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]), and a continuous external torque datum
$\tau:I_0\to\mathbb R^{3}$ with respect to which the adopted balance of
[[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iii) holds along the motion. Then:

1. **Euler's equations with torque.** Writing $l:=I\omega$, one has
   $l'=R^{\mathsf T}\tau-\omega\times I\omega$ and
   $$I\omega'(t)+\omega(t)\times I\omega(t)=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\tau(t)\qquad(t\in I_0).$$
2. **Principal-axis components.** If $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ is a positively oriented orthonormal
   eigenbasis of $I$ with $Ie_{j}=I_{j}e_{j}$ ([[pthm-cm10-principal-axes]]
   clause (a)) and $\omega=\sum_{j}\omega_{j}e_{j}$,
   $R^{\mathsf T}\tau=\sum_{j}\tau_{j}e_{j}$, then the equations are
   componentwise
   $$I_{1}\omega_{1}'=(I_{2}-I_{3})\omega_{2}\omega_{3}+\tau_{1},\qquad I_{2}\omega_{2}'=(I_{3}-I_{1})\omega_{3}\omega_{1}+\tau_{2},\qquad I_{3}\omega_{3}'=(I_{1}-I_{2})\omega_{1}\omega_{2}+\tau_{3}.$$
3. **Rotational power identity.** The rotational kinetic energy
   $K_{\mathrm{rot}}(t):=\tfrac12\omega(t)^{\mathsf T}I\omega(t)$ is
   differentiable on $I_0$ with
   $$\frac{d}{dt}K_{\mathrm{rot}}(t)=\omega(t)\cdot R(t)^{\mathsf T}\tau(t)\qquad(t\in I_0);$$
   in particular, if $\tau\equiv0$, then $K_{\mathrm{rot}}$ is constant on
   $I_0$, and $K_{\mathrm{rot}}$ coincides with the rotational term
   $\tfrac12\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega$ of the model's kinetic energy in
   clause 3 of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]].
4. **Torque-free reduction and nondegeneracy.** Suppose $\tau\equiv0$ and the
   model is nondegenerate in the sense of [[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] clause
   (a), so that $I$ is invertible with $I^{-1}l=\omega$. Then, writing
   $\omega$ as a function of $l$,
   $$l'=l\times(I^{-1}l),\qquad \omega'=F(\omega):=-I^{-1}\bigl(\omega\times I\omega\bigr);$$
   the second form exhibits the torque-free body angular velocity as a
   solution of the autonomous field $F$ on $\mathbb R^{3}$.
5. **Frame covariance.** Let a second inertial frame be related to the first
   by $t'=t+b$, $x'=Qx+ut+a$ with $b\in\mathbb R$, $a,u\in\mathbb R^{3}$,
   $Q\in SO(3)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]] clause (iv)), and let
   $\tilde x(t',\rho):=Qx(t'-b,\rho)+u(t'-b)+a$, $\tilde\tau(t'):=Q\tau(t'-b)$
   be the transformed motion and datum of [[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause
   (vii). Then the balance holds in the second frame, and
   $$I\tilde\omega'(t')+\tilde\omega(t')\times I\tilde\omega(t')=\tilde R(t')^{\mathsf T}\tilde\tau(t')\qquad(t'\in I_0+b),$$
   where $\tilde\omega(t')=\omega(t'-b)$ and
   $\tilde R(t')=QR(t'-b)$; the body-frame torque is unchanged:
   $\tilde R(t')^{\mathsf T}\tilde\tau(t')=R(t'-b)^{\mathsf T}\tau(t'-b)$.

The statement is conditional on the adopted model and torque balance; it
asserts no force law for $\tau$, no conservation of $L_c$ and no measured
value.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only to make the integrals finite. Adopt the
model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] and its inertia data
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]): the reference mass distribution $\nu$ with
total mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates, the body inertia matrix $I$,
the spatial inertia tensor $I(t)=R(t)IR(t)^{\mathsf T}$ of a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$, and the inertia tensor $I(t,p)$ about a spatial
point $p$ ([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]). Then:

**(a) Principal basis.** There is an orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of
$\mathbb R^3$ and real numbers $I_1,I_2,I_3$, the **principal axes** and
**principal moments** of the model, with
$$Ie_j=I_je_j\qquad(j=1,2,3).$$

**(b) Quadratic form and rotational term.** For every
$\omega=\sum_j\omega_je_j\in\mathbb R^3$ one has
$I\omega=\sum_jI_j\omega_je_j$ and
$$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\sum_jI_j\omega_j^{2}=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)\ \ge 0,$$
and each principal moment is
$I_j=e_j^{\mathsf T}Ie_j=\int\lVert e_j\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)$.

**(c) Axis moments.** For every unit vector $n\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$n^{\mathsf T}In=\int\lVert n\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho);$$
for every spatial point $p$ and unit vector $n$, with $x=x(t,\cdot)$ the
placement at time $t$,
$$n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n=\int\lVert n\times\bigl(x(t,\rho)-p\bigr)\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho).$$
Consequently the number $\Theta_\ell(t)=n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n$ of
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] depends only on the spatial line $\ell$
$\{p+sn:s\in\mathbb R\}$ and not on the choice of the point $p$ on it nor on
the sign of the unit direction $n$.

**(d) Vanishing and positivity.** Each principal moment satisfies $I_j\ge0$,
and $I_j=0$ exactly when $\nu$ is supported on the line $\mathbb Re_j$ of the
principal axis, that is $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Re_j\bigr)=0$.
If the model is nondegenerate, that is if
$\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega\bigr)>0$ for every
$\omega\neq0$, then every $I_j>0$ and $I$ is invertible. If $\nu$ is
supported on some line through the origin (such a line exists whenever the
support of a centred $\nu$ is contained in a line, because the mean of $\nu$
is the origin), then $I$ is not invertible.

**(e) Extremal moments.** For every unit vector
$n=\sum_jc_je_j$ one has $n^{\mathsf T}In=\sum_jI_jc_j^{2}$ and therefore
$$\min_jI_j\ \le\ n^{\mathsf T}In\ \le\ \max_jI_j,$$
with the value $\max_jI_j$ attained at a unit eigenvector for a maximal
principal moment and the value $\min_jI_j$ attained at a unit eigenvector for
a minimal principal moment. Hence the largest and smallest principal moments
are the maximum and minimum of the rotational-inertia quadratic form over the
unit sphere.

The identities are conditional on the model data and the stated choice
assumption; no equation of motion and no conservation statement is used or
asserted.

Adopt the model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: the reference mass
distribution $\nu$, its total mass $m=\nu(\mathbb R^3)$ and its centred
reference coordinates $\int\rho\,d\nu(\rho)=0$. Assume the Axiom of Countable
Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, used only through
[[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]] to make the polynomial moments of $\nu$ of
degree at most two finite real numbers. Fix an inertial frame and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^2$
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]).

**(a) Body inertia matrix.** The **body inertia matrix** of the model is the
inertia matrix of the reference mass distribution,
$$I:=I(\nu)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}I_3-\rho\rho^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
with entries $I_{jk}=\int(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}\delta_{jk}-\rho_j\rho_k)\,d\nu$
as in [[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]; the matrix is expressed
in the standard basis of the reference coordinates. Its entries are finite
real numbers, it is symmetric, and for every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)\ \ge 0$$
by [[lem-cm-inertia-matrix-properties]] clauses 1-2; hence $I$ is symmetric
and its quadratic form is positive semidefinite. The dimension is
$[I]=\mu\ell^{2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]), read in kilogram metres squared. The
model is **nondegenerate** when no line through the origin carries the whole
mass, that is $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega\bigr)>0$ for every
$\omega\neq0$, and **degenerate** otherwise; the connection between this
criterion and the strict positivity and invertibility of $I$ is proved in the
principal-axes theorem of this page.

**(b) Spatial inertia tensor at the centre of mass.** The **spatial inertia
tensor** of the model at time $t$ is
$$I(t):=R(t)\,I\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
the matrix of the same quadratic form in the frame's spatial coordinates: for
every $n\in\mathbb R^3$,
$n^{\mathsf T}I(t)n=(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)^{\mathsf T}I(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)$. Its
entries are $C^2$ functions of $t$, since $R$ is of class $C^2$ and $I$ is
constant; the matrix rotates with the body and returns to $I$ in the
body-fixed frame, where $R=I_3$.

**(c) Inertia tensor about a spatial point.** For a spatial point
$p\in\mathbb R^3$ let
$$a(t,p):=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\bigl(p-c(t)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^3$$
be the **reference coordinate of $p$**, that is the label of the material
point of the reference placement that is placed at $p$ at time $t$. The
**inertia tensor of the model about $p$** at time $t$ is
$$I(t,p):=R(t)\,I_\nu\bigl(a(t,p)\bigr)\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
where
$$I_\nu(a)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho-a\rVert_2^{2}I_3-(\rho-a)(\rho-a)^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)$$
is the inertia tensor of the mass distribution about the point $a$ of the
reference coordinates ([[def-cm-inertia-tensor-about-a-point]]). Since the
label of a spatial point is uniquely determined by the placement, this is
well defined; for the centre of mass, $a(t,c(t))=0$ and
$I(t,c(t))=I(t)$. The dimension is again $\mu\ell^{2}$, read in kilogram
metres squared.

**(d) Moment of inertia about an axis.** Let $\ell$ be a spatial line at time
$t$, given by a point $p\in\mathbb R^3$ and a unit direction $n\in\mathbb R^3$
($\lVert n\rVert_2=1$). The **moment of inertia of the model about $\ell$** is
$$\Theta_\ell(t):=n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n .$$
Its invariance under the choices entering the description of the line and
its identification with the integral defining the physical moment of inertia
about the line are statements, not conventions; they are proved in clause
(c) of the principal-axes theorem of this page. For a **body-fixed
axis**, that is a line through the centre of mass whose direction in
reference coordinates is a constant unit vector $n_0$, the moment is
$$n_0^{\mathsf T}I n_0=\int\lVert n_0\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),$$
by clause (a), and is independent of time, because $I$ and $n_0$ are model
data.

**(e) What is constant and what moves.** The body inertia matrix $I$ is
determined by the model's reference mass distribution alone and does not
depend on the time, the frame or the motion; the spatial inertia tensor
$I(t)$ depends on the motion through the orientation $R(t)$; the inertia
tensor $I(t,p)$ about a spatial point depends on the motion through both the
orientation and the position of $p$. Principal axes and principal moments of
$I$ are the subject of the principal-axes theorem of this page.

Let $I_1<I_2<I_3$ be positive reals and let $I:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be the linear map with $Ie_j=I_je_j$ on the standard orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$. Consider the autonomous first-order system
$$l'(t)=F(l(t)),\qquad F(l):=l\times(I^{-1}l),$$
on $U:=\mathbb R^3$, read as in [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]] with the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and $I^{-1}$ the inverse of $I$ ([[cor-cm-principal-axes-of-the-inertia-matrix]]); this is the torque-free Euler system of [[thm-cm-euler-equations-and-torque-free-invariants]] in angular-momentum variables. Let $L\ne0$. Then:

$Le_1$ and $Le_3$ are equilibria of $F$ and each is Lyapunov stable in the sense of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]: for $j=1$ and $j=3$ and for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta\in(0,\varepsilon]$ such that every maximal solution $l$ with $\lVert l(0)-Le_j\rVert_2<\delta$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $\lVert l(t)-Le_j\rVert_2<\varepsilon$ for every $t\ge0$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a map. Consider the autonomous first-order system

$$z'(t)=F(z(t)),$$

read as the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] with $D=\mathbb R\times U$ and right-hand side $(t,z)\mapsto F(z)$. A **solution** below means a solution of this system on an interval containing $0$; a solution whose interval is $[0,\infty)$ or contains it is said to be **defined for all $t\ge0$**.

A solution $\tilde z:J\to U$ **extends** $z:I\to U$ when $I\subseteq J$ and $\tilde z|_I=z$; the extension is proper if $I\subsetneq J$. A solution is **maximal** when it has no proper extension ([[def-maximal-ode-solution]]). All stability predicates below quantify over maximal solutions whose intervals contain $0$; their local restrictions remain solutions. This convention asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of maximal solutions for an arbitrary map $F$.

A point $z_*\in U$ is an **equilibrium** (also **fixed point** or **zero**) of $F$ when $F(z_*)=0$; then the constant function $z(t)=z_*$ is a solution on every interval containing $0$.

Let $z_*\in U$ be an equilibrium.

1. $z_*$ is **Lyapunov stable** (or simply **stable**) when for every Euclidean ball $B_\varepsilon(z_*)$ with $\overline{B_\varepsilon(z_*)}\subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) there is $\delta\in(0,\varepsilon]$ such that every maximal solution $z$ with $\|z(0)-z_*\|_2<\delta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies

$$\|z(t)-z_*\|_2<\varepsilon\qquad(t\ge0).$$

2. $z_*$ is **asymptotically stable** when it is Lyapunov stable and in addition there is $\delta_0>0$ such that every maximal solution $z$ with $\|z(0)-z_*\|_2<\delta_0$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $\|z(t)-z_*\|_2\to0$ as $t\to\infty$.

An equilibrium which is not Lyapunov stable is **unstable**. An equilibrium is **globally asymptotically stable** when it is asymptotically stable and every maximal solution of the system is defined for all $t\ge0$ and converges to it as $t\to\infty$.

Let $I_1<I_2<I_3$ be positive reals, let $I:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be the linear map with $Ie_j=I_je_j$ on the standard orthonormal basis, and consider the torque-free Euler system $l'=F(l)$, $F(l)=l\times(I^{-1}l)$, on $U=\mathbb R^3$ ([[thm-cm-euler-equations-and-torque-free-invariants]], [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]). Let $L\ne0$. Then $l_0:=Le_2$ is an equilibrium of $F$ and is **not Lyapunov stable**: with $$\varepsilon_0:=\frac{|L|}{2},\qquad a:=\sqrt{\frac{1/I_1-1/I_2}{1/I_2-1/I_3}}>0,\qquad c_0:=a\Bigl(\frac1{I_2}-\frac1{I_3}\Bigr)\frac{\sqrt3}{2}|L|>0,$$ for every $\delta>0$ there is a solution $l$ with $\lVert l(0)-l_0\rVert_2<\delta$ and some $t\ge0$ with $\lVert l(t)-l_0\rVert_2\ge\varepsilon_0$; Moreover, with $\delta_0:=|L|/(2\sqrt{1+a^2})$, the escape can be arranged at a time $t\le c_0^{-1}\log(\delta_0/\eta)$ where $\eta=l_1(0)>0$ may be chosen as small as desired.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate open interval, let $\omega:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous, and consider on the open time-state domain $D:=I\times\mathbb H\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb H$ the initial value problem

$$q'(t)=\tfrac12\,q(t)\,\varphi\bigl(\omega(t)\bigr),\qquad q(t_0)=q_0,$$

read as the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] with time-state domain $D$, state space $\mathbb H$, and right-hand side $F:D\to\mathbb H$, $F(t,q)=\tfrac12q\,\varphi(\omega(t))$, where $\varphi$, $S^3$ and $\rho$ are those of [[def-cm-quaternion-rotation-map-and-cover]].

1. If $q:I\to\mathbb H$ is a $C^1$ solution of $q'=\tfrac12q\,\varphi(\omega(t))$, then $N\circ q$ is constant on $I$; if $q(t_0)\in S^3$ for one $t_0\in I$, then $q(I)\subseteq S^3$ and the curve

$$R:=\rho\circ q:I\longrightarrow SO(3),\qquad R(t):=\rho(q(t)),$$

is of class $C^1$ with $R'(t)=R(t)\,\Omega_{\omega(t)}$ for every $t\in I$; consequently $\omega$ is the body angular velocity of $R$ in the sense of [[lem-cm-body-angular-velocity-of-a-rotation-path]].
2. For every $t_0\in I$ and $q_0\in S^3$ the problem has exactly one maximal solution, and its domain is all of $I$; that is, there is exactly one $C^1$ curve $q:I\to S^3$ with $q(t_0)=q_0$ and $q'=\tfrac12q\,\varphi(\omega(t))$ on $I$, and clause 1 applies to it.

Let $\mathbb H$ be the quaternion algebra with its product, conjugation $x\mapsto\bar x$, real-valued norm $N:\mathbb H\to\mathbb R$, and real embedding $r\mapsto\hat r=(r,0,0,0)$, in the notation of [[def-quaternions]]. Thus $x=x_0+x_1i+x_2j+x_3k$ with the multiplication formula of [[def-quaternions]], and

$$N(x)=x_0^2+x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2,\qquad \widehat{N(x)}=x\bar x=\bar x x.$$

In particular, $N(x)>0$ for $x\ne0$, and the imported division-ring theorem gives the typed inverse formula $x^{-1}=\widehat{N(x)^{-1}}\,\bar x$ ([[thm-quaternions-form-a-division-ring]]). Under the identification of $\mathbb H$ with $\mathbb R^4$ by the coordinates $x_0,\dots,x_3$ one has $N(x)=\|x\|_2^2$ for the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

**Imaginary quaternions and the vector identification.** Put

$$\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H:=\{x\in\mathbb H:\bar x=-x\}=\mathbb Ri\oplus\mathbb Rj\oplus\mathbb Rk,\qquad \varphi:\mathbb R^3\to\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H,\quad \varphi(v_1,v_2,v_3):=v_1i+v_2j+v_3k .$$

Then $\varphi$ is a linear isomorphism with $N(\varphi(v))=\|v\|_2^2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^3$. Throughout the collection, $\varphi$ translates between vectors of $\mathbb R^3$ (their inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$, norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ and cross product) and imaginary quaternions inside quaternion products.

**The unit sphere.** Define

$$S^3:=\{q\in\mathbb H:N(q)=1\},$$

the unit sphere of $\mathbb H\cong\mathbb R^4$. The identification of $S^3$ with $SU(2)$ is the one of the published covering example `ex-su-two-to-so-three-as-a-covering-homomorphism`, which is also the source of the covering statement recorded in the second remark below; that example is linked from the page summary of this pair.

**Conjugation and the rotation map.** For $q\in\mathbb H$ with $q\ne0$ let $c_q:\mathbb H\to\mathbb H$ be

$$c_q(x):=qxq^{-1}=qx\,\widehat{N(q)^{-1}}\,\bar q,$$

where the real scalar is embedded by $r\mapsto\hat r$, and define

$$\rho(q):=c_q|_{\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H}:\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H\longrightarrow\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H .$$

Both the $\mathbb R$-linear map $\rho(q)$ and its matrix in the ordered basis $(i,j,k)$ of $\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H$ are written $\rho(q)$; the equality $\rho(q)\in SO(3)$ for $q\in S^3$ is part of the cited covering statement, and the matrix is the one meant whenever $\rho(q)$ is composed with the identifications above. The map $\rho$ itself is never linear in $q$ and no such structure is used.

**Quaternion lifts.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let $R:I\to SO(3)$ be a map, with $SO(3)$ as in [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]. A **quaternion lift** of $R$ is a map $q:I\to S^3$ with $\rho(q(t))=R(t)$ for every $t\in I$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points, let $t_0\in I$ and let $A,B:I\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be **differentiable at $t_0$**, meaning ([[def-matrix-space]]) that every entry function $t\mapsto A(t)_{ij}$ and $t\mapsto B(t)_{ij}$ is differentiable at $t_0$ in the sense of [[def-derivative]]; write $A'(t_0)$ for the matrix with entries $A'(t_0)_{ij}:=(t\mapsto A(t)_{ij})'(t_0)$, and similarly for $B$.

1. $A+B$ and $A^{\mathsf T}$ are differentiable at $t_0$, with $(A+B)'(t_0)=A'(t_0)+B'(t_0)$ and $(A^{\mathsf T})'(t_0)=(A'(t_0))^{\mathsf T}$.
2. $AB$ is differentiable at $t_0$, with $(AB)'(t_0)=A'(t_0)B(t_0)+A(t_0)B'(t_0)$.
3. If $A(t)\in SO(3)$ for every $t\in I$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]), then the matrix $A(t_0)^{\mathsf T}A'(t_0)$ is skew-symmetric, i.e. $(A^{\mathsf T}A')^{\mathsf T}=-A^{\mathsf T}A'$ at $t_0$, and likewise $A'(t_0)A(t_0)^{\mathsf T}$ is skew-symmetric. In particular the trace of each of these two matrices vanishes.

Use the standard basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ and coordinates $\omega=\omega_1e_1+\omega_2e_2+\omega_3e_3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], [[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Define the map $[\cdot]_\times:\mathbb R^3\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ by
$$[\omega]_\times:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\omega_3&\omega_2\\ \omega_3&0&-\omega_1\\ -\omega_2&\omega_1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then:

1. $[\omega]_\times z=\omega\times z$ for all $\omega,z\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].
2. $[\omega]_\times^{\mathsf T}=-[\omega]_\times$ for every $\omega$; the map $\omega\mapsto[\omega]_\times$ is linear and injective, and its image is exactly the set of skew-symmetric matrices of $M_3(\mathbb R)$. Consequently every skew-symmetric $\Omega\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ equals $[\omega]_\times$ for exactly one $\omega$, namely $\omega=(\Omega_{32},\Omega_{13},\Omega_{21})$.
3. For every $R\in SO(3)$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]) and every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$, $$R[\omega]_\times R^{\mathsf T}=[R\omega]_\times.$$
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Adopt the model data, the time window $I_0$, the inertial frame and the
notation of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: the reference mass distribution
$\nu$ with total mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates, and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^2$.

**(a) Configuration and configuration space.** The **configuration** of the
model at time $t$ in the frame is the pair $(c(t),R(t))$; the pair
$(c,R)$ is a **configuration path**. The **configuration space** of the model
is the set
$$\mathcal C:=\mathbb R^3\times SO(3),$$
read through the identification of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ with $\mathbb R^{9}$
([[def-matrix-space]]) so that $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathbb R^{12}$. The
configuration determines the placement $x=c+R\,\cdot$ at that time, and the
reference placement is $(c,R)=(0,I_3)$. Under the identification of
$M_3(\mathbb R)$ with $\mathbb R^{9}$, the group $SO(3)$ is a compact
three-dimensional embedded submanifold of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ and a subgroup of
the general linear group ([[lem-cm-so3-is-a-compact-three-dimensional-embedded-submanifold]]
clauses 1 and 3, [[lem-cm-so3-is-a-matrix-group]]); consequently
$\mathcal C=\mathbb R^3\times SO(3)$ is a six-dimensional smooth manifold
with the product structure. Its dimension $3+3=6$ is read as three
translation coordinates of $c$ and three orientation degrees of freedom of
$R$; the model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] has no other configuration
degrees of freedom, since deformation and internal variables are excluded by
that postulate.

**(b) Centre of mass, orientation, body frame.** Because
$\int\rho\,d\nu=0$, the configuration's translation is the position of the
centre of mass of the model,
$\int x(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho)=mc(t)$. The rotation $R(t)$ is the **orientation**
of the model at time $t$: the linear map that carries reference coordinates
into the frame's spatial coordinates, so that a material point whose
reference coordinate is $\rho$ is found at the spatial position $x(t,\rho)$.
The **body-fixed frame** at time $t$ is the ordered orthonormal basis
$(R(t)e_1,R(t)e_2,R(t)e_3)$ of the spatial space, obtained by applying the
orientation to the standard basis; the basis is $g$-orthonormal because
$R(t)\in O(3)$ preserves the Euclidean inner product
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]). The
material point of reference coordinate $\rho$ has **spatial position**
$x(t,\rho)$ and **reference coordinates** $\rho$.

**(c) Physical labels and faithfulness.** The **physical label set** is
$S:=\operatorname{supp}\nu$, defined here as the complement of the union of
all open $\nu$-null subsets of $\mathbb R^3$. Thus $\rho\in S$ exactly when
every open neighbourhood of $\rho$ has positive mass. This is a closed set
carrying all mass: the rational open boxes form a countable basis
([[thm-rational-points-and-boxes-in-rn]], $n=3$), so its complement is the
union of the countably many null basis boxes. Disjointifying this union and
using countable additivity ([[def-measure]]) gives $\nu(\mathbb R^3\setminus S)=0$.
In particular $S\neq\varnothing$ because $m>0$.

If two configurations satisfy $c+R\rho=\bar c+\bar R\rho$ for every
$\rho\in S$, integration against the centred measure gives $mc=m\bar c$,
hence $c=\bar c$. Their exact orientation ambiguity is therefore
$$\bar R^{-1}R\in\operatorname{Stab}_{SO(3)}(S):=\{H\in SO(3):H\rho=\rho\text{ for every }\rho\in S\},$$
the pointwise stabilizer of [[lem-cm-rigid-labeling-stabilizer]]. Conversely,
$c=\bar c$ and this stabilizer condition give equality of the placements on
$S$ by multiplication. A **nondegenerate physical labeling** is one whose
$S$ contains two linearly independent vectors; its stabilizer is $\{I_3\}$
by that lemma, so the physical placement determines $(c,R)$ uniquely.
The same injectivity conclusion holds for any auxiliary label set containing
the origin and two independent vectors, by evaluation at the origin followed
by the lemma, as in [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] clause (iii).

A **degenerate physical labeling** has no two independent vectors. If
$S$ contains a nonzero vector $u$, then $S\subseteq\mathbb Ru$, and its
stabilizer is exactly $\{H\in SO(3):Hu=u\}$, the rotations fixing the line
$\mathbb Ru$ pointwise; the orientation is determined only up to right
composition with this subgroup. If $S$ contains no nonzero vector, then
$S=\{0\}$ and its stabilizer is all of $SO(3)$. More generally a singleton
support $\{q\}$ must have $q=0$, since centring gives $mq=0$.
Thus a centred point mass has no distinguished orientation axis. These are
all the degenerate cases: after choosing any nonzero $u\in S$, failure of
independence forces every vector in $S$ to be a multiple of $u$.
Configuration pairs remain model data in every case, including orientation
data invisible in the placed physical labels.

**(d) Description in another inertial frame.** Let a second inertial frame be
related to the first by the transformation $t'=t+b$, $x'=Qx+ut+a$ of
[[post-cm01-frames]] clause (iv), with $b\in\mathbb R$, $a,u\in\mathbb R^3$
and $Q\in SO(3)$
([[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]] clause 1); the letters
$Q$ and $u$ are the rotation and the boost velocity written $R$ and $v$ in
[[post-cm01-frames]], renamed to avoid clashes with the orientation path
$R(t)$ and the material velocity field of clause (e). The
**description of the same motion in the second frame** assigns to the same
material label $\rho$ the events of the motion in the new coordinates,
$$\tilde x(t',\rho):=Q\,x(t'-b,\rho)+u\,(t'-b)+a .$$
Substituting $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ and using distributivity of the matrix
product over sums expresses the description as a motion of the same model in
the second frame, with configuration path
$$\tilde c(t')=Qc(t'-b)+u\,(t'-b)+a,\qquad \tilde R(t')=Q\,R(t'-b),$$
where $\tilde R(t')\in SO(3)$ for every $t'$ because $SO(3)$ is closed under
matrix multiplication ([[lem-cm-so3-is-a-matrix-group]]); the pair
$(\tilde c,\tilde R)$ is again of class $C^2$. This description is a
convention forced by the frame change,
not a dynamical statement; the transformation laws of the velocity field, the
angular velocity and the inertia data are proved in the frame-covariance
theorem of this page.

**(e) Material velocities.** For a motion with configuration path $(c,R)$, the
**material velocity** of the label $\rho$ at time $t$ is the derivative
$$\partial_tx(t,\rho):=c'(t)+R'(t)\rho,$$
which exists by differentiability of $c$ and of the entries of $R$
([[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]]). The **velocity field
of the motion** at time $t$ is the map
$p\mapsto v(t,p)$ assigning to a spatial point the velocity of the material
point currently placed there, defined on the image of the placement. Neither
the configuration nor the placement by itself asserts a dynamics: the pair
$(c,R)$ is a description of the position and orientation of the body, and the
material velocity is its kinematic derivative.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following **rigid-material
model** branch, in the spacetime and frames of [[post-cm01-spacetime]] and
[[post-cm01-frames]].

**(i) Reference mass distribution.** A rigid-material model carries, besides
the framework's time and frame structure, a **reference mass distribution**: a
measure $\nu$ on the Borel space $(\mathbb R^3,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3))$ that
is a mass distribution in the sense of
[[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]] — finite and bounded, with
$\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline B_R(0)\bigr)=0$ for some real $R>0$,
and of total mass $m:=\nu(\mathbb R^3)\in(0,+\infty)$ — whose reference
coordinates are **centred**,
$$\int\rho\,d\nu(\rho)=0\in\mathbb R^3 .$$
The label variable $\rho$ is a coordinate of the model's reference placement
and has dimension $\ell$, each component read in metres; the total mass $m$
has dimension $\mu$, read in kilograms, and $R$ has dimension $\ell$ and is
the model's **reference size**
([[def-cm01-units]]). Under the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$,
used only through [[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]] to make the polynomial
moments of $\nu$ of degree at most two finite, the first and second moments
of $\nu$ are finite real numbers. The measure $\nu$ and the number $m$ are
model data: no distribution of mass of any concrete body and no measured mass
is asserted.

**(ii) Time window and motions.** A model carries a **time window**
$I_0\subseteq\mathbb R$, a nondegenerate open interval $(a,b)$ with
$-\infty\le a<b\le+\infty$ and at least two points, read in seconds. Fix an
**inertial frame** of the model, that is the adapted chart
$(o,u,(e_1,e_2,e_3))$ with coordinates $(t,x)$ of [[post-cm01-frames]]. A
**motion** of the model in this frame is a map
$x:I_0\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ for which there exist a map
$c:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ and a map $R:I_0\to SO(3)$, both of class $C^2$
(componentwise derivatives, [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] for the coordinates
and [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]] for the target), such that
$$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho\qquad(t\in I_0,\ \rho\in\mathbb R^3).$$
Adopt: the motions of the model are the maps of this form, and the pair
$(c,R)$ is the **configuration path** of the motion. The map
$x(t,\cdot):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is the **placement** at time $t$ and is
the rigid placement of [[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]]
with translation $c$ and rotation $R$; its material velocity is
$\partial_tx(t,\rho)=c'(t)+R'(t)\rho$, defined by differentiability of $c$ and
of the entries of $R$. The time window $I_0$ is the interval on which the
model's configuration path is considered; the model's time coordinate is
the frame time $t$.

**(iii) Rigidity idealization.** The idealization adopted is that the model
describes a body that does not deform, and its content is the representation
(ii): a placement of the form $x=c+R\rho$ with $R\in SO(3)$ preserves every
mutual distance, since $R(t)$ preserves the Euclidean norm
([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]), so for all $\rho,\rho'\in\mathbb R^3$
the number $\lVert x(t,\rho)-x(t,\rho')\rVert_2=\lVert\rho-\rho'\rVert_2$ is
independent of $t$. The model class (ii) is *adopted* as the definition of a
rigid-material placement; a motion of material points that preserves all
mutual distances but whose label set fails to determine a rotation is not
claimed to be of this form, and the general characterization of
distance-preserving placements is neither asserted nor used on this page.
For a **nondegenerate labeling** — a label set containing the origin and two
linearly independent material vectors — distinct configurations $(c,R)$ and
$(\bar c,\bar R)$ give distinct placements, by [[lem-cm-rigid-labeling-stabilizer]];
the configuration data of (ii) therefore do not overcount for such a body.
Degenerate labelings and degenerate mass distributions are not excluded by
this postulate; the later items of the pair state where invertibility of the
inertial data must be assumed.

**(iv) Centre of mass and orientation.** Because the reference coordinates are
centred, the identity
$$\int x(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho)=mc(t)$$
holds for every motion, by linearity of the integral and
$\int\rho\,d\nu=0$; the physical reading is that $c(t)$ is the position of the
centre of mass of the model in the placement at time $t$. The rotation
$R(t)$ is the model's **orientation**: it carries reference coordinates into
the frame's spatial coordinates, and the **body-fixed frame** at time $t$ is
the ordered orthonormal basis $(R(t)e_1,R(t)e_2,R(t)e_3)$ of the spatial
space. The reading of $R(t)$ as the orientation of the placement uses the
nondegeneracy of (iii): for a nondegenerate labeling the material points
determine $R(t)$ uniquely, so the orientation is an attribute of the body's
placement and not of the choice of label coordinates.

**(v) Frame changes.** The description of a motion in a second inertial frame
is obtained by the change of coordinates $t'=t+b$, $x'=Qx+ut+a$ of
[[post-cm01-frames]] clause (iv), applied to every event of the motion; here
$Q\in SO(3)$ and $u\in\mathbb R^3$ are the rotation and the boost velocity of
that clause, written $R$ and $v$ there and renamed here to avoid a clash with
the orientation path $R(t)$ of clause (ii) and with the material velocity
field of the pair's definition. With the same $\rho$ labelling a material
point, the description in the second frame is
$$\tilde x(t',\rho):=Q\,x(t'-b,\rho)+u\,(t'-b)+a .$$
This description is again a motion of the model, with configuration path
$$\tilde c(t')=Qc(t'-b)+u\,(t'-b)+a,\qquad \tilde R(t')=Q\,R(t'-b),$$
because $SO(3)$ is closed under multiplication
([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]); this is a consistency requirement of
the model's frame language, exactly as for the particle worldlines of
[[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (ii). The derived transformation laws of the
angular velocity, of the inertia data and of the kinetic splitting are
theorems of this pair's page, not part of this postulate.

**(vi) No dynamics.** This postulate fixes the kinematic class of the model
and its mass data only. It asserts no force law, no torque law, no equation of
motion for the pair $(c,R)$, and no balance or conservation law; in
particular the model does not by itself constrain the configuration path,
and the effect of forces and torques on a body is a separate model
assumption. It also asserts no measured value of any mass, length, duration
or orientation.

**(vii) Scope and exclusions.** The branch excludes deformation, internal
degrees of freedom such as temperature, chemical state or an independent spin
variable, variable mass, ablation and impact events, contact, friction and
dissipative constitutive laws, and any relativistic or quantum description.
It excludes bodies whose mass distribution is not a bounded finite Borel
measure of the stated kind. A rigid-material model is not a system of
finitely many particle labels: the continuum measure $\nu$ carries the mass
data of the model, and the situations of point masses are the special cases
of measures supported on finitely many points. All physical statements about
the model weight material points by $\nu$; properties of $\nu$-null sets of
labels are not physical properties of the body.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), carried through [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]
clause (i) and [[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] for finite mass moments, through
[[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]] and [[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (i)
for the finite inertial integrals, and through the double-cover supplier of
[[def-cm-quaternion-rotation-map-and-cover]] (its second remark) for the
surjectivity used to choose an initial unit quaternion. Adopt a **nondegenerate** model of the
rigid-material branch [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: a reference mass
distribution $\nu$ with total mass $m$, centred reference coordinates and no
line through the origin carrying the whole mass
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] clause (a)). Fix an orthonormal principal basis
$(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ with $Ie_{j}=I_{j}e_{j}$ and $I_{j}>0$
([[pthm-cm10-principal-axes]] clauses (a) and (d)), use the model in the
**torque-free** branch of [[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iv), and fix
an index $j\in\{1,2,3\}$ and a rate $\Omega\in\mathbb R$. Use the model's nondegenerate open
time window $I_0$ ([[def-interval]] and
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] clause (ii)), and fix a time $t_{0}\in I_0$ and an orientation
$R_{0}\in SO(3)$. Then:

1. **Existence of the uniform rotation.** There is a path
   $R:I_0\to SO(3)$ of class $C^{1}$ with $R(t_{0})=R_{0}$ and
   $$R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)=[\Omega e_{j}]_\times\qquad(t\in I_0),$$
   that is, with constant body angular velocity $\omega\equiv\Omega e_{j}$
   ([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]] clause (a)).
2. **It is a torque-free motion.** For every such path $R$ and every curve
   $c:I_0\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{2}$, the map
   $x(t,\rho):=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ is a motion of the torque-free model of the
   branch: its angular momentum about the centre of mass is
   $$L_c(t)=\Omega I_{j}\,R(t)e_{j},$$
   it is constant on $I_0$, and the adopted balance $L_c'=0$ holds. (Here $R$
   is automatically of class $C^{2}$, because $R'=R[\Omega e_{j}]_\times$ is
   the product of the $C^{1}$ curve $R$ with a constant matrix, so the
   configuration path $(c,R)$ has the regularity required of a motion.)
3. **Geometry and invariants.** In the motions of clause 2 one has
   $l=I\omega=\Omega I_{j}e_{j}$ constant,
   $$C=\lVert L_c\rVert_2^{2}=\Omega^{2}I_{j}^{2},\qquad E=\tfrac12\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\tfrac12\Omega^{2}I_{j};$$
   if $\Omega\neq0$, define the spatial line of the body-fixed axis by
   $\ell_j(t):=\{c(t)+sR(t)e_j:s\in\mathbb R\}$ and its unit direction by
   $n_j(t):=R(t)e_j$. Then $n_j(t)=L_c/(\Omega I_j)$ for every $t$, so this
   direction is **fixed in the inertial frame** and the spatial angular
   velocity $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t):=R(t)\omega(t)=\Omega n_j$ of
   [[def-cm10-angular-velocity]] clause (b) is constant; the line
   $\ell_j(t)$ need not be fixed because $c$ is arbitrary. If $\Omega=0$,
   then $R$ is constant on $I_0$.
4. **Converse classification.** Conversely, let a motion of a nondegenerate
   torque-free model have **constant** body angular velocity
   $\omega\equiv\omega_{0}$ on its time window. Then
   $I\omega_{0}=\lambda\omega_{0}$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb R$: either
   $\omega_{0}=0$ and the orientation path is constant, or $\omega_{0}\neq0$
   and $\omega_{0}$ lies along a principal axis; in the latter case an orthonormal principal basis can be chosen with one vector $e_j=\omega_0/\|\omega_0\|_2$ and $\Omega=\|\omega_0\|_2\ne0$, and the conclusions of clauses 2 and 3 hold in that adapted basis. It can be made positively oriented by negating a different basis vector. No alignment with the initially fixed basis is asserted when eigenvalues repeat.

The statement is conditional on the adopted model and zero-torque balance; it
asserts no force, no measurement and no empirical law, and the existence
clause is a statement about the model's kinematic class, not about nature.

Let $\mathbb H$ be the quaternion algebra with its product, conjugation $x\mapsto\bar x$, real-valued norm $N:\mathbb H\to\mathbb R$, and real embedding $r\mapsto\hat r=(r,0,0,0)$, in the notation of [[def-quaternions]]. Thus $x=x_0+x_1i+x_2j+x_3k$ with the multiplication formula of [[def-quaternions]], and

$$N(x)=x_0^2+x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2,\qquad \widehat{N(x)}=x\bar x=\bar x x.$$

In particular, $N(x)>0$ for $x\ne0$, and the imported division-ring theorem gives the typed inverse formula $x^{-1}=\widehat{N(x)^{-1}}\,\bar x$ ([[thm-quaternions-form-a-division-ring]]). Under the identification of $\mathbb H$ with $\mathbb R^4$ by the coordinates $x_0,\dots,x_3$ one has $N(x)=\|x\|_2^2$ for the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

**Imaginary quaternions and the vector identification.** Put

$$\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H:=\{x\in\mathbb H:\bar x=-x\}=\mathbb Ri\oplus\mathbb Rj\oplus\mathbb Rk,\qquad \varphi:\mathbb R^3\to\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H,\quad \varphi(v_1,v_2,v_3):=v_1i+v_2j+v_3k .$$

Then $\varphi$ is a linear isomorphism with $N(\varphi(v))=\|v\|_2^2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^3$. Throughout the collection, $\varphi$ translates between vectors of $\mathbb R^3$ (their inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$, norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ and cross product) and imaginary quaternions inside quaternion products.

**The unit sphere.** Define

$$S^3:=\{q\in\mathbb H:N(q)=1\},$$

the unit sphere of $\mathbb H\cong\mathbb R^4$. The identification of $S^3$ with $SU(2)$ is the one of the published covering example `ex-su-two-to-so-three-as-a-covering-homomorphism`, which is also the source of the covering statement recorded in the second remark below; that example is linked from the page summary of this pair.

**Conjugation and the rotation map.** For $q\in\mathbb H$ with $q\ne0$ let $c_q:\mathbb H\to\mathbb H$ be

$$c_q(x):=qxq^{-1}=qx\,\widehat{N(q)^{-1}}\,\bar q,$$

where the real scalar is embedded by $r\mapsto\hat r$, and define

$$\rho(q):=c_q|_{\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H}:\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H\longrightarrow\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H .$$

Both the $\mathbb R$-linear map $\rho(q)$ and its matrix in the ordered basis $(i,j,k)$ of $\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H$ are written $\rho(q)$; the equality $\rho(q)\in SO(3)$ for $q\in S^3$ is part of the cited covering statement, and the matrix is the one meant whenever $\rho(q)$ is composed with the identifications above. The map $\rho$ itself is never linear in $q$ and no such structure is used.

**Quaternion lifts.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let $R:I\to SO(3)$ be a map, with $SO(3)$ as in [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]. A **quaternion lift** of $R$ is a map $q:I\to S^3$ with $\rho(q(t))=R(t)$ for every $t\in I$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: The positively oriented principal basis has a basis matrix $Q\in SO(3)$; the skew/cross correspondence of [L5] gives $Q(u\times v)=(Qu)\times(Qv)$, so $l\mapsto l\times(I^{-1}l)$ is the supplier's positive diagonal field in those coordinates. Clause 1 of [L2] gives for $j=1$ and $j=3$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ a $\delta\in(0,\varepsilon]$ such that every maximal solution with $\lVert l(0)-Le_{j}\rVert_2<\delta$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $\lVert l(t)-Le_{j}\rVert_2<\varepsilon$; by [L1] a maximal solution is a solution defined on $\mathbb R$, so this is exactly the Lyapunov stability of $Le_{j}$ for the $l$-system, and the equilibrium property $F(Le_{j})=0$ holds by the alternation of the cross product in [L5].

The functions $D_{1}$ and $D_{3}$ of clause 2 are nonnegative, since in the principal basis with $l=\sum_{k}l_{k}e_{k}$ one has $D_{1}(l)=\tfrac12\sum_{k}(1/I_{1}-1/I_{k})l_{k}^{2}$ and $D_{3}(l)=\tfrac12\sum_{k}(1/I_{k}-1/I_{3})l_{k}^{2}$ with all coefficients nonnegative by $I_{1}<I_{2}<I_{3}$; and $2D_{1}(l)\ge(1/I_{1}-1/I_{2})(l_{2}^{2}+l_{3}^{2})$ and $2D_{3}(l)\ge(1/I_{2}-1/I_{3})(l_{1}^{2}+l_{2}^{2})$ because the remaining coefficients are at least these. By [L1] the two combinations $\langle l,l\rangle$ and $\langle l,I^{-1}l\rangle$ are constant along every solution, so $D_{1}$ and $D_{3}$ are constant along solutions and the two displayed inequalities of clause 2 follow.

Fix an admissible prescribed $\eta$ from clause 3. Let a torque-free motion have time window containing $[0,\infty)$ and datum with $\lVert l(0)-Le_{j}\rVert_2<\delta$, $j\in\{1,3\}$, for the $\delta$ of step 1.1. Let $l:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{3}$ be the global solution of the $l$-system with datum $l(0)=l^{\eta}$ (global by [L1]), and put $\omega:=I^{-1}l$, which is continuous and of class $C^{1}$ because $l$ solves a locally Lipschitz equation; by [L4] there is a $C^{2}$ rotation path $R:\mathbb R\to SO(3)$ with body angular velocity $\omega$, with any prescribed initial orientation $R(0)=R_0\in SO(3)$ by choosing a preimage $q_0$ of $R_0$. citations.quote:
Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following **heavy symmetric
top branch** of the rigid-material model, in the setting of
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]].

**(i) Setting.** A model of the branch carries the data of
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: a reference mass distribution $\nu$ with total
mass $m>0$ and centred reference coordinates, a time window $I_0$, an
inertial frame with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]),
whose origin is chosen at the pivot point of clause (iii), and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^{2}$
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]). Assume the Axiom of Countable
Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), used only through the
integrals of the model's inertial quantities. Fix once and for all an
orthonormal basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ of the reference coordinates.

**(ii) Axisymmetry and the declared parameters.** The body inertia matrix of
the model ([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] clause (a)) is
$$I=A_{c}\,(e_{1}e_{1}^{\mathsf T}+e_{2}e_{2}^{\mathsf T})+C_{c}\,e_{3}e_{3}^{\mathsf T},\qquad A_{c}>0,\ C_{c}>0,$$
so that $e_{3}$ is the **symmetry axis**; the numbers $A_{c}$, $C_{c}$ are
declared model parameters of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}$, read in kilogram metres
squared, and are not measured within the framework. The branch also declares
a **pivot distance** $d>0$ of dimension $\ell$ and a **field strength**
$g>0$ of dimension $\ell\tau^{-2}$, read in metres per second squared
([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(iii) The pivot constraint.** The material point of reference coordinate
$\rho_{p}:=-d\,e_{3}$ is the **pivot material point**; it lies on the
symmetry axis at distance $d$ from the centre of mass. The motions of the
branch are those satisfying
$$c(t)+R(t)\rho_{p}=0\qquad(t\in I_{0}),$$
    that is $c(t)=d\,R(t)e_{3}$: the pivot material point is held fixed at the
    origin of the inertial frame for the whole time window, and the centre of
    mass lies on the sphere of radius $d$ about the origin. The
constraint is maintained by a mechanism (a bearing, a hinge or a fine
support) whose force system is **ideal** in the sense adopted for
frictionless hinges in [[post-cm06-ideal-reaction-law]] clause (iii) together
with the virtual-work law of its clause (i): the mechanism exerts on the body
a force system equivalent to a single force applied at the pivot point, so
that its total torque about the origin **vanishes**. The holonomic-constraint
vocabulary of [[def-cm06-holonomic-constraint-model]] — constrained curve
families, reaction fields and the declaration that the constraint is
maintained by an additional force contribution — is the framework's account
for finitely many particle labels; the present model is a continuum, and this
clause adopts the analogous idealisation for it. No friction, damping or
driving torque at the pivot is asserted; such torques are excluded and would
have to be declared as part of a torque datum with their own model.

**(iv) The uniform gravitational field.** The model declares a **uniform
gravitational acceleration** $G:=-g\,e_{3}$ of dimension $\ell\tau^{-2}$:
every material point of the body is subject to the external force
$G\,d\nu$, that is, the force per unit mass is the constant vector $-g e_{3}$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] for the
spatial vectors). The field is a model idealisation: it asserts neither a
particular direction in any absolute sense (the direction $e_{3}$ is a
declared frame direction) nor a measured value of $g$, and it is not
asserted to represent the Earth's or any planet's field. The resultant of
this force system and its total torque about a point are computed in
the reduction theorem of this page; in particular the resultant is the total weight
$-mg e_{3}$ applied at the centre of mass.

**(v) The adopted dynamics.** Along every motion of the branch adopt the
**balance of angular momentum about the pivot**: with
$$J_{p}(t):=\int\bigl(x(t,\rho)-0\bigr)\times\partial_{t}x(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho)$$
the angular momentum of the model about the origin, and with $\tau_{p}(t)$
the total external torque about the origin — the sum of the gravitational
torque and of the pivot reaction torque, the latter vanishing by clause
(iii) — adopt
$$J_{p}'(t)=\tau_{p}(t)\qquad(t\in I_{0}).$$
This is an adopted dynamical law of the branch, analogous to but distinct
from the balance of [[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iii) about the
centre of mass; it acquires content only together with the kinematic
constraint of clause (iii) and the external force system of clause (iv). No
equation of motion for the pivot reaction is asserted: the reaction is
whatever force the ideal mechanism supplies, and its torque about the origin
is zero by clause (iii).

**(vi) Scope and exclusions.** The branch excludes non-axisymmetric bodies
($A_{c}$ and $C_{c}$ are the two transverse and the axial moment and no other
inertia data are used), bodies whose mass distribution fails to produce this
inertia matrix, non-uniform gravitational fields, friction and driving
torques at the pivot, rolling or sliding contacts, impacts, deformable
bodies and variable mass, and every relativistic or quantum description. It
asserts no force law for the pivot reaction, no conservation law and no
measured value of $A_{c}$, $C_{c}$, $m$, $d$ or $g$. Whether the branch is
adequate for a given apparatus — a top on a bearing, a gyroscope in a gimbal,
a spinning shell — is decided by comparing the model's conditional
predictions with reported observations of that apparatus under its stated
regime, and agreement is evidence about the combined model and apparatus, not
a proof of the idealisation.

**(vii) Relation to the other balances.** The balance of clause (v) is not
claimed to be a consequence of the centre-of-mass balance of
[[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iii), nor conversely; the two are
separate adopted laws about different points, and neither is deduced from the
framework's particle balances. A model may use both simultaneously, and the
reduction theorem of this page uses only clause (v) together with clauses
(ii)-(iv).

Adopt the model data, the time window $I_0$, the inertial frame and the
notation of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: the reference mass distribution
$\nu$ with total mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates, and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^2$.

**(a) Configuration and configuration space.** The **configuration** of the
model at time $t$ in the frame is the pair $(c(t),R(t))$; the pair
$(c,R)$ is a **configuration path**. The **configuration space** of the model
is the set
$$\mathcal C:=\mathbb R^3\times SO(3),$$
read through the identification of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ with $\mathbb R^{9}$
([[def-matrix-space]]) so that $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathbb R^{12}$. The
configuration determines the placement $x=c+R\,\cdot$ at that time, and the
reference placement is $(c,R)=(0,I_3)$. Under the identification of
$M_3(\mathbb R)$ with $\mathbb R^{9}$, the group $SO(3)$ is a compact
three-dimensional embedded submanifold of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ and a subgroup of
the general linear group ([[lem-cm-so3-is-a-compact-three-dimensional-embedded-submanifold]]
clauses 1 and 3, [[lem-cm-so3-is-a-matrix-group]]); consequently
$\mathcal C=\mathbb R^3\times SO(3)$ is a six-dimensional smooth manifold
with the product structure. Its dimension $3+3=6$ is read as three
translation coordinates of $c$ and three orientation degrees of freedom of
$R$; the model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] has no other configuration
degrees of freedom, since deformation and internal variables are excluded by
that postulate.

**(b) Centre of mass, orientation, body frame.** Because
$\int\rho\,d\nu=0$, the configuration's translation is the position of the
centre of mass of the model,
$\int x(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho)=mc(t)$. The rotation $R(t)$ is the **orientation**
of the model at time $t$: the linear map that carries reference coordinates
into the frame's spatial coordinates, so that a material point whose
reference coordinate is $\rho$ is found at the spatial position $x(t,\rho)$.
The **body-fixed frame** at time $t$ is the ordered orthonormal basis
$(R(t)e_1,R(t)e_2,R(t)e_3)$ of the spatial space, obtained by applying the
orientation to the standard basis; the basis is $g$-orthonormal because
$R(t)\in O(3)$ preserves the Euclidean inner product
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]). The
material point of reference coordinate $\rho$ has **spatial position**
$x(t,\rho)$ and **reference coordinates** $\rho$.

**(c) Physical labels and faithfulness.** The **physical label set** is
$S:=\operatorname{supp}\nu$, defined here as the complement of the union of
all open $\nu$-null subsets of $\mathbb R^3$. Thus $\rho\in S$ exactly when
every open neighbourhood of $\rho$ has positive mass. This is a closed set
carrying all mass: the rational open boxes form a countable basis
([[thm-rational-points-and-boxes-in-rn]], $n=3$), so its complement is the
union of the countably many null basis boxes. Disjointifying this union and
using countable additivity ([[def-measure]]) gives $\nu(\mathbb R^3\setminus S)=0$.
In particular $S\neq\varnothing$ because $m>0$.

If two configurations satisfy $c+R\rho=\bar c+\bar R\rho$ for every
$\rho\in S$, integration against the centred measure gives $mc=m\bar c$,
hence $c=\bar c$. Their exact orientation ambiguity is therefore
$$\bar R^{-1}R\in\operatorname{Stab}_{SO(3)}(S):=\{H\in SO(3):H\rho=\rho\text{ for every }\rho\in S\},$$
the pointwise stabilizer of [[lem-cm-rigid-labeling-stabilizer]]. Conversely,
$c=\bar c$ and this stabilizer condition give equality of the placements on
$S$ by multiplication. A **nondegenerate physical labeling** is one whose
$S$ contains two linearly independent vectors; its stabilizer is $\{I_3\}$
by that lemma, so the physical placement determines $(c,R)$ uniquely.
The same injectivity conclusion holds for any auxiliary label set containing
the origin and two independent vectors, by evaluation at the origin followed
by the lemma, as in [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] clause (iii).

A **degenerate physical labeling** has no two independent vectors. If
$S$ contains a nonzero vector $u$, then $S\subseteq\mathbb Ru$, and its
stabilizer is exactly $\{H\in SO(3):Hu=u\}$, the rotations fixing the line
$\mathbb Ru$ pointwise; the orientation is determined only up to right
composition with this subgroup. If $S$ contains no nonzero vector, then
$S=\{0\}$ and its stabilizer is all of $SO(3)$. More generally a singleton
support $\{q\}$ must have $q=0$, since centring gives $mq=0$.
Thus a centred point mass has no distinguished orientation axis. These are
all the degenerate cases: after choosing any nonzero $u\in S$, failure of
independence forces every vector in $S$ to be a multiple of $u$.
Configuration pairs remain model data in every case, including orientation
data invisible in the placed physical labels.

**(d) Description in another inertial frame.** Let a second inertial frame be
related to the first by the transformation $t'=t+b$, $x'=Qx+ut+a$ of
[[post-cm01-frames]] clause (iv), with $b\in\mathbb R$, $a,u\in\mathbb R^3$
and $Q\in SO(3)$
([[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]] clause 1); the letters
$Q$ and $u$ are the rotation and the boost velocity written $R$ and $v$ in
[[post-cm01-frames]], renamed to avoid clashes with the orientation path
$R(t)$ and the material velocity field of clause (e). The
**description of the same motion in the second frame** assigns to the same
material label $\rho$ the events of the motion in the new coordinates,
$$\tilde x(t',\rho):=Q\,x(t'-b,\rho)+u\,(t'-b)+a .$$
Substituting $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ and using distributivity of the matrix
product over sums expresses the description as a motion of the same model in
the second frame, with configuration path
$$\tilde c(t')=Qc(t'-b)+u\,(t'-b)+a,\qquad \tilde R(t')=Q\,R(t'-b),$$
where $\tilde R(t')\in SO(3)$ for every $t'$ because $SO(3)$ is closed under
matrix multiplication ([[lem-cm-so3-is-a-matrix-group]]); the pair
$(\tilde c,\tilde R)$ is again of class $C^2$. This description is a
convention forced by the frame change,
not a dynamical statement; the transformation laws of the velocity field, the
angular velocity and the inertia data are proved in the frame-covariance
theorem of this page.

**(e) Material velocities.** For a motion with configuration path $(c,R)$, the
**material velocity** of the label $\rho$ at time $t$ is the derivative
$$\partial_tx(t,\rho):=c'(t)+R'(t)\rho,$$
which exists by differentiability of $c$ and of the entries of $R$
([[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]]). The **velocity field
of the motion** at time $t$ is the map
$p\mapsto v(t,p)$ assigning to a spatial point the velocity of the material
point currently placed there, defined on the image of the placement. Neither
the configuration nor the placement by itself asserts a dynamics: the pair
$(c,R)$ is a description of the position and orientation of the body, and the
material velocity is its kinematic derivative.

Adopt the model, inertial frame and notation of
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] and [[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]], and
let a motion $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ have configuration path $(c,R)$ of
class $C^2$ on the time window $I_0$ ([[def-interval]]).

**(a) Body angular velocity.** By
[[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]], the matrix
$R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)$ is skew-symmetric at every $t\in I_0$
([[lem-cm-matrix-curve-derivative-rules]] clause 3), and by
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]] clause 2 there is exactly
one vector $\omega(t)\in\mathbb R^3$ with
$$R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)=[\omega(t)]_\times .$$
The map $\omega:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ is the **body angular velocity** of the
motion. Since $R$ is of class $C^2$, the entries of $R^{\mathsf T}R'$ are
differentiable and hence $\omega$ is of class $C^1$; its derivative is the
**body angular acceleration**. The dimension is $[\omega]=\tau^{-1}$
([[def-cm01-units]]), read in radians per second under the radian convention,
in which angles are dimensionless.

**(b) Spatial angular velocity.** The **spatial angular velocity** of the
motion is
$$\omega_{\mathrm s}(t):=R(t)\omega(t)\in\mathbb R^3,$$
of the same dimension $\tau^{-1}$. By the conjugation clause of
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]],
$R'(t)R(t)^{\mathsf T}=[\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)]_\times$; this is the
space-frame rate matrix of the motion.

**(c) Material velocity field.** For every material label $\rho$,
$$\partial_tx(t,\rho)=c'(t)+R(t)\bigl(\omega(t)\times\rho\bigr),$$
because $R'(t)=R(t)[\omega(t)]_\times$ and
$[\omega]_\times\rho=\omega\times\rho$
([[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]],
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]] clause 1). Writing
$p=x(t,\rho)$ for the spatial position of the label and using
$R(\omega\times\rho)=(R\omega)\times(R\rho)$, the same identity reads
$$\partial_tx(t,\rho)=c'(t)+\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\times\bigl(p-c(t)\bigr):$$
the material velocity field is that of a translation $c'(t)$ composed with a
rotation of angular velocity $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ about the centre of mass
$c(t)$. The motion is a **pure translation** at time $t$ exactly when
$\omega(t)=0$, equivalently $R'(t)=0$; then every material velocity equals
$c'(t)$.

**(d) Uniqueness of the velocity data.** The velocity field determines
$c'(t)$ and $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ uniquely: if a motion has material
velocity field $p\mapsto v(t,p)=c'(t)+\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\times(p-c(t))$,
then evaluating at $p=c(t)$ gives $c'(t)=v(t,c(t))$, and for $u\in\mathbb R^3$
the difference $v(t,c(t)+u)-v(t,c(t))=\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\times u$ is a
linear map of $u$; testing it on two linearly independent vectors determines
$\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ by the injectivity clause of
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]], and then
$\omega(t)=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$. The pair
$\bigl(c'(t),\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\bigr)$ is therefore an intrinsic
description of the velocity field; the body angular velocity is its
description in the body-fixed frame, and the choice of reference coordinates
is part of the model data fixed in [[post-cm10-rigid-material]].

**(e) Instantaneous rotation axis.** If $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\neq0$, the line
$$\bigl\{c(t)+s\,\omega_{\mathrm s}(t):s\in\mathbb R\bigr\}$$
is the **instantaneous rotation axis** of the motion at time $t$: it is the
set of spatial points whose material velocity equals $c'(t)$, as follows from
$\omega_{\mathrm s}\times(\omega_{\mathrm s}s)=0$. Conversely, write
$w=\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ and $z=p-c(t)$. If $w\times z=0$, choose a
coordinate $i$ with $w_i\neq0$; the cross-product coordinate equations
([[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]] clause 1) give
$w_i z_j=w_j z_i$ for every $j$, hence $z=(z_i/w_i)w$.
This proves that the zero relative-velocity set is exactly the displayed
line. The velocity field is
constant on lines parallel to $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ and rotates about this
axis; if also $c'(t)=0$ at that instant, every point of the axis is
instantaneously at rest and the motion is an instantaneous rotation about it.
No claim is made that the axis is fixed in time or in space.

**(f) Conventions and scope.** The convention fixed here is the body-fixed
one of the cited mathematical definition: $\Omega=R^{\mathsf T}R'=[\omega]_\times$
and $R'=R\Omega$. A consumer using the space-fixed convention must state the
change, which is the rotation by $R$ recorded in (b); the two vectors agree
only when $R(t)$ fixes $\omega(t)$. Both vectors are kinematic quantities of
the motion: no torque, no angular momentum and no equation of motion for
$\omega$ is asserted, and no measured angular velocity is recorded. The
behaviour of $\omega$ under a change of inertial frame is proved in the
frame-covariance theorem of this page.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only to make the integrals below finite.
Adopt the model and notation of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: a reference
mass distribution $\nu$ with total mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates,
a fixed inertial frame, and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^{2}$ on
the time window $I_0$, body angular velocity $\omega$
([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]]) and body inertia matrix $I$
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]). Define the **total momentum**, **kinetic
energy** and **angular momentum about the centre of mass** of the model along
the motion by the componentwise integrals
$$P(t):=\int\partial_tx(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho),\qquad K(t):=\frac12\int\lVert\partial_tx(t,\rho)\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),$$
$$L_c(t):=\int\bigl(x(t,\rho)-c(t)\bigr)\times\bigl(\partial_tx(t,\rho)-c'(t)\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho),$$
with dimensions $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$, $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ and
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). Then for every $t\in I_0$:

1. the three integrands are $\nu$-integrable, so $P(t)$, $K(t)$ and
   $L_c(t)$ are a well-defined finite vector and finite real numbers;
2. $P(t)=m\,c'(t)$;
3. $K(t)=\dfrac12m\lVert c'(t)\rVert_2^{2}+\dfrac12\omega(t)^{\mathsf T}I\omega(t)$;
4. $L_c(t)=R(t)\,I\,\omega(t)$.

The identities hold for every $C^{2}$ configuration path; no equation of
motion, force law or conservation statement is used or asserted.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

u(\mathbb R^3)<+\infty$ and $

1. for all $j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$ the functions $ho\mapstoho_j$ and $ho\mapstoho_jho_k$ are Borel measurable and $

u\le R^2\,
u(\mathbb R^3)$;
2. consequently $m:=
u(\mathbb R^3)$ and the scalar integrals $\intho_j\,d

u)$ and inertia matrix $I(
u)$ of [[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]. When $m=0$, all these integrals vanish; the zero measure is not called a mass distribution.

Let $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3)$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) and let $
u$ be a measure on the measurable space $(\mathbb R^3,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3))$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-measure-space]]) that is **finite**, $
u(\mathbb R^3)<+\infty$, and **bounded**, meaning that there is a real $R>0$ with
$$
u igl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline B_R(0) igr)=0,$$
the closed ball being that of [[def-metric-ball]]. Throughout, integrals are Lebesgue integrals against $
u$ in the sense of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] and [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], and for a measurable vector- or matrix-valued function the integral is defined **componentwise**: $\int F\,d
u:= igl(\int F_1\,d
u,\int F_2\,d
u,\int F_3\,d
u igr)$ and $ igl(\int M\,d
u igr)_{jk}:=\int M_{jk}\,d
u$, whenever every displayed scalar integral is finite.

A **mass distribution on $\mathbb R^3$** is a bounded finite Borel measure $
u$ with $m:=
u(\mathbb R^3)\in(0,+\infty)$; the number $m$ is its **total mass**. Writing points of $\mathbb R^3$ as $ho$ and using the Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdotangle$ and norm $\lVerthoVert_2=\sqrt{\langleho,hoangle}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], define:

u):=\intho\,d
u\in\mathbb R^3$, read componentwise as $\mu(

2. the **inertia matrix** $I(

The mass distribution is **centred** when $\mu(
u)=0$. Under the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), each of the integrals above is a finite real number: on $\overline B_R(0)$ one has $|ho_j|\le R$ and $|ho_jho_k|\le R^2$, and $

The assumption is used there exactly once, to obtain the Borel measurability of the polynomial integrands from the published continuity criterion; every later item that invokes this finiteness carries the assumption explicitly.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following **heavy symmetric
top branch** of the rigid-material model, in the setting of
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]].

**(i) Setting.** A model of the branch carries the data of
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: a reference mass distribution $\nu$ with total
mass $m>0$ and centred reference coordinates, a time window $I_0$, an
inertial frame with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]),
whose origin is chosen at the pivot point of clause (iii), and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^{2}$
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]). Assume the Axiom of Countable
Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), used only through the
integrals of the model's inertial quantities. Fix once and for all an
orthonormal basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ of the reference coordinates.

**(ii) Axisymmetry and the declared parameters.** The body inertia matrix of
the model ([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] clause (a)) is
$$I=A_{c}\,(e_{1}e_{1}^{\mathsf T}+e_{2}e_{2}^{\mathsf T})+C_{c}\,e_{3}e_{3}^{\mathsf T},\qquad A_{c}>0,\ C_{c}>0,$$
so that $e_{3}$ is the **symmetry axis**; the numbers $A_{c}$, $C_{c}$ are
declared model parameters of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}$, read in kilogram metres
squared, and are not measured within the framework. The branch also declares
a **pivot distance** $d>0$ of dimension $\ell$ and a **field strength**
$g>0$ of dimension $\ell\tau^{-2}$, read in metres per second squared
([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(iii) The pivot constraint.** The material point of reference coordinate
$\rho_{p}:=-d\,e_{3}$ is the **pivot material point**; it lies on the
symmetry axis at distance $d$ from the centre of mass. The motions of the
branch are those satisfying
$$c(t)+R(t)\rho_{p}=0\qquad(t\in I_{0}),$$
    that is $c(t)=d\,R(t)e_{3}$: the pivot material point is held fixed at the
    origin of the inertial frame for the whole time window, and the centre of
    mass lies on the sphere of radius $d$ about the origin. The
constraint is maintained by a mechanism (a bearing, a hinge or a fine
support) whose force system is **ideal** in the sense adopted for
frictionless hinges in [[post-cm06-ideal-reaction-law]] clause (iii) together
with the virtual-work law of its clause (i): the mechanism exerts on the body
a force system equivalent to a single force applied at the pivot point, so
that its total torque about the origin **vanishes**. The holonomic-constraint
vocabulary of [[def-cm06-holonomic-constraint-model]] — constrained curve
families, reaction fields and the declaration that the constraint is
maintained by an additional force contribution — is the framework's account
for finitely many particle labels; the present model is a continuum, and this
clause adopts the analogous idealisation for it. No friction, damping or
driving torque at the pivot is asserted; such torques are excluded and would
have to be declared as part of a torque datum with their own model.

**(iv) The uniform gravitational field.** The model declares a **uniform
gravitational acceleration** $G:=-g\,e_{3}$ of dimension $\ell\tau^{-2}$:
every material point of the body is subject to the external force
$G\,d\nu$, that is, the force per unit mass is the constant vector $-g e_{3}$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] for the
spatial vectors). The field is a model idealisation: it asserts neither a
particular direction in any absolute sense (the direction $e_{3}$ is a
declared frame direction) nor a measured value of $g$, and it is not
asserted to represent the Earth's or any planet's field. The resultant of
this force system and its total torque about a point are computed in
the reduction theorem of this page; in particular the resultant is the total weight
$-mg e_{3}$ applied at the centre of mass.

**(v) The adopted dynamics.** Along every motion of the branch adopt the
**balance of angular momentum about the pivot**: with
$$J_{p}(t):=\int\bigl(x(t,\rho)-0\bigr)\times\partial_{t}x(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho)$$
the angular momentum of the model about the origin, and with $\tau_{p}(t)$
the total external torque about the origin — the sum of the gravitational
torque and of the pivot reaction torque, the latter vanishing by clause
(iii) — adopt
$$J_{p}'(t)=\tau_{p}(t)\qquad(t\in I_{0}).$$
This is an adopted dynamical law of the branch, analogous to but distinct
from the balance of [[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iii) about the
centre of mass; it acquires content only together with the kinematic
constraint of clause (iii) and the external force system of clause (iv). No
equation of motion for the pivot reaction is asserted: the reaction is
whatever force the ideal mechanism supplies, and its torque about the origin
is zero by clause (iii).

**(vi) Scope and exclusions.** The branch excludes non-axisymmetric bodies
($A_{c}$ and $C_{c}$ are the two transverse and the axial moment and no other
inertia data are used), bodies whose mass distribution fails to produce this
inertia matrix, non-uniform gravitational fields, friction and driving
torques at the pivot, rolling or sliding contacts, impacts, deformable
bodies and variable mass, and every relativistic or quantum description. It
asserts no force law for the pivot reaction, no conservation law and no
measured value of $A_{c}$, $C_{c}$, $m$, $d$ or $g$. Whether the branch is
adequate for a given apparatus — a top on a bearing, a gyroscope in a gimbal,
a spinning shell — is decided by comparing the model's conditional
predictions with reported observations of that apparatus under its stated
regime, and agreement is evidence about the combined model and apparatus, not
a proof of the idealisation.

**(vii) Relation to the other balances.** The balance of clause (v) is not
claimed to be a consequence of the centre-of-mass balance of
[[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iii), nor conversely; the two are
separate adopted laws about different points, and neither is deduced from the
framework's particle balances. A model may use both simultaneously, and the
reduction theorem of this page uses only clause (v) together with clauses
(ii)-(iv).

Adopt the model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: the reference mass
distribution $\nu$, its total mass $m=\nu(\mathbb R^3)$ and its centred
reference coordinates $\int\rho\,d\nu(\rho)=0$. Assume the Axiom of Countable
Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, used only through
[[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]] to make the polynomial moments of $\nu$ of
degree at most two finite real numbers. Fix an inertial frame and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^2$
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]).

**(a) Body inertia matrix.** The **body inertia matrix** of the model is the
inertia matrix of the reference mass distribution,
$$I:=I(\nu)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}I_3-\rho\rho^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
with entries $I_{jk}=\int(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}\delta_{jk}-\rho_j\rho_k)\,d\nu$
as in [[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]; the matrix is expressed
in the standard basis of the reference coordinates. Its entries are finite
real numbers, it is symmetric, and for every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)\ \ge 0$$
by [[lem-cm-inertia-matrix-properties]] clauses 1-2; hence $I$ is symmetric
and its quadratic form is positive semidefinite. The dimension is
$[I]=\mu\ell^{2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]), read in kilogram metres squared. The
model is **nondegenerate** when no line through the origin carries the whole
mass, that is $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega\bigr)>0$ for every
$\omega\neq0$, and **degenerate** otherwise; the connection between this
criterion and the strict positivity and invertibility of $I$ is proved in the
principal-axes theorem of this page.

**(b) Spatial inertia tensor at the centre of mass.** The **spatial inertia
tensor** of the model at time $t$ is
$$I(t):=R(t)\,I\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
the matrix of the same quadratic form in the frame's spatial coordinates: for
every $n\in\mathbb R^3$,
$n^{\mathsf T}I(t)n=(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)^{\mathsf T}I(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)$. Its
entries are $C^2$ functions of $t$, since $R$ is of class $C^2$ and $I$ is
constant; the matrix rotates with the body and returns to $I$ in the
body-fixed frame, where $R=I_3$.

**(c) Inertia tensor about a spatial point.** For a spatial point
$p\in\mathbb R^3$ let
$$a(t,p):=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\bigl(p-c(t)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^3$$
be the **reference coordinate of $p$**, that is the label of the material
point of the reference placement that is placed at $p$ at time $t$. The
**inertia tensor of the model about $p$** at time $t$ is
