$$I(t,p):=R(t)\,I_\nu\bigl(a(t,p)\bigr)\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
where
$$I_\nu(a)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho-a\rVert_2^{2}I_3-(\rho-a)(\rho-a)^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)$$
is the inertia tensor of the mass distribution about the point $a$ of the
reference coordinates ([[def-cm-inertia-tensor-about-a-point]]). Since the
label of a spatial point is uniquely determined by the placement, this is
well defined; for the centre of mass, $a(t,c(t))=0$ and
$I(t,c(t))=I(t)$. The dimension is again $\mu\ell^{2}$, read in kilogram
metres squared.

**(d) Moment of inertia about an axis.** Let $\ell$ be a spatial line at time
$t$, given by a point $p\in\mathbb R^3$ and a unit direction $n\in\mathbb R^3$
($\lVert n\rVert_2=1$). The **moment of inertia of the model about $\ell$** is
$$\Theta_\ell(t):=n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n .$$
Its invariance under the choices entering the description of the line and
its identification with the integral defining the physical moment of inertia
about the line are statements, not conventions; they are proved in clause
(c) of the principal-axes theorem of this page. For a **body-fixed
axis**, that is a line through the centre of mass whose direction in
reference coordinates is a constant unit vector $n_0$, the moment is
$$n_0^{\mathsf T}I n_0=\int\lVert n_0\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),$$
by clause (a), and is independent of time, because $I$ and $n_0$ are model
data.

**(e) What is constant and what moves.** The body inertia matrix $I$ is
determined by the model's reference mass distribution alone and does not
depend on the time, the frame or the motion; the spatial inertia tensor
$I(t)$ depends on the motion through the orientation $R(t)$; the inertia
tensor $I(t,p)$ about a spatial point depends on the motion through both the
orientation and the position of $p$. Principal axes and principal moments of
$I$ are the subject of the principal-axes theorem of this page.

Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points, let $\varphi,\theta,\psi:J\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable with $\theta(J)\subseteq(0,\pi)$, and put
$$R(t):=\Theta\bigl(\varphi(t),\theta(t),\psi(t)\bigr)=R_z(\varphi(t))\,R_y(\theta(t))\,R_z(\psi(t)),$$
the Euler-angle parametrization of [[def-cm-euler-angle-parametrization-and-heavy-top-system]]. Then $R$ is a differentiable $SO(3)$-valued curve, and its **body angular velocity** $\omega:J\to\mathbb R^3$ in the sense of [[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]] (the unique vector with $R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)=[\omega(t)]_\times$) is, in the standard basis,
$$\omega=\bigl(-\varphi'\sin\theta\cos\psi+\theta'\sin\psi\bigr)e_1+\bigl(\varphi'\sin\theta\sin\psi+\theta'\cos\psi\bigr)e_2+\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)e_3,$$
all functions evaluated at $t$. Consequently
$$\omega_3=\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta,\qquad \omega_1^2+\omega_2^2=\theta'^2+\varphi'^2\sin^2\theta,\qquad \lVert\omega\rVert_2^2=\theta'^2+\varphi'^2\sin^2\theta+\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)^2.$$
Moreover, if $A,C>0$ and $I:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is the linear map with $Ie_1=Ae_1$, $Ie_2=Ae_2$, $Ie_3=Ce_3$, then $\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=A\bigl(\theta'^2+\varphi'^2\sin^2\theta\bigr)+C\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)^2$.

For $a\in\mathbb R$ define, in the standard basis of $\mathbb R^3$,
$$R_z(a):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos a&-\sin a&0\\ \sin a&\cos a&0\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad R_y(a):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos a&0&\sin a\\ 0&1&0\\ -\sin a&0&\cos a\end{pmatrix}\in M_3(\mathbb R).$$
Then:

1. $R_z(a)\in SO(3)$ and $R_y(a)\in SO(3)$ for every $a$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]), $R_z(a)e_3=e_3$ and $R_y(a)e_2=e_2$, and $R_z(0)=R_y(0)=I_3$.
2. $R_z(a)R_z(b)=R_z(a+b)$ and $R_y(a)R_y(b)=R_y(a+b)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$.
3. For every differentiable $a:I\to\mathbb R$ on an interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-derivative]], [[def-interval]]), the matrix-valued curves $t\mapsto R_z(a(t))$ and $t\mapsto R_y(a(t))$ are differentiable with $$(R_z\circ a)'=a'\,R_z(a)\,[e_3]_\times=a'\,[e_3]_\times R_z(a),\qquad (R_y\circ a)'=a'\,R_y(a)\,[e_2]_\times=a'\,[e_2]_\times R_y(a),$$ where $[e_3]_\times,[e_2]_\times$ are the cross-product matrices of [[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]].

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

**Euler-angle parametrization.** Let $R_z,R_y$ be the coordinate rotation matrices of [[lem-cm-coordinate-rotation-matrices]]. The **Euler-angle parametrization** is the map
$$\Theta:\mathbb R\times(0,\pi)\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow SO(3),\qquad \Theta(\varphi,\theta,\psi):=R_z(\varphi)\,R_y(\theta)\,R_z(\psi),$$
which is $SO(3)$-valued by [[lem-cm-coordinate-rotation-matrices]] and [[lem-cm-so3-is-a-matrix-group]]. The numbers $(\varphi,\theta,\psi)$ are the **Euler angles** and the open set $\mathbb R\times(0,\pi)\times\mathbb R$ is its **domain**; $\theta$ is restricted to the open interval $(0,\pi)$ so that $\sin\theta>0$, with $\pi$ defined as twice the smallest positive cosine zero ([[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]]) and positivity supplied by [[cor-pi-is-the-first-positive-sine-zero]]. No injectivity and no chart or diffeomorphism property of $\Theta$ is asserted or used here, and no periodicity of the angles is imposed — the real parameters stand for themselves.

**Parameters.** Fix reals $A>0$, $C>0$, $m>0$, $d>0$ and $g>0$; they are mathematical parameters, not identified with any physical quantity in this item.

**The heavy-top function.** Write $q=(\varphi,\theta,\psi)$ for a point of the domain and $v=(\varphi',\theta',\psi')$ for a triple of reals. The **heavy-top function** is
$$L(q,v):=\tfrac12A\bigl(\theta'^2+\varphi'^2\sin^2\theta\bigr)+\tfrac12C\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)^2-mgd\cos\theta,$$
using the sine and cosine of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]. Repeated application of the sine/cosine derivative identities ([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]]) and the finite sum, product and chain rules ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule]]) gives continuous partial derivatives of every order, so it is $C^\infty$ on the domain times $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); its relevant partial derivatives are, explicitly,
$$\partial_{\varphi'}L=A\varphi'\sin^2\theta+C\cos\theta\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr),\qquad \partial_\varphi L=0,$$
$$\partial_{\theta'}L=A\theta',\qquad \partial_\theta L=A\varphi'^2\sin\theta\cos\theta-C\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)\varphi'\sin\theta+mgd\sin\theta,$$
$$\partial_{\psi'}L=C\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr),\qquad \partial_\psi L=0.$$

**The heavy-top system.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points. A **heavy-top trajectory** for these parameters is a twice-differentiable curve $q=(\varphi,\theta,\psi):I\to\mathbb R\times(0,\pi)\times\mathbb R$ such that, with $q'=(\varphi',\theta',\psi')$ its derivative, the three second-order equations
$$\frac{d}{dt}\Bigl(A\varphi'\sin^2\theta+C\cos\theta\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)\Bigr)=0,\qquad \frac{d}{dt}\bigl(A\theta'\bigr)=A\varphi'^2\sin\theta\cos\theta-C\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)\varphi'\sin\theta+mgd\sin\theta,$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}\Bigl(C\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)\Bigr)=0$$
hold on $I$, all functions being evaluated at $t$. These displayed equations are the definition of the system; they are written out so that no separate definition of a variational principle is needed. The first and third are the statements that $\partial_{\varphi'}L$ and $\partial_{\psi'}L$ are constant along the trajectory.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points, let $t_0\in I$ and let $A,B:I\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be **differentiable at $t_0$**, meaning ([[def-matrix-space]]) that every entry function $t\mapsto A(t)_{ij}$ and $t\mapsto B(t)_{ij}$ is differentiable at $t_0$ in the sense of [[def-derivative]]; write $A'(t_0)$ for the matrix with entries $A'(t_0)_{ij}:=(t\mapsto A(t)_{ij})'(t_0)$, and similarly for $B$.

1. $A+B$ and $A^{\mathsf T}$ are differentiable at $t_0$, with $(A+B)'(t_0)=A'(t_0)+B'(t_0)$ and $(A^{\mathsf T})'(t_0)=(A'(t_0))^{\mathsf T}$.
2. $AB$ is differentiable at $t_0$, with $(AB)'(t_0)=A'(t_0)B(t_0)+A(t_0)B'(t_0)$.
3. If $A(t)\in SO(3)$ for every $t\in I$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]), then the matrix $A(t_0)^{\mathsf T}A'(t_0)$ is skew-symmetric, i.e. $(A^{\mathsf T}A')^{\mathsf T}=-A^{\mathsf T}A'$ at $t_0$, and likewise $A'(t_0)A(t_0)^{\mathsf T}$ is skew-symmetric. In particular the trace of each of these two matrices vanishes.

Use the standard basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ and coordinates $\omega=\omega_1e_1+\omega_2e_2+\omega_3e_3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], [[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Define the map $[\cdot]_\times:\mathbb R^3\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ by
$$[\omega]_\times:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\omega_3&\omega_2\\ \omega_3&0&-\omega_1\\ -\omega_2&\omega_1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then:

1. $[\omega]_\times z=\omega\times z$ for all $\omega,z\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].
2. $[\omega]_\times^{\mathsf T}=-[\omega]_\times$ for every $\omega$; the map $\omega\mapsto[\omega]_\times$ is linear and injective, and its image is exactly the set of skew-symmetric matrices of $M_3(\mathbb R)$. Consequently every skew-symmetric $\Omega\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ equals $[\omega]_\times$ for exactly one $\omega$, namely $\omega=(\Omega_{32},\Omega_{13},\Omega_{21})$.
3. For every $R\in SO(3)$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]) and every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$, $$R[\omega]_\times R^{\mathsf T}=[R\omega]_\times.$$

Let $M_3(\mathbb R)$ be the set of $3\times3$ matrices over $\mathbb R$ ([[def-matrix-space]]), with identity $I_3$ and product as in [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], transpose $R^{\mathsf T}$ as in [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]], and determinant $\det R$ as in [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]].

The **orthogonal group** and the **special orthogonal group** are the subsets

$$O(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\},\qquad SO(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\ \text{and}\ \det R=1\}.$$

Equivalently $SO(3)=O(3)\cap\{R:\det R=1\}$. Elements of $SO(3)$ are called **rotations**. The identification of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ with the function space $\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ and hence with $\mathbb R^9$ is the one of [[def-matrix-space]]; when $M_3(\mathbb R)$ is regarded as a metric or topological space, this is always the Euclidean metric of that identification.
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

derivations.claim: By [L1] the constraint gives $c(t)=dR(t)e_{3}$, and since $R$ is $C^{1}$ with $R'=R[\omega]_{\times}$ by [L6] one has $c'=dR'e_{3}=dR[\omega]_{\times}e_{3}=dR(\omega\times e_{3})$.

By [L4], reading the columns of the three factors and using $\theta(I_0)\subseteq(0,\pi)$, the vector $\gamma=R^{\mathsf T}e_{3}=R_{z}(\psi)^{\mathsf T}R_{y}(\theta)^{\mathsf T}R_{z}(\varphi)^{\mathsf T}e_{3}=R_{z}(-\psi)R_{y}(-\theta)e_{3}$ equals $R_{z}(-\psi)\bigl(-\sin\theta\,e_{1}+\cos\theta\,e_{3}\bigr)=\bigl(-\sin\theta\cos\psi,\ \sin\theta\sin\psi,\ \cos\theta\bigr)$, and $\omega_{3}=\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta$.

By [L1] the gravitational force system of the branch acts as the total force $-mge_{3}$ applied at the centre of mass, whose torque about the origin is $\tau_{p}=mc\times(-ge_{3})$; with $c=dRe_{3}$ from step 1.1 this is $\tau_{p}=-mgd(Re_{3})\times e_{3}$, and $\tau_{p}\cdot e_{3}=0$ because the cross product is orthogonal to its factors by [L6].

By [L2] one has $J_{p}=L_{c}+c\times P=RI\omega+mc\times c'$. Substituting $c=dRe_{3}$ and $c'=dR(\omega\times e_{3})$ from step 1.1 and using $I e_{3}=C e_{3}$, $Ie_{1}=A_{c}e_{1}$, $Ie_{2}=A_{c}e_{2}$ from [L3] gives $mc\times c'=md^{2}\,(Re_{3})\times R(\omega\times e_{3})=md^{2}R\bigl(e_{3}\times(\omega\times e_{3})\bigr)=md^{2}R(\omega-\omega_{3}e_{3})$ by [L6] and the vector triple product with $\lVert e_{3}\rVert_2=1$, so $J_{p}=R\bigl(I\omega+md^{2}(\omega-\omega_{3}e_{3})\bigr)=R\tilde I\omega$ with $\tilde I=\mathrm{diag}(A,A,C)$ and $A=A_{c}+md^{2}$, $C=C_{c}$. Hence the balance of [L1] reads $J_{p}'=\tau_{p}$ with $\tau_{p}$ as in step 2.1, completing clause 1.

Since $R$ is $C^{1}$ and $\omega$ is $C^{1}$, the product $\tilde I\omega$ is $C^{1}$ and $J_{p}=R\tilde I\omega$ from step 3.1 gives $R(\tilde I\omega'+\omega\times\tilde I\omega)=J_{p}'$ by [L6]; with the balance $J_{p}'=\tau_{p}$ of step 3.1 and $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_{3}$ one gets $\tilde I\omega'+\omega\times\tilde I\omega=R^{\mathsf T}\tau_{p}$. By step 2.1 and [L6], $R^{\mathsf T}\bigl((Re_{3})\times e_{3}\bigr)=e_{3}\times(R^{\mathsf T}e_{3})=e_{3}\times\gamma$ with $\gamma$ of step 1.2, so $\tilde I\omega'+\omega\times\tilde I\omega=-mgd(e_{3}\times\gamma)$. Componentwise, $(e_{3}\times\gamma)_{1}=-\gamma_{2}$, $(e_{3}\times\gamma)_{2}=\gamma_{1}$, $(e_{3}\times\gamma)_{3}=0$ and $(\omega\times\tilde I\omega)_{1}=(C-A)\omega_{2}\omega_{3}$, $(\omega\times\tilde I\omega)_{2}=(A-C)\omega_{1}\omega_{3}$, $(\omega\times\tilde I\omega)_{3}=0$, giving the three displayed equations of clause 2.

The third of the equations of step 4.1 gives $C\omega_{3}'=0$, and $C>0$, so $\omega_{3}$ is constant on the interval $I_0$ by [L6]; by step 1.2, $b=C(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta)=C\omega_{3}$ is constant on $I_0$.

By step 3.1 and [L6], $\frac{d}{dt}(J_{p}\cdot e_{3})=J_{p}'\cdot e_{3}=\tau_{p}\cdot e_{3}=0$ by step 2.1, so $J_{p}\cdot e_{3}$ is constant on $I_0$; and by steps 3.1 and 1.2, $J_{p}\cdot e_{3}=(R\tilde I\omega)\cdot e_{3}=\tilde I\omega\cdot\gamma=A(\omega_{1}\gamma_{1}+\omega_{2}\gamma_{2})+C\omega_{3}\gamma_{3}$. Substituting the components of [L4] and step 1.2 and using $\sin^{2}\psi+\cos^{2}\psi=1$ from [L4] gives $\omega_{1}\gamma_{1}+\omega_{2}\gamma_{2}=\varphi'\sin^{2}\theta$ and $\omega_{3}\gamma_{3}=(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta)\cos\theta$, so $J_{p}\cdot e_{3}=A\varphi'\sin^{2}\theta+b\cos\theta=a$ is constant on $I_0$.

Put $n:=\sin\psi\,e_{1}+\cos\psi\,e_{2}$, so that $n$ has $\lVert n\rVert_2=1$ and, by [L4] and $R'=R[\omega]_{\times}$, the identity $\theta'=\omega\cdot n$ holds. Differentiating $\theta'$ with [L6] gives $A\theta''=A(\omega'\cdot n)+A(\omega\cdot n')$, where $n'=\psi'(\cos\psi\,e_{1}-\sin\psi\,e_{2})$; using the first two equations of step 4.1, the components of [L4] and the values $\omega_{1}\cos\psi-\omega_{2}\sin\psi=-\varphi'\sin\theta$, $\omega_{2}\sin\psi-\omega_{1}\cos\psi=\varphi'\sin\theta$ and $\gamma_{2}\sin\psi-\gamma_{1}\cos\psi=\sin\theta$ of step 1.2, one computes $A(\omega'\cdot n)=(A-C)\omega_{3}\,\varphi'\sin\theta+mgd\,\sin\theta$ and $A(\omega\cdot n')=-A\varphi'\psi'\sin\theta$, hence $A\theta''=(A-C)\omega_{3}\varphi'\sin\theta+mgd\sin\theta-A\varphi'\psi'\sin\theta=A\varphi'^{2}\sin\theta\cos\theta-b\varphi'\sin\theta+mgd\sin\theta$, the last equality by $\omega_{3}-\psi'=\varphi'\cos\theta$ from step 1.2 and $b=C\omega_{3}$ from step 5.1.

The three equations of the definition of [L5] hold: the first is $\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(A\varphi'\sin^{2}\theta+C\cos\theta(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta)\bigr)=a'=0$ by step 6.1, the third is $\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(C(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta)\bigr)=b'=0$ by step 5.1, and the second is $A\theta''=A\varphi'^{2}\sin\theta\cos\theta-C(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta)\varphi'\sin\theta+mgd\sin\theta$ by step 6.2 with $C(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta)=b$. Therefore $(\varphi,\theta,\psi)$ is a heavy-top trajectory of [L5] with parameters $(A,C,m,d,g)$, and clauses 1-4 of [[thm-cm-heavy-top-reduction]] apply: $a$ and $b$ are constant, $\varphi'$ and $\psi'$ are given by the displayed formulas, the reduced energy $E$ is constant, and $A\theta''=-U'(\theta)$. This proves clauses 3 and 4.

boundaries.reason: The hypotheses are satisfiable: any axisymmetric mass distribution with positive moments, any d>0 and any g>0 gives a model of the branch, and the chart description is a hypothesis on the interval; step 7.1 concludes the system for the given data.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 4.1–5.1 use positive pivot inertias A,C and allow instantaneous zero angular velocity; step 6.1 obtains the conserved vertical momentum without dividing by it. The time-derivative symbol dt is not a vanishing denominator. The Euler chart instead excludes sin(theta)=0 by theta in (0,pi).

boundaries.reason: One interval and one description: the statement fixes one motion and one Euler-angle description on I_0, and steps 1.1-7.1 use only that data; the chart caveat records that on a subinterval the conclusions hold there.

The pole case theta in {0,pi} is excluded by the hypothesis theta(I_0) in (0,pi), and the statement and remark state explicitly that the sleeping-top and hanging configurations are not covered; degenerate inertia data are excluded by A_c>0 and C_c>0.
The time-window endpoints: all constancy statements are on the open interval I_0; steps 5.1, 6.1 and 7.1 apply the zero-derivative lemma on intervals, and no boundary value is used.
AC_omega is declared and used only for the finiteness of the defining integrals in [L2] via pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting; the reduction identities are choice-free.
The forward direction is the reduction from the branch to the heavy-top system (steps 1.1-7.1).

The reverse direction - that every heavy-top trajectory arises from a motion of the branch - is not asserted; the example on the companion page verifies the pivot balance directly on its explicit data, and no general converse is claimed.

risk_review.notes: All nine steps checked against pivot postulate, Euler-angle velocity and exact heavy-top system/reduction. J_p=L_c+c cross mc prime follows centred integral linearity; c=dRe3 adds md^2 only transversely. Torque sign is -mgd(Re3) cross e3; gamma=(-sin(theta)cos(psi),sin(theta)sin(psi),cos(theta)). Projection on n=(sin(psi),cos(psi),0) yields A theta second=A phi prime squared sin(theta)cos(theta)-b phi prime sin(theta)+mgd sin(theta). a,b conservation and supplier energy hold for C^2 angles with 0<theta<pi, never at poles; A,C,m,d,g positive and AC_omega met. Sphere repair affects no actual use. No empirical premise.

citations.quote:
Adopt the model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: the reference mass
distribution $\nu$, its total mass $m=\nu(\mathbb R^3)$ and its centred
reference coordinates $\int\rho\,d\nu(\rho)=0$. Assume the Axiom of Countable
Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, used only through
[[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]] to make the polynomial moments of $\nu$ of
degree at most two finite real numbers. Fix an inertial frame and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^2$
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]).

**(a) Body inertia matrix.** The **body inertia matrix** of the model is the
inertia matrix of the reference mass distribution,
$$I:=I(\nu)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}I_3-\rho\rho^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
with entries $I_{jk}=\int(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}\delta_{jk}-\rho_j\rho_k)\,d\nu$
as in [[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]; the matrix is expressed
in the standard basis of the reference coordinates. Its entries are finite
real numbers, it is symmetric, and for every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)\ \ge 0$$
by [[lem-cm-inertia-matrix-properties]] clauses 1-2; hence $I$ is symmetric
and its quadratic form is positive semidefinite. The dimension is
$[I]=\mu\ell^{2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]), read in kilogram metres squared. The
model is **nondegenerate** when no line through the origin carries the whole
mass, that is $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega\bigr)>0$ for every
$\omega\neq0$, and **degenerate** otherwise; the connection between this
criterion and the strict positivity and invertibility of $I$ is proved in the
principal-axes theorem of this page.

**(b) Spatial inertia tensor at the centre of mass.** The **spatial inertia
tensor** of the model at time $t$ is
$$I(t):=R(t)\,I\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
the matrix of the same quadratic form in the frame's spatial coordinates: for
every $n\in\mathbb R^3$,
$n^{\mathsf T}I(t)n=(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)^{\mathsf T}I(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)$. Its
entries are $C^2$ functions of $t$, since $R$ is of class $C^2$ and $I$ is
constant; the matrix rotates with the body and returns to $I$ in the
body-fixed frame, where $R=I_3$.

**(c) Inertia tensor about a spatial point.** For a spatial point
$p\in\mathbb R^3$ let
$$a(t,p):=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\bigl(p-c(t)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^3$$
be the **reference coordinate of $p$**, that is the label of the material
point of the reference placement that is placed at $p$ at time $t$. The
**inertia tensor of the model about $p$** at time $t$ is
$$I(t,p):=R(t)\,I_\nu\bigl(a(t,p)\bigr)\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
where
$$I_\nu(a)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho-a\rVert_2^{2}I_3-(\rho-a)(\rho-a)^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)$$
is the inertia tensor of the mass distribution about the point $a$ of the
reference coordinates ([[def-cm-inertia-tensor-about-a-point]]). Since the
label of a spatial point is uniquely determined by the placement, this is
well defined; for the centre of mass, $a(t,c(t))=0$ and
$I(t,c(t))=I(t)$. The dimension is again $\mu\ell^{2}$, read in kilogram
metres squared.

**(d) Moment of inertia about an axis.** Let $\ell$ be a spatial line at time
$t$, given by a point $p\in\mathbb R^3$ and a unit direction $n\in\mathbb R^3$
($\lVert n\rVert_2=1$). The **moment of inertia of the model about $\ell$** is
$$\Theta_\ell(t):=n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n .$$
Its invariance under the choices entering the description of the line and
its identification with the integral defining the physical moment of inertia
about the line are statements, not conventions; they are proved in clause
(c) of the principal-axes theorem of this page. For a **body-fixed
axis**, that is a line through the centre of mass whose direction in
reference coordinates is a constant unit vector $n_0$, the moment is
$$n_0^{\mathsf T}I n_0=\int\lVert n_0\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),$$
by clause (a), and is independent of time, because $I$ and $n_0$ are model
data.

**(e) What is constant and what moves.** The body inertia matrix $I$ is
determined by the model's reference mass distribution alone and does not
depend on the time, the frame or the motion; the spatial inertia tensor
$I(t)$ depends on the motion through the orientation $R(t)$; the inertia
tensor $I(t,p)$ about a spatial point depends on the motion through both the
orientation and the position of $p$. Principal axes and principal moments of
$I$ are the subject of the principal-axes theorem of this page.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only to make the integrals finite. Adopt the
model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] and its inertia data
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]): the reference mass distribution $\nu$ with
total mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates, the body inertia matrix $I$,
the spatial inertia tensor $I(t)=R(t)IR(t)^{\mathsf T}$ of a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$, and the inertia tensor $I(t,p)$ about a spatial
point $p$ ([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]). Then:

**(a) Principal basis.** There is an orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of
$\mathbb R^3$ and real numbers $I_1,I_2,I_3$, the **principal axes** and
**principal moments** of the model, with
$$Ie_j=I_je_j\qquad(j=1,2,3).$$

**(b) Quadratic form and rotational term.** For every
$\omega=\sum_j\omega_je_j\in\mathbb R^3$ one has
$I\omega=\sum_jI_j\omega_je_j$ and
$$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\sum_jI_j\omega_j^{2}=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)\ \ge 0,$$
and each principal moment is
$I_j=e_j^{\mathsf T}Ie_j=\int\lVert e_j\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)$.

**(c) Axis moments.** For every unit vector $n\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$n^{\mathsf T}In=\int\lVert n\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho);$$
for every spatial point $p$ and unit vector $n$, with $x=x(t,\cdot)$ the
placement at time $t$,
$$n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n=\int\lVert n\times\bigl(x(t,\rho)-p\bigr)\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho).$$
Consequently the number $\Theta_\ell(t)=n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n$ of
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] depends only on the spatial line $\ell$
$\{p+sn:s\in\mathbb R\}$ and not on the choice of the point $p$ on it nor on
the sign of the unit direction $n$.

**(d) Vanishing and positivity.** Each principal moment satisfies $I_j\ge0$,
and $I_j=0$ exactly when $\nu$ is supported on the line $\mathbb Re_j$ of the
principal axis, that is $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Re_j\bigr)=0$.
If the model is nondegenerate, that is if
$\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega\bigr)>0$ for every
$\omega\neq0$, then every $I_j>0$ and $I$ is invertible. If $\nu$ is
supported on some line through the origin (such a line exists whenever the
support of a centred $\nu$ is contained in a line, because the mean of $\nu$
is the origin), then $I$ is not invertible.

**(e) Extremal moments.** For every unit vector
$n=\sum_jc_je_j$ one has $n^{\mathsf T}In=\sum_jI_jc_j^{2}$ and therefore
$$\min_jI_j\ \le\ n^{\mathsf T}In\ \le\ \max_jI_j,$$
with the value $\max_jI_j$ attained at a unit eigenvector for a maximal
principal moment and the value $\min_jI_j$ attained at a unit eigenvector for
a minimal principal moment. Hence the largest and smallest principal moments
are the maximum and minimum of the rotational-inertia quadratic form over the
unit sphere.

The identities are conditional on the model data and the stated choice
assumption; no equation of motion and no conservation statement is used or
asserted.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), carried through [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]
clause (i) and [[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] for finite mass moments, through
[[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]] and [[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (i)
for the finite inertial integrals, and through the double-cover supplier of
[[def-cm-quaternion-rotation-map-and-cover]] (its second remark) for the
surjectivity used to choose an initial unit quaternion. Adopt a **nondegenerate** model of the
rigid-material branch [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: a reference mass
distribution $\nu$ with total mass $m$, centred reference coordinates and no
line through the origin carrying the whole mass
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] clause (a)). Fix an orthonormal principal basis
$(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ with $Ie_{j}=I_{j}e_{j}$ and $I_{j}>0$
([[pthm-cm10-principal-axes]] clauses (a) and (d)), use the model in the
**torque-free** branch of [[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iv), and fix
an index $j\in\{1,2,3\}$ and a rate $\Omega\in\mathbb R$. Use the model's nondegenerate open
time window $I_0$ ([[def-interval]] and
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] clause (ii)), and fix a time $t_{0}\in I_0$ and an orientation
$R_{0}\in SO(3)$. Then:

1. **Existence of the uniform rotation.** There is a path
   $R:I_0\to SO(3)$ of class $C^{1}$ with $R(t_{0})=R_{0}$ and
   $$R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)=[\Omega e_{j}]_\times\qquad(t\in I_0),$$
   that is, with constant body angular velocity $\omega\equiv\Omega e_{j}$
   ([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]] clause (a)).
2. **It is a torque-free motion.** For every such path $R$ and every curve
   $c:I_0\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{2}$, the map
   $x(t,\rho):=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ is a motion of the torque-free model of the
   branch: its angular momentum about the centre of mass is
   $$L_c(t)=\Omega I_{j}\,R(t)e_{j},$$
   it is constant on $I_0$, and the adopted balance $L_c'=0$ holds. (Here $R$
   is automatically of class $C^{2}$, because $R'=R[\Omega e_{j}]_\times$ is
   the product of the $C^{1}$ curve $R$ with a constant matrix, so the
   configuration path $(c,R)$ has the regularity required of a motion.)
3. **Geometry and invariants.** In the motions of clause 2 one has
   $l=I\omega=\Omega I_{j}e_{j}$ constant,
   $$C=\lVert L_c\rVert_2^{2}=\Omega^{2}I_{j}^{2},\qquad E=\tfrac12\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\tfrac12\Omega^{2}I_{j};$$
   if $\Omega\neq0$, define the spatial line of the body-fixed axis by
   $\ell_j(t):=\{c(t)+sR(t)e_j:s\in\mathbb R\}$ and its unit direction by
   $n_j(t):=R(t)e_j$. Then $n_j(t)=L_c/(\Omega I_j)$ for every $t$, so this
   direction is **fixed in the inertial frame** and the spatial angular
   velocity $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t):=R(t)\omega(t)=\Omega n_j$ of
   [[def-cm10-angular-velocity]] clause (b) is constant; the line
   $\ell_j(t)$ need not be fixed because $c$ is arbitrary. If $\Omega=0$,
   then $R$ is constant on $I_0$.
4. **Converse classification.** Conversely, let a motion of a nondegenerate
   torque-free model have **constant** body angular velocity
   $\omega\equiv\omega_{0}$ on its time window. Then
   $I\omega_{0}=\lambda\omega_{0}$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb R$: either
   $\omega_{0}=0$ and the orientation path is constant, or $\omega_{0}\neq0$
   and $\omega_{0}$ lies along a principal axis; in the latter case an orthonormal principal basis can be chosen with one vector $e_j=\omega_0/\|\omega_0\|_2$ and $\Omega=\|\omega_0\|_2\ne0$, and the conclusions of clauses 2 and 3 hold in that adapted basis. It can be made positively oriented by negating a different basis vector. No alignment with the initially fixed basis is asserted when eigenvalues repeat.

The statement is conditional on the adopted model and zero-torque balance; it
asserts no force, no measurement and no empirical law, and the existence
clause is a statement about the model's kinematic class, not about nature.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only through the integrals of
[[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]]. Adopt a model of the rigid-material branch
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] that is **nondegenerate** in the sense of
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] clause (a) (no line through the origin carries
the whole mass), and use it in the **torque-free** external-torque branch of
[[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iv): the datum vanishes, so along every
motion of the resulting model the adopted balance reads $L_c'=0$ on the time
window $I_0$. Let $\omega$ be the body angular velocity, $I$ the body inertia
matrix and $l:=I\omega$ ([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]],
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]). Then:

1. **Conservation of angular momentum.** The angular momentum about the
   centre of mass $L_c(t)=R(t)l(t)$ of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]] clause
   4 is constant on $I_0$; in particular $\lVert L_c\rVert_2$ is constant.
2. **Energy-momentum invariants and principal components.** The scalars
   $$C:=\langle l,l\rangle=\lVert L_c\rVert_2^{2},\qquad E:=\tfrac12\,\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\tfrac12\,\langle l,I^{-1}l\rangle$$
   are constant on $I_0$, and $l$ satisfies the torque-free equation
   $$l'=l\times(I^{-1}l).$$
   If $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ is a positively oriented orthonormal eigenbasis of $I$ with
   $Ie_{j}=I_{j}e_{j}$ and $l=\sum_{j}l_{j}e_{j}$
   ([[pthm-cm10-principal-axes]] clauses (a)-(b)), then
   $$C=\sum_{j}l_{j}^{2},\qquad E=\sum_{j}\frac{l_{j}^{2}}{2I_{j}},$$
   and the component equations are
   $$l_{1}'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_{3}}-\frac1{I_{2}}\Bigr)l_{2}l_{3},\qquad l_{2}'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_{1}}-\frac1{I_{3}}\Bigr)l_{1}l_{3},\qquad l_{3}'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_{2}}-\frac1{I_{1}}\Bigr)l_{1}l_{2}.$$
3. **The energy invariant is the rotational kinetic energy.** $E$ equals the
   rotational term $\tfrac12\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega$ of the model's kinetic
   energy in clause 3 of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]]; and with
   $I_{\min}:=\min_{j}I_{j}>0$ one has
   $$\lVert\omega(t)\rVert_2^{2}\le\frac{2E}{I_{\min}}\qquad(t\in I_0).$$
   In particular both $l$ and $\omega$ are bounded on $I_0$.
4. **The spin field is globally solvable.** The autonomous field
   $F(l)=l\times(I^{-1}l)$ on $\mathbb R^{3}$ is locally Lipschitz in the
   state variable ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]), and
   every solution of $l'=F(l)$ has a unique maximal extension defined
   on all of $\mathbb R$, and that extension satisfies $\lVert l(t)\rVert_2=\lVert l(0)\rVert_2$
   for every $t$. Consequently the $l$-path of a torque-free motion is the
   restriction to $I_0$ of a solution defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and its
   path is contained in the compact level set
   $$\Lambda(C,E):=\bigl\{z\in\mathbb R^{3}:\langle z,z\rangle=C,\ \tfrac12\langle z,I^{-1}z\rangle=E\bigr\},$$
   which is nonempty because it contains the datum at any chosen time of the motion.

The statement is conditional on the adopted model, its nondegeneracy and the
zero-torque balance; it asserts no orientation of the body in space, no
measured value and no empirical law.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only through the integrals of
[[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]]; the theorems below neither use nor imply any
other choice principle. Adopt a model of the rigid-material branch
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] with the external-torque branch
[[post-cm11-torque-balance]]: a reference mass distribution $\nu$ with total
mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates, a time window $I_0$
([[def-interval]]), an inertial frame, a motion $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with
configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^{2}$
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]), body angular velocity $\omega$
([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]]) and body inertia matrix $I$
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]), and a continuous external torque datum
$\tau:I_0\to\mathbb R^{3}$ with respect to which the adopted balance of
[[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iii) holds along the motion. Then:

1. **Euler's equations with torque.** Writing $l:=I\omega$, one has
   $l'=R^{\mathsf T}\tau-\omega\times I\omega$ and
   $$I\omega'(t)+\omega(t)\times I\omega(t)=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\tau(t)\qquad(t\in I_0).$$
2. **Principal-axis components.** If $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ is a positively oriented orthonormal
   eigenbasis of $I$ with $Ie_{j}=I_{j}e_{j}$ ([[pthm-cm10-principal-axes]]
   clause (a)) and $\omega=\sum_{j}\omega_{j}e_{j}$,
   $R^{\mathsf T}\tau=\sum_{j}\tau_{j}e_{j}$, then the equations are
   componentwise
   $$I_{1}\omega_{1}'=(I_{2}-I_{3})\omega_{2}\omega_{3}+\tau_{1},\qquad I_{2}\omega_{2}'=(I_{3}-I_{1})\omega_{3}\omega_{1}+\tau_{2},\qquad I_{3}\omega_{3}'=(I_{1}-I_{2})\omega_{1}\omega_{2}+\tau_{3}.$$
3. **Rotational power identity.** The rotational kinetic energy
   $K_{\mathrm{rot}}(t):=\tfrac12\omega(t)^{\mathsf T}I\omega(t)$ is
   differentiable on $I_0$ with
   $$\frac{d}{dt}K_{\mathrm{rot}}(t)=\omega(t)\cdot R(t)^{\mathsf T}\tau(t)\qquad(t\in I_0);$$
   in particular, if $\tau\equiv0$, then $K_{\mathrm{rot}}$ is constant on
   $I_0$, and $K_{\mathrm{rot}}$ coincides with the rotational term
   $\tfrac12\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega$ of the model's kinetic energy in
   clause 3 of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]].
4. **Torque-free reduction and nondegeneracy.** Suppose $\tau\equiv0$ and the
   model is nondegenerate in the sense of [[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] clause
   (a), so that $I$ is invertible with $I^{-1}l=\omega$. Then, writing
   $\omega$ as a function of $l$,
   $$l'=l\times(I^{-1}l),\qquad \omega'=F(\omega):=-I^{-1}\bigl(\omega\times I\omega\bigr);$$
   the second form exhibits the torque-free body angular velocity as a
   solution of the autonomous field $F$ on $\mathbb R^{3}$.
5. **Frame covariance.** Let a second inertial frame be related to the first
   by $t'=t+b$, $x'=Qx+ut+a$ with $b\in\mathbb R$, $a,u\in\mathbb R^{3}$,
   $Q\in SO(3)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]] clause (iv)), and let
   $\tilde x(t',\rho):=Qx(t'-b,\rho)+u(t'-b)+a$, $\tilde\tau(t'):=Q\tau(t'-b)$
   be the transformed motion and datum of [[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause
   (vii). Then the balance holds in the second frame, and
   $$I\tilde\omega'(t')+\tilde\omega(t')\times I\tilde\omega(t')=\tilde R(t')^{\mathsf T}\tilde\tau(t')\qquad(t'\in I_0+b),$$
   where $\tilde\omega(t')=\omega(t'-b)$ and
   $\tilde R(t')=QR(t'-b)$; the body-frame torque is unchanged:
   $\tilde R(t')^{\mathsf T}\tilde\tau(t')=R(t'-b)^{\mathsf T}\tau(t'-b)$.

The statement is conditional on the adopted model and torque balance; it
asserts no force law for $\tau$, no conservation of $L_c$ and no measured
value.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate open interval, let $\omega:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous, and consider on the open time-state domain $D:=I\times\mathbb H\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb H$ the initial value problem

$$q'(t)=\tfrac12\,q(t)\,\varphi\bigl(\omega(t)\bigr),\qquad q(t_0)=q_0,$$

read as the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] with time-state domain $D$, state space $\mathbb H$, and right-hand side $F:D\to\mathbb H$, $F(t,q)=\tfrac12q\,\varphi(\omega(t))$, where $\varphi$, $S^3$ and $\rho$ are those of [[def-cm-quaternion-rotation-map-and-cover]].

1. If $q:I\to\mathbb H$ is a $C^1$ solution of $q'=\tfrac12q\,\varphi(\omega(t))$, then $N\circ q$ is constant on $I$; if $q(t_0)\in S^3$ for one $t_0\in I$, then $q(I)\subseteq S^3$ and the curve

$$R:=\rho\circ q:I\longrightarrow SO(3),\qquad R(t):=\rho(q(t)),$$

is of class $C^1$ with $R'(t)=R(t)\,\Omega_{\omega(t)}$ for every $t\in I$; consequently $\omega$ is the body angular velocity of $R$ in the sense of [[lem-cm-body-angular-velocity-of-a-rotation-path]].
2. For every $t_0\in I$ and $q_0\in S^3$ the problem has exactly one maximal solution, and its domain is all of $I$; that is, there is exactly one $C^1$ curve $q:I\to S^3$ with $q(t_0)=q_0$ and $q'=\tfrac12q\,\varphi(\omega(t))$ on $I$, and clause 1 applies to it.

Let $\mathbb H$ be the quaternion algebra with its product, conjugation $x\mapsto\bar x$, real-valued norm $N:\mathbb H\to\mathbb R$, and real embedding $r\mapsto\hat r=(r,0,0,0)$, in the notation of [[def-quaternions]]. Thus $x=x_0+x_1i+x_2j+x_3k$ with the multiplication formula of [[def-quaternions]], and

$$N(x)=x_0^2+x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2,\qquad \widehat{N(x)}=x\bar x=\bar x x.$$

In particular, $N(x)>0$ for $x\ne0$, and the imported division-ring theorem gives the typed inverse formula $x^{-1}=\widehat{N(x)^{-1}}\,\bar x$ ([[thm-quaternions-form-a-division-ring]]). Under the identification of $\mathbb H$ with $\mathbb R^4$ by the coordinates $x_0,\dots,x_3$ one has $N(x)=\|x\|_2^2$ for the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

**Imaginary quaternions and the vector identification.** Put

$$\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H:=\{x\in\mathbb H:\bar x=-x\}=\mathbb Ri\oplus\mathbb Rj\oplus\mathbb Rk,\qquad \varphi:\mathbb R^3\to\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H,\quad \varphi(v_1,v_2,v_3):=v_1i+v_2j+v_3k .$$

Then $\varphi$ is a linear isomorphism with $N(\varphi(v))=\|v\|_2^2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^3$. Throughout the collection, $\varphi$ translates between vectors of $\mathbb R^3$ (their inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$, norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ and cross product) and imaginary quaternions inside quaternion products.

**The unit sphere.** Define

$$S^3:=\{q\in\mathbb H:N(q)=1\},$$

the unit sphere of $\mathbb H\cong\mathbb R^4$. The identification of $S^3$ with $SU(2)$ is the one of the published covering example `ex-su-two-to-so-three-as-a-covering-homomorphism`, which is also the source of the covering statement recorded in the second remark below; that example is linked from the page summary of this pair.

**Conjugation and the rotation map.** For $q\in\mathbb H$ with $q\ne0$ let $c_q:\mathbb H\to\mathbb H$ be

$$c_q(x):=qxq^{-1}=qx\,\widehat{N(q)^{-1}}\,\bar q,$$

where the real scalar is embedded by $r\mapsto\hat r$, and define

$$\rho(q):=c_q|_{\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H}:\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H\longrightarrow\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H .$$

Both the $\mathbb R$-linear map $\rho(q)$ and its matrix in the ordered basis $(i,j,k)$ of $\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H$ are written $\rho(q)$; the equality $\rho(q)\in SO(3)$ for $q\in S^3$ is part of the cited covering statement, and the matrix is the one meant whenever $\rho(q)$ is composed with the identifications above. The map $\rho$ itself is never linear in $q$ and no such structure is used.

**Quaternion lifts.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let $R:I\to SO(3)$ be a map, with $SO(3)$ as in [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]. A **quaternion lift** of $R$ is a map $q:I\to S^3$ with $\rho(q(t))=R(t)$ for every $t\in I$.

Adopt a **nondegenerate** model of the rigid-material branch
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] with **pairwise distinct** principal moments in
a positively oriented principal basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$, $Ie_{j}=I_{j}e_{j}$ with $I_{j}>0$
([[pthm-cm10-principal-axes]] clauses (a) and (d)), and use it in the
**torque-free** branch of [[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iv). In the
body-angular-velocity variable $\omega$ the torque-free dynamics is the
autonomous field
$$F(\omega):=-I^{-1}\bigl(\omega\times I\omega\bigr),\qquad \omega\in\mathbb R^{3},$$
on $\mathbb R^{3}$ ([[pthm-cm11-euler-equations]] clause 4), and for every
axis $j$ and every $\Omega\neq0$ the constant path
$\bar\omega\equiv\Omega e_{j}$ is a solution ([[pthm-cm11-principal-rotations]]
clauses 1-3). Fix such $j$ and $\Omega$, and choose $(a,b,j)$ cyclically:
$(a,b,j)=(2,3,1)$, $(3,1,2)$ or $(1,2,3)$. Thus $(e_a,e_b,e_j)$
is positively oriented. Put
$$\lambda_{j}:=\frac{\Omega^{2}\,(I_{a}-I_{j})(I_{j}-I_{b})}{I_{a}I_{b}}\neq0,\qquad \kappa_{j}:=\sqrt{\lvert\lambda_{j}\rvert}.$$
Then:

1. **The linearized field.** $F$ is totally differentiable at $\Omega e_{j}$
   in the sense of [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], with total
   derivative $A_{j}$ given on the principal basis by
   $$A_{j}e_{a}=\frac{\Omega(I_{j}-I_{a})}{I_{b}}\,e_{b},\qquad A_{j}e_{b}=\frac{\Omega(I_{b}-I_{j})}{I_{a}}\,e_{a},\qquad A_{j}e_{j}=0,$$
   and there is a constant $C\ge0$ with
   $\lVert F(\Omega e_{j}+\delta)-A_{j}\delta\rVert_2\le C\lVert\delta\rVert_2^{2}$
   for all $\delta\in\mathbb R^{3}$.
2. **The linearized system and its dichotomy.** Write
   $\delta=\delta_{a}e_{a}+\delta_{b}e_{b}+\delta_{j}e_{j}$.
   - If $I_{j}$ is a **largest or smallest** principal moment, then
     $\lambda_{j}<0$, every solution of the linearized system
     $\delta'=A_{j}\delta$ has a unique maximal extension defined on all of $\mathbb R$ and bounded on
     $[0,\infty)$, with
     $$\delta_{a}(t)=\delta_{a}(0)\cos(\kappa_{j}t)+\frac{\Omega(I_{b}-I_{j})}{I_{a}\kappa_{j}}\,\delta_{b}(0)\sin(\kappa_{j}t),$$
     $$\delta_{b}(t)=\delta_{b}(0)\cos(\kappa_{j}t)+\frac{\Omega(I_{j}-I_{a})}{I_{b}\kappa_{j}}\,\delta_{a}(0)\sin(\kappa_{j}t),$$
     and $\delta_{j}$ constant; consequently the spin is **linearly stable** in
     the sense of [[def-cm-orbital-and-linear-stability]].
   - If $I_{j}$ lies **strictly between** $I_{a}$ and $I_{b}$, then
     $\lambda_{j}>0$, the same two formulas hold with $\cosh$ and $\sinh$ in
     place of $\cos$ and $\sin$ and $\kappa_{j}=\sqrt{\lambda_{j}}$, the
     linearized system has unbounded solutions (for instance with
     $\delta_{b}(0)=0$ and $\delta_{a}(0)\neq0$ satisfying
     $\delta_{a}(0)+\frac{\Omega(I_{b}-I_{j})}{I_{a}\kappa_{j}}\delta_{b}(0)\neq0$),
     and the spin is **not linearly stable**.

The statement is a statement about the linearized system at the spin; the
corresponding nonlinear Lyapunov statements are separate items of this page,
and no conclusion about the nonlinear stability of the spin is drawn here.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $\gamma$ be the unique smallest positive zero of cosine supplied by [[thm-cosine-has-a-smallest-positive-zero]]. Define
$$\pi:=2\gamma.$$

Thus $\pi>0$ and $\pi/2=\gamma$.
There is a unique $\gamma\in(0,2)$ with $\cos\gamma=0$. It is the smallest positive zero of cosine.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

derivations.claim: By [L2] applied to each model, each $j$ and each $\Omega$ there is a torque-free motion with constant body angular velocity $\Omega e_{j}$, and $l=\Omega I_{j}e_{j}$, $C=\Omega^{2}I_{j}^{2}$, $E=\tfrac12\Omega^{2}I_{j}$ along it; for Model S with $I_{3}=2$, $j=3$, $\Omega=2$ this gives $l=4e_{3}$, $C=(2\cdot2)^{2}=16$, $E=\tfrac12\cdot4\cdot2=4$, and for Model A with $I_{1}=1$, $j=1$, $\Omega=1$ it gives $l=e_{1}$, $C=1$, $E=\tfrac12$, which is claim 1.

For the path $\omega$ of claim 2 in Model S, $l=I\omega=(\tfrac12\cos t,\tfrac12\sin t,2)$ by [L1], so $l'=(-\tfrac12\sin t,\tfrac12\cos t,0)$ by [L6], while $l\times(I^{-1}l)=l\times(\tfrac12\cos t,\tfrac12\sin t,1)$ has components $(\tfrac12\sin t\cdot1-2\cdot\tfrac12\sin t,\ -( \tfrac12\cos t\cdot1-2\cdot\tfrac12\cos t),\ \tfrac12\cos t\cdot\tfrac12\sin t-\tfrac12\sin t\cdot\tfrac12\cos t)=(-\tfrac12\sin t,\tfrac12\cos t,0)$ by the coordinate formula for the cross product in [L6]; hence $l'=l\times(I^{-1}l)$, so $l$ solves the torque-free equations and $\omega$ satisfies the Euler equations by [L3].

For claim 3, [L5] gives $\lambda_{j}=\Omega^{2}(I_{a}-I_{j})(I_{j}-I_{b})/(I_{a}I_{b})$; for Model A and $j=1$, with $a=2$, $b=3$: $\lambda_{1}=\tfrac{(2-1)(1-3)}{2\cdot3}=-\tfrac13$ and $\kappa_{1}=1/\sqrt3$; for $j=2$, with the cyclic choice $a=3$, $b=1$: $\lambda_{2}=\tfrac{(3-2)(2-1)}{3\cdot1}=\tfrac13$ and $\kappa_{2}=1/\sqrt3$; for $j=3$, with $a=1$, $b=2$: $\lambda_{3}=\tfrac{(1-3)(3-2)}{1\cdot2}=-1$ and $\kappa_{3}=1$. In the first case the linearized field of [L5] satisfies $Ae_{2}=-\tfrac13e_{3}$ and $Ae_{3}=e_{2}$, and the pair $\delta_{2}(t)=\cos(t/\sqrt3)$, $\delta_{3}(t)=-\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\sin(t/\sqrt3)$ satisfies $\delta_{2}'=\delta_{3}$ and $\delta_{3}'=-\tfrac13\delta_{2}$ by [L6], so it solves the transverse linearized equations.

The quantities of claim 2: $\lVert\omega(t)\rVert_2^{2}=\tfrac14\cos^{2}t+\tfrac14\sin^{2}t+1=\tfrac14+1=\tfrac54$ and $C=\langle l,l\rangle=\tfrac14\cos^{2}t+\tfrac14\sin^{2}t+4=\tfrac{17}4$ by the Pythagorean identity in [L6]; and $E=\tfrac12\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\tfrac12(\tfrac14\cos^{2}t+\tfrac14\sin^{2}t+2\cdot1)=\tfrac12(\tfrac14+2)=\tfrac98$. The difference $\omega(\tfrac\pi2)-\omega(0)=(-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,0)\neq0$ has norm $\tfrac{\sqrt2}2$, so $\omega$ is not constant.

Since $\omega$ is $C^{\infty}$, hence $C^{1}$, [L4] supplies a $C^{1}$ rotation path $R:\mathbb R\to SO(3)$ with body angular velocity $\omega$ and any prescribed initial orientation; then $R'=R[\omega]_\times$ is $C^{1}$, so $R$ is of class $C^{2}$, and $x:I_0\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, $x(t,\rho):=R(t)\rho$ (that is, $c\equiv0$), is a motion of Model S on its declared window $I_0=\mathbb R$ by [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] clause (ii) with body angular velocity $\omega$ and $l$ as in step 1.2. Its balance holds: $L_c=Rl$ by [L3], so $(Rl)'=R'l+Rl'=R(\omega\times l+l')=0$ because $l'=l\times(I^{-1}l)=l\times\omega=-\omega\times l$ from step 1.2 and the alternation of the cross product in [L6]; hence the motion is torque-free and realizes claim 2.

In the intermediate case $j=2$, the same formulas give $Ae_{1}=-\tfrac13e_{3}$ and $Ae_{3}=-e_{1}$, so the transverse system is $\delta_{1}'=-\delta_{3}$, $\delta_{3}'=-\tfrac13\delta_{1}$; with $\delta_{1}(0)=1$, $\delta_{3}(0)=0$ the $\cosh,\sinh$ solution of [L5] is $\delta_{1}(t)=\cosh(t/\sqrt3)$, $\delta_{3}(t)=-\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\sinh(t/\sqrt3)$, and $\delta_{1}$ is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$ by [L6]; hence the linearized system at the intermediate spin of Model A has an unbounded solution, which is claim 3.

boundaries.reason: The declared data are satisfiable: both matrices are symmetric positive definite and the models exist; step 1.1 instantiates the principal-axis claims on them.
Zero cases: Omega=0 is included in claim 1 and gives the zero angular velocity with C=E=0; the constant m and the zero of the cross product are used in step 1.2.
One axis and one model at a time: each claim fixes a single model and axis, and steps 1.1-3.2 treat each case separately.

Degeneracy: the symmetric model has I_1=I_2, which is why claim 3 is checked on the asymmetric model with distinct moments; the two coincident moments of model S are used only through the explicit solution of steps 1.2-2.1 and never through the linearization theorem.
The interval is all of R in every claim, so the endpoints play no role; the sine and cosine functions used in steps 1.2-1.3 are global.

The arithmetic introduces no choice principle. AC_omega is inherited for finite mass moments and inertial integrals through the model and principal-spin suppliers used in step 1.1, and for quaternion-cover surjectivity and the lift used in step 3.1.
The forward direction is the verification of the displayed values and equations, carried out in steps 1.1-3.2.
The reverse reading (that the displayed data are the only ones with those invariants) is not claimed and is false in general; no converse appears in the statement.

risk_review.notes: All six steps checked: Model S l=(cos(t)/2,sin(t)/2,2) gives derivative (-sin(t)/2,cos(t)/2,0)=l cross omega; C=17/4,E=9/8,omega norm squared=5/4. Quaternion reconstruction on R with C^1 omega yields C^2 R and zero torque balance. Model A lambda values -1/3,1/3,-1 and transverse equations match trig/hyperbolic solutions. Refuter:27:1 confirmed missing dimensional time scale and repaired by explicit numerical SI convention t=T/T_* with T_*=1 s, omega_phys=omega/T_* and rates/frequencies restored; pi/2 means physical pi T_*/2.
