Added exact quarter-turn/pi and square-root suppliers for previously unstated special-value use; all claims unchanged numerically. Direct consumers are counterexample, intermediate escape and B-page summary; each requires inherited numerical SI convention, within batch only. No measurements.

citations.quote:
Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following **rigid-material
model** branch, in the spacetime and frames of [[post-cm01-spacetime]] and
[[post-cm01-frames]].

**(i) Reference mass distribution.** A rigid-material model carries, besides
the framework's time and frame structure, a **reference mass distribution**: a
measure $\nu$ on the Borel space $(\mathbb R^3,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3))$ that
is a mass distribution in the sense of
[[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]] — finite and bounded, with
$\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline B_R(0)\bigr)=0$ for some real $R>0$,
and of total mass $m:=\nu(\mathbb R^3)\in(0,+\infty)$ — whose reference
coordinates are **centred**,
$$\int\rho\,d\nu(\rho)=0\in\mathbb R^3 .$$
The label variable $\rho$ is a coordinate of the model's reference placement
and has dimension $\ell$, each component read in metres; the total mass $m$
has dimension $\mu$, read in kilograms, and $R$ has dimension $\ell$ and is
the model's **reference size**
([[def-cm01-units]]). Under the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$,
used only through [[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]] to make the polynomial
moments of $\nu$ of degree at most two finite, the first and second moments
of $\nu$ are finite real numbers. The measure $\nu$ and the number $m$ are
model data: no distribution of mass of any concrete body and no measured mass
is asserted.

**(ii) Time window and motions.** A model carries a **time window**
$I_0\subseteq\mathbb R$, a nondegenerate open interval $(a,b)$ with
$-\infty\le a<b\le+\infty$ and at least two points, read in seconds. Fix an
**inertial frame** of the model, that is the adapted chart
$(o,u,(e_1,e_2,e_3))$ with coordinates $(t,x)$ of [[post-cm01-frames]]. A
**motion** of the model in this frame is a map
$x:I_0\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ for which there exist a map
$c:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ and a map $R:I_0\to SO(3)$, both of class $C^2$
(componentwise derivatives, [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] for the coordinates
and [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]] for the target), such that
$$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho\qquad(t\in I_0,\ \rho\in\mathbb R^3).$$
Adopt: the motions of the model are the maps of this form, and the pair
$(c,R)$ is the **configuration path** of the motion. The map
$x(t,\cdot):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is the **placement** at time $t$ and is
the rigid placement of [[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]]
with translation $c$ and rotation $R$; its material velocity is
$\partial_tx(t,\rho)=c'(t)+R'(t)\rho$, defined by differentiability of $c$ and
of the entries of $R$. The time window $I_0$ is the interval on which the
model's configuration path is considered; the model's time coordinate is
the frame time $t$.

**(iii) Rigidity idealization.** The idealization adopted is that the model
describes a body that does not deform, and its content is the representation
(ii): a placement of the form $x=c+R\rho$ with $R\in SO(3)$ preserves every
mutual distance, since $R(t)$ preserves the Euclidean norm
([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]), so for all $\rho,\rho'\in\mathbb R^3$
the number $\lVert x(t,\rho)-x(t,\rho')\rVert_2=\lVert\rho-\rho'\rVert_2$ is
independent of $t$. The model class (ii) is *adopted* as the definition of a
rigid-material placement; a motion of material points that preserves all
mutual distances but whose label set fails to determine a rotation is not
claimed to be of this form, and the general characterization of
distance-preserving placements is neither asserted nor used on this page.
For a **nondegenerate labeling** — a label set containing the origin and two
linearly independent material vectors — distinct configurations $(c,R)$ and
$(\bar c,\bar R)$ give distinct placements, by [[lem-cm-rigid-labeling-stabilizer]];
the configuration data of (ii) therefore do not overcount for such a body.
Degenerate labelings and degenerate mass distributions are not excluded by
this postulate; the later items of the pair state where invertibility of the
inertial data must be assumed.

**(iv) Centre of mass and orientation.** Because the reference coordinates are
centred, the identity
$$\int x(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho)=mc(t)$$
holds for every motion, by linearity of the integral and
$\int\rho\,d\nu=0$; the physical reading is that $c(t)$ is the position of the
centre of mass of the model in the placement at time $t$. The rotation
$R(t)$ is the model's **orientation**: it carries reference coordinates into
the frame's spatial coordinates, and the **body-fixed frame** at time $t$ is
the ordered orthonormal basis $(R(t)e_1,R(t)e_2,R(t)e_3)$ of the spatial
space. The reading of $R(t)$ as the orientation of the placement uses the
nondegeneracy of (iii): for a nondegenerate labeling the material points
determine $R(t)$ uniquely, so the orientation is an attribute of the body's
placement and not of the choice of label coordinates.

**(v) Frame changes.** The description of a motion in a second inertial frame
is obtained by the change of coordinates $t'=t+b$, $x'=Qx+ut+a$ of
[[post-cm01-frames]] clause (iv), applied to every event of the motion; here
$Q\in SO(3)$ and $u\in\mathbb R^3$ are the rotation and the boost velocity of
that clause, written $R$ and $v$ there and renamed here to avoid a clash with
the orientation path $R(t)$ of clause (ii) and with the material velocity
field of the pair's definition. With the same $\rho$ labelling a material
point, the description in the second frame is
$$\tilde x(t',\rho):=Q\,x(t'-b,\rho)+u\,(t'-b)+a .$$
This description is again a motion of the model, with configuration path
$$\tilde c(t')=Qc(t'-b)+u\,(t'-b)+a,\qquad \tilde R(t')=Q\,R(t'-b),$$
because $SO(3)$ is closed under multiplication
([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]); this is a consistency requirement of
the model's frame language, exactly as for the particle worldlines of
[[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (ii). The derived transformation laws of the
angular velocity, of the inertia data and of the kinetic splitting are
theorems of this pair's page, not part of this postulate.

**(vi) No dynamics.** This postulate fixes the kinematic class of the model
and its mass data only. It asserts no force law, no torque law, no equation of
motion for the pair $(c,R)$, and no balance or conservation law; in
particular the model does not by itself constrain the configuration path,
and the effect of forces and torques on a body is a separate model
assumption. It also asserts no measured value of any mass, length, duration
or orientation.

**(vii) Scope and exclusions.** The branch excludes deformation, internal
degrees of freedom such as temperature, chemical state or an independent spin
variable, variable mass, ablation and impact events, contact, friction and
dissipative constitutive laws, and any relativistic or quantum description.
It excludes bodies whose mass distribution is not a bounded finite Borel
measure of the stated kind. A rigid-material model is not a system of
finitely many particle labels: the continuum measure $\nu$ carries the mass
data of the model, and the situations of point masses are the special cases
of measures supported on finitely many points. All physical statements about
the model weight material points by $\nu$; properties of $\nu$-null sets of
labels are not physical properties of the body.

Adopt the model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: the reference mass
distribution $\nu$, its total mass $m=\nu(\mathbb R^3)$ and its centred
reference coordinates $\int\rho\,d\nu(\rho)=0$. Assume the Axiom of Countable
Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, used only through
[[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]] to make the polynomial moments of $\nu$ of
degree at most two finite real numbers. Fix an inertial frame and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^2$
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]).

**(a) Body inertia matrix.** The **body inertia matrix** of the model is the
inertia matrix of the reference mass distribution,
$$I:=I(\nu)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}I_3-\rho\rho^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
with entries $I_{jk}=\int(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}\delta_{jk}-\rho_j\rho_k)\,d\nu$
as in [[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]; the matrix is expressed
in the standard basis of the reference coordinates. Its entries are finite
real numbers, it is symmetric, and for every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)\ \ge 0$$
by [[lem-cm-inertia-matrix-properties]] clauses 1-2; hence $I$ is symmetric
and its quadratic form is positive semidefinite. The dimension is
$[I]=\mu\ell^{2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]), read in kilogram metres squared. The
model is **nondegenerate** when no line through the origin carries the whole
mass, that is $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega\bigr)>0$ for every
$\omega\neq0$, and **degenerate** otherwise; the connection between this
criterion and the strict positivity and invertibility of $I$ is proved in the
principal-axes theorem of this page.

**(b) Spatial inertia tensor at the centre of mass.** The **spatial inertia
tensor** of the model at time $t$ is
$$I(t):=R(t)\,I\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
the matrix of the same quadratic form in the frame's spatial coordinates: for
every $n\in\mathbb R^3$,
$n^{\mathsf T}I(t)n=(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)^{\mathsf T}I(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)$. Its
entries are $C^2$ functions of $t$, since $R$ is of class $C^2$ and $I$ is
constant; the matrix rotates with the body and returns to $I$ in the
body-fixed frame, where $R=I_3$.

**(c) Inertia tensor about a spatial point.** For a spatial point
$p\in\mathbb R^3$ let
$$a(t,p):=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\bigl(p-c(t)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^3$$
be the **reference coordinate of $p$**, that is the label of the material
point of the reference placement that is placed at $p$ at time $t$. The
**inertia tensor of the model about $p$** at time $t$ is
$$I(t,p):=R(t)\,I_\nu\bigl(a(t,p)\bigr)\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
where
$$I_\nu(a)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho-a\rVert_2^{2}I_3-(\rho-a)(\rho-a)^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)$$
is the inertia tensor of the mass distribution about the point $a$ of the
reference coordinates ([[def-cm-inertia-tensor-about-a-point]]). Since the
label of a spatial point is uniquely determined by the placement, this is
well defined; for the centre of mass, $a(t,c(t))=0$ and
$I(t,c(t))=I(t)$. The dimension is again $\mu\ell^{2}$, read in kilogram
metres squared.

**(d) Moment of inertia about an axis.** Let $\ell$ be a spatial line at time
$t$, given by a point $p\in\mathbb R^3$ and a unit direction $n\in\mathbb R^3$
($\lVert n\rVert_2=1$). The **moment of inertia of the model about $\ell$** is
$$\Theta_\ell(t):=n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n .$$
Its invariance under the choices entering the description of the line and
its identification with the integral defining the physical moment of inertia
about the line are statements, not conventions; they are proved in clause
(c) of the principal-axes theorem of this page. For a **body-fixed
axis**, that is a line through the centre of mass whose direction in
reference coordinates is a constant unit vector $n_0$, the moment is
$$n_0^{\mathsf T}I n_0=\int\lVert n_0\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),$$
by clause (a), and is independent of time, because $I$ and $n_0$ are model
data.

**(e) What is constant and what moves.** The body inertia matrix $I$ is
determined by the model's reference mass distribution alone and does not
depend on the time, the frame or the motion; the spatial inertia tensor
$I(t)$ depends on the motion through the orientation $R(t)$; the inertia
tensor $I(t,p)$ about a spatial point depends on the motion through both the
orientation and the position of $p$. Principal axes and principal moments of
$I$ are the subject of the principal-axes theorem of this page.

**Numerical SI convention.** Let $T$ denote physical elapsed time and fix
$T_*=1\,\mathrm s$, $M_*=1\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $D_*=1\,\mathrm m$.
Below $t:=T/T_*$ is dimensionless and all quantities are numerical SI
values: inertia is divided by $M_*D_*^2$, angular velocity and its
perturbations by $T_*^{-1}$, angular momentum by $M_*D_*^2/T_*$,
and energy by $M_*D_*^2/T_*^2$. Primes differentiate with respect to $t$.
Restore physical angular velocity by
$\omega_{\rm phys}(T)=\omega(T/T_*)/T_*$ and angular momentum by
$l_{\rm phys}(T)=(M_*D_*^2/T_*)l(T/T_*)$.
The displayed numerical rates $1$, $2$, $1/\sqrt3$ mean physical rates
$1/T_*$, $2/T_*$, $1/(\sqrt3 T_*)$; $\lambda_j$ is restored by
$\lambda_{j,\rm phys}=\lambda_j/T_*^2$.
Thus $\cos t$, $\sin t$, $\cos(t/\sqrt3)$ and the hyperbolic functions
have dimensionless arguments; $t=\pi/2$ means $T=\pi T_*/2$.
For the reconstructed motion use
$x_{\rm phys}(T,\rho_{\rm phys})=D_*x(T/T_*,\rho_{\rm phys}/D_*)$;
the chain rule restores $R_{\rm phys}^{\mathsf T}dR_{\rm phys}/dT
=[\omega_{\rm phys}]_\times$ and the dimensioned torque-free equation.
This convention uses [[def-cm01-units]] and reports no measurement.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), inherited for finite mass moments and inertial
integrals through the rigid-material and torque-balance suppliers, and for
the double-cover surjectivity used in the quaternion constructions below. Consider two **declared** models of the rigid-material branch
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]], each with body inertia matrix diagonal in the
declared positively oriented orthonormal basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ and no other inertia data,
each with time window $I_0=\mathbb R$ (equivalently all physical times $T\in\mathbb R$),
each used in the torque-free branch of [[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause
(iv):

- **Model S** (symmetric): $I=\mathrm{diag}(1,1,2)$ in kilogram metres
  squared in the declared units ([[def-cm01-units]]); the principal moments
  are $I_{1}=I_{2}=1$, $I_{3}=2$.
- **Model A** (asymmetric): $I=\mathrm{diag}(1,2,3)$; the principal moments
  are $I_{1}=1<I_{2}=2<I_{3}=3$.

Verify the following.

1. **Principal-axis spins.** For each model, each $j$ and each $\Omega\in\mathbb R$,
   the constant path $\omega\equiv\Omega e_{j}$ is the body angular velocity
   of a torque-free motion; along it $l=\Omega I_{j}e_{j}$ is constant,
   $C=\Omega^{2}I_{j}^{2}$ and $E=\tfrac12\Omega^{2}I_{j}$. In Model S with
   $j=3$ and $\Omega=2$ this gives $l=4e_{3}$, $C=16$, $E=4$; in Model A with
   $j=1$ and $\Omega=1$ it gives $l=e_{1}$, $C=1$, $E=\tfrac12$.
2. **A non-uniform symmetric-top motion.** For Model S the path
   $$\omega(t)=\bigl(\tfrac12\cos t,\ \tfrac12\sin t,\ 1\bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R)$$
   satisfies the torque-free Euler equations
   $l'=l\times(I^{-1}l)$ and is the body angular velocity of a torque-free
   motion of Model S; along it
   $$l(t)=\bigl(\tfrac12\cos t,\ \tfrac12\sin t,\ 2\bigr),\qquad C=\frac{17}{4},\qquad E=\frac98,\qquad\lVert\omega(t)\rVert_2^{2}=\frac54,$$
   and $\omega$ is not constant: $\omega(\tfrac\pi2)-\omega(0)=(-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,0)$.
3. **Linearization of Model A at its principal-axis spins.** At the spin
   $\Omega e_{1}$ with $\Omega=1$ the linearized system of
   [[pthm-cm11-linearized-spin]] has $\lambda_{1}=-\tfrac13$, $\kappa_{1}=1/\sqrt3$, and the
   pair $(\delta_{2},\delta_{3})=(\cos(t/\sqrt3),\ -\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\sin(t/\sqrt3))$
   solves the transverse equations; at the intermediate spin $e_{2}$ with
   $\Omega=1$ the linearized system has $\lambda_{2}=\tfrac13>0$ and the
   solution with $\delta_{1}(0)=1$, $\delta_{3}(0)=0$ has $\delta_{1}(t)=\cosh(t/\sqrt3)$,
   which is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$; at the extreme spin $e_{3}$ with
   $\Omega=1$ one has $\kappa_{3}=1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only through the integrals of
[[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]]. Adopt a model of the rigid-material branch
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] that is **nondegenerate** in the sense of
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] clause (a) (no line through the origin carries
the whole mass), and use it in the **torque-free** external-torque branch of
[[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iv): the datum vanishes, so along every
motion of the resulting model the adopted balance reads $L_c'=0$ on the time
window $I_0$. Let $\omega$ be the body angular velocity, $I$ the body inertia
matrix and $l:=I\omega$ ([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]],
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]). Then:

1. **Conservation of angular momentum.** The angular momentum about the
   centre of mass $L_c(t)=R(t)l(t)$ of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]] clause
   4 is constant on $I_0$; in particular $\lVert L_c\rVert_2$ is constant.
2. **Energy-momentum invariants and principal components.** The scalars
   $$C:=\langle l,l\rangle=\lVert L_c\rVert_2^{2},\qquad E:=\tfrac12\,\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\tfrac12\,\langle l,I^{-1}l\rangle$$
   are constant on $I_0$, and $l$ satisfies the torque-free equation
   $$l'=l\times(I^{-1}l).$$
   If $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ is a positively oriented orthonormal eigenbasis of $I$ with
   $Ie_{j}=I_{j}e_{j}$ and $l=\sum_{j}l_{j}e_{j}$
   ([[pthm-cm10-principal-axes]] clauses (a)-(b)), then
   $$C=\sum_{j}l_{j}^{2},\qquad E=\sum_{j}\frac{l_{j}^{2}}{2I_{j}},$$
   and the component equations are
   $$l_{1}'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_{3}}-\frac1{I_{2}}\Bigr)l_{2}l_{3},\qquad l_{2}'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_{1}}-\frac1{I_{3}}\Bigr)l_{1}l_{3},\qquad l_{3}'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_{2}}-\frac1{I_{1}}\Bigr)l_{1}l_{2}.$$
3. **The energy invariant is the rotational kinetic energy.** $E$ equals the
   rotational term $\tfrac12\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega$ of the model's kinetic
   energy in clause 3 of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]]; and with
   $I_{\min}:=\min_{j}I_{j}>0$ one has
   $$\lVert\omega(t)\rVert_2^{2}\le\frac{2E}{I_{\min}}\qquad(t\in I_0).$$
   In particular both $l$ and $\omega$ are bounded on $I_0$.
4. **The spin field is globally solvable.** The autonomous field
   $F(l)=l\times(I^{-1}l)$ on $\mathbb R^{3}$ is locally Lipschitz in the
   state variable ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]), and
   every solution of $l'=F(l)$ has a unique maximal extension defined
   on all of $\mathbb R$, and that extension satisfies $\lVert l(t)\rVert_2=\lVert l(0)\rVert_2$
   for every $t$. Consequently the $l$-path of a torque-free motion is the
   restriction to $I_0$ of a solution defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and its
   path is contained in the compact level set
   $$\Lambda(C,E):=\bigl\{z\in\mathbb R^{3}:\langle z,z\rangle=C,\ \tfrac12\langle z,I^{-1}z\rangle=E\bigr\},$$
   which is nonempty because it contains the datum at any chosen time of the motion.

The statement is conditional on the adopted model, its nondegeneracy and the
zero-torque balance; it asserts no orientation of the body in space, no
measured value and no empirical law.

**Numerical SI convention.** Let $T$ denote physical elapsed time and fix
$T_*=1\,\mathrm s$, $M_*=1\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $D_*=1\,\mathrm m$.
Below $t:=T/T_*$ is dimensionless and all quantities are numerical SI
values: inertia is divided by $M_*D_*^2$, angular velocity and its
perturbations by $T_*^{-1}$, angular momentum by $M_*D_*^2/T_*$,
and energy by $M_*D_*^2/T_*^2$. Primes differentiate with respect to $t$.
Restore physical angular velocity by
$\omega_{\rm phys}(T)=\omega(T/T_*)/T_*$ and angular momentum by
$l_{\rm phys}(T)=(M_*D_*^2/T_*)l(T/T_*)$.
The displayed numerical rates $1$, $2$, $1/\sqrt3$ mean physical rates
$1/T_*$, $2/T_*$, $1/(\sqrt3 T_*)$; $\lambda_j$ is restored by
$\lambda_{j,\rm phys}=\lambda_j/T_*^2$.
Thus $\cos t$, $\sin t$, $\cos(t/\sqrt3)$ and the hyperbolic functions
have dimensionless arguments; $t=\pi/2$ means $T=\pi T_*/2$.
For the reconstructed motion use
$x_{\rm phys}(T,\rho_{\rm phys})=D_*x(T/T_*,\rho_{\rm phys}/D_*)$;
the chain rule restores $R_{\rm phys}^{\mathsf T}dR_{\rm phys}/dT
=[\omega_{\rm phys}]_\times$ and the dimensioned torque-free equation.
This convention uses [[def-cm01-units]] and reports no measurement.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), inherited for finite mass moments and inertial
integrals through the rigid-material and torque-balance suppliers, and for
the double-cover surjectivity used in the quaternion constructions below. Consider two **declared** models of the rigid-material branch
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]], each with body inertia matrix diagonal in the
declared positively oriented orthonormal basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ and no other inertia data,
each with time window $I_0=\mathbb R$ (equivalently all physical times $T\in\mathbb R$),
each used in the torque-free branch of [[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause
(iv):

- **Model S** (symmetric): $I=\mathrm{diag}(1,1,2)$ in kilogram metres
  squared in the declared units ([[def-cm01-units]]); the principal moments
  are $I_{1}=I_{2}=1$, $I_{3}=2$.
- **Model A** (asymmetric): $I=\mathrm{diag}(1,2,3)$; the principal moments
  are $I_{1}=1<I_{2}=2<I_{3}=3$.

Verify the following.

1. **Principal-axis spins.** For each model, each $j$ and each $\Omega\in\mathbb R$,
   the constant path $\omega\equiv\Omega e_{j}$ is the body angular velocity
   of a torque-free motion; along it $l=\Omega I_{j}e_{j}$ is constant,
   $C=\Omega^{2}I_{j}^{2}$ and $E=\tfrac12\Omega^{2}I_{j}$. In Model S with
   $j=3$ and $\Omega=2$ this gives $l=4e_{3}$, $C=16$, $E=4$; in Model A with
   $j=1$ and $\Omega=1$ it gives $l=e_{1}$, $C=1$, $E=\tfrac12$.
2. **A non-uniform symmetric-top motion.** For Model S the path
   $$\omega(t)=\bigl(\tfrac12\cos t,\ \tfrac12\sin t,\ 1\bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R)$$
   satisfies the torque-free Euler equations
   $l'=l\times(I^{-1}l)$ and is the body angular velocity of a torque-free
   motion of Model S; along it
   $$l(t)=\bigl(\tfrac12\cos t,\ \tfrac12\sin t,\ 2\bigr),\qquad C=\frac{17}{4},\qquad E=\frac98,\qquad\lVert\omega(t)\rVert_2^{2}=\frac54,$$
   and $\omega$ is not constant: $\omega(\tfrac\pi2)-\omega(0)=(-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,0)$.
3. **Linearization of Model A at its principal-axis spins.** At the spin
   $\Omega e_{1}$ with $\Omega=1$ the linearized system of
   [[pthm-cm11-linearized-spin]] has $\lambda_{1}=-\tfrac13$, $\kappa_{1}=1/\sqrt3$, and the
   pair $(\delta_{2},\delta_{3})=(\cos(t/\sqrt3),\ -\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\sin(t/\sqrt3))$
   solves the transverse equations; at the intermediate spin $e_{2}$ with
   $\Omega=1$ the linearized system has $\lambda_{2}=\tfrac13>0$ and the
   solution with $\delta_{1}(0)=1$, $\delta_{3}(0)=0$ has $\delta_{1}(t)=\cosh(t/\sqrt3)$,
   which is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$; at the extreme spin $e_{3}$ with
   $\Omega=1$ one has $\kappa_{3}=1$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

Let $\gamma$ be the unique smallest positive zero of cosine supplied by [[thm-cosine-has-a-smallest-positive-zero]]. Define
$$\pi:=2\gamma.$$

Thus $\pi>0$ and $\pi/2=\gamma$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

derivations.claim: The motion of [F2] is a torque-free motion of model S on $\mathbb R$, its angular momentum about the centre of mass is constant (with $\lVert L_c\rVert_2^{2}=\tfrac{17}4$), and its rotational kinetic energy is constantly $\tfrac98$; hence all hypotheses of the refuted statement are satisfied.

By [F3], $\omega(\tfrac\pi2)-\omega(0)=(-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,0)$, whose Euclidean norm is $\tfrac{\sqrt2}2\neq0$; hence $\omega(\tfrac\pi2)\neq\omega(0)$, so the body angular velocity of the motion is not constant in time.
The hypotheses of the refuted statement hold along the motion by step 1.1, while its asserted conclusion fails by step 2.1; therefore the statement is false.

boundaries.reason: The counterexample is nonempty: the model and motion of the companion example exist, and step 1.1 verifies that they meet the hypotheses of the refuted statement.
The zero case of the difference used to refute the conclusion is treated in step 2.1: the displayed two times give a nonzero difference, so the negation is witnessed by a nonzero value.
One motion and one model suffice to refute a universally quantified statement, and step 1.1 fixes exactly one model and one motion.
Degeneracy of the inertia data is immaterial here: the model diag(1,1,2) has repeated transverse moments but is nondegenerate, and the refutation uses only the explicit solution.
The endpoints of the time interval are not used: the motion is defined on all of R and the two times 0 and pi/2 are interior points.
No choice principle is used in the refutation itself; the realisability of the path as a motion is quoted from the companion example under its declared hypothesis.
The forward direction is the verification that the hypotheses of the refuted statement hold (step 1.1).
The reverse direction is the exhibition of the failure of its conclusion (steps 2.1 and 3.1), which is what makes the statement false.

risk_review.notes: Three steps checked against Model S witness: zero torque balance and constant spatial L_c with C=17/4,E=9/8 but omega(pi/2)-omega(0)=(-1/2,1/2,0), norm sqrt(2)/2. Refuter:27:2 confirmed inherited dimensional defect and repaired by explicit numerical SI convention; physical comparison times 0 and pi T_*/2 and nonzero velocity difference divided by T_* preserve counterexample. Added exact quarter-turn/pi and square-root suppliers, explicit AC_omega hypothesis for witness construction and units supplier. Refuted universal statement unchanged; no stronger claim against model. Page-only consumer receives same convention; no outside consumer found.

citations.quote:
Adopt the model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: the reference mass
distribution $\nu$, its total mass $m=\nu(\mathbb R^3)$ and its centred
reference coordinates $\int\rho\,d\nu(\rho)=0$. Assume the Axiom of Countable
Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, used only through
[[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]] to make the polynomial moments of $\nu$ of
degree at most two finite real numbers. Fix an inertial frame and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^2$
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]).

**(a) Body inertia matrix.** The **body inertia matrix** of the model is the
inertia matrix of the reference mass distribution,
$$I:=I(\nu)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}I_3-\rho\rho^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
with entries $I_{jk}=\int(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}\delta_{jk}-\rho_j\rho_k)\,d\nu$
as in [[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]; the matrix is expressed
in the standard basis of the reference coordinates. Its entries are finite
real numbers, it is symmetric, and for every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)\ \ge 0$$
by [[lem-cm-inertia-matrix-properties]] clauses 1-2; hence $I$ is symmetric
and its quadratic form is positive semidefinite. The dimension is
$[I]=\mu\ell^{2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]), read in kilogram metres squared. The
model is **nondegenerate** when no line through the origin carries the whole
mass, that is $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega\bigr)>0$ for every
$\omega\neq0$, and **degenerate** otherwise; the connection between this
criterion and the strict positivity and invertibility of $I$ is proved in the
principal-axes theorem of this page.

**(b) Spatial inertia tensor at the centre of mass.** The **spatial inertia
tensor** of the model at time $t$ is
$$I(t):=R(t)\,I\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
the matrix of the same quadratic form in the frame's spatial coordinates: for
every $n\in\mathbb R^3$,
$n^{\mathsf T}I(t)n=(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)^{\mathsf T}I(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)$. Its
entries are $C^2$ functions of $t$, since $R$ is of class $C^2$ and $I$ is
constant; the matrix rotates with the body and returns to $I$ in the
body-fixed frame, where $R=I_3$.

**(c) Inertia tensor about a spatial point.** For a spatial point
$p\in\mathbb R^3$ let
$$a(t,p):=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\bigl(p-c(t)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^3$$
be the **reference coordinate of $p$**, that is the label of the material
point of the reference placement that is placed at $p$ at time $t$. The
**inertia tensor of the model about $p$** at time $t$ is
$$I(t,p):=R(t)\,I_\nu\bigl(a(t,p)\bigr)\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
where
$$I_\nu(a)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho-a\rVert_2^{2}I_3-(\rho-a)(\rho-a)^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)$$
is the inertia tensor of the mass distribution about the point $a$ of the
reference coordinates ([[def-cm-inertia-tensor-about-a-point]]). Since the
label of a spatial point is uniquely determined by the placement, this is
well defined; for the centre of mass, $a(t,c(t))=0$ and
$I(t,c(t))=I(t)$. The dimension is again $\mu\ell^{2}$, read in kilogram
metres squared.

**(d) Moment of inertia about an axis.** Let $\ell$ be a spatial line at time
$t$, given by a point $p\in\mathbb R^3$ and a unit direction $n\in\mathbb R^3$
($\lVert n\rVert_2=1$). The **moment of inertia of the model about $\ell$** is
$$\Theta_\ell(t):=n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n .$$
Its invariance under the choices entering the description of the line and
its identification with the integral defining the physical moment of inertia
about the line are statements, not conventions; they are proved in clause
(c) of the principal-axes theorem of this page. For a **body-fixed
axis**, that is a line through the centre of mass whose direction in
reference coordinates is a constant unit vector $n_0$, the moment is
$$n_0^{\mathsf T}I n_0=\int\lVert n_0\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),$$
by clause (a), and is independent of time, because $I$ and $n_0$ are model
data.

**(e) What is constant and what moves.** The body inertia matrix $I$ is
determined by the model's reference mass distribution alone and does not
depend on the time, the frame or the motion; the spatial inertia tensor
$I(t)$ depends on the motion through the orientation $R(t)$; the inertia
tensor $I(t,p)$ about a spatial point depends on the motion through both the
orientation and the position of $p$. Principal axes and principal moments of
$I$ are the subject of the principal-axes theorem of this page.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only to make the integrals finite. Adopt the
model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] and its inertia data
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]): the reference mass distribution $\nu$ with
total mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates, the body inertia matrix $I$,
the spatial inertia tensor $I(t)=R(t)IR(t)^{\mathsf T}$ of a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$, and the inertia tensor $I(t,p)$ about a spatial
point $p$ ([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]). Then:

**(a) Principal basis.** There is an orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of
$\mathbb R^3$ and real numbers $I_1,I_2,I_3$, the **principal axes** and
**principal moments** of the model, with
$$Ie_j=I_je_j\qquad(j=1,2,3).$$

**(b) Quadratic form and rotational term.** For every
$\omega=\sum_j\omega_je_j\in\mathbb R^3$ one has
$I\omega=\sum_jI_j\omega_je_j$ and
$$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\sum_jI_j\omega_j^{2}=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)\ \ge 0,$$
and each principal moment is
$I_j=e_j^{\mathsf T}Ie_j=\int\lVert e_j\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)$.

**(c) Axis moments.** For every unit vector $n\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$n^{\mathsf T}In=\int\lVert n\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho);$$
for every spatial point $p$ and unit vector $n$, with $x=x(t,\cdot)$ the
placement at time $t$,
$$n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n=\int\lVert n\times\bigl(x(t,\rho)-p\bigr)\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho).$$
Consequently the number $\Theta_\ell(t)=n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n$ of
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] depends only on the spatial line $\ell$
$\{p+sn:s\in\mathbb R\}$ and not on the choice of the point $p$ on it nor on
the sign of the unit direction $n$.

**(d) Vanishing and positivity.** Each principal moment satisfies $I_j\ge0$,
and $I_j=0$ exactly when $\nu$ is supported on the line $\mathbb Re_j$ of the
principal axis, that is $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Re_j\bigr)=0$.
If the model is nondegenerate, that is if
$\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega\bigr)>0$ for every
$\omega\neq0$, then every $I_j>0$ and $I$ is invertible. If $\nu$ is
supported on some line through the origin (such a line exists whenever the
support of a centred $\nu$ is contained in a line, because the mean of $\nu$
is the origin), then $I$ is not invertible.

**(e) Extremal moments.** For every unit vector
$n=\sum_jc_je_j$ one has $n^{\mathsf T}In=\sum_jI_jc_j^{2}$ and therefore
$$\min_jI_j\ \le\ n^{\mathsf T}In\ \le\ \max_jI_j,$$
with the value $\max_jI_j$ attained at a unit eigenvector for a maximal
principal moment and the value $\min_jI_j$ attained at a unit eigenvector for
a minimal principal moment. Hence the largest and smallest principal moments
are the maximum and minimum of the rotational-inertia quadratic form over the
unit sphere.

The identities are conditional on the model data and the stated choice
assumption; no equation of motion and no conservation statement is used or
asserted.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following **rigid-material
model** branch, in the spacetime and frames of [[post-cm01-spacetime]] and
[[post-cm01-frames]].

**(i) Reference mass distribution.** A rigid-material model carries, besides
the framework's time and frame structure, a **reference mass distribution**: a
measure $\nu$ on the Borel space $(\mathbb R^3,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3))$ that
is a mass distribution in the sense of
[[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]] — finite and bounded, with
$\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline B_R(0)\bigr)=0$ for some real $R>0$,
and of total mass $m:=\nu(\mathbb R^3)\in(0,+\infty)$ — whose reference
coordinates are **centred**,
$$\int\rho\,d\nu(\rho)=0\in\mathbb R^3 .$$
The label variable $\rho$ is a coordinate of the model's reference placement
and has dimension $\ell$, each component read in metres; the total mass $m$
has dimension $\mu$, read in kilograms, and $R$ has dimension $\ell$ and is
the model's **reference size**
([[def-cm01-units]]). Under the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$,
used only through [[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]] to make the polynomial
moments of $\nu$ of degree at most two finite, the first and second moments
of $\nu$ are finite real numbers. The measure $\nu$ and the number $m$ are
model data: no distribution of mass of any concrete body and no measured mass
is asserted.

**(ii) Time window and motions.** A model carries a **time window**
$I_0\subseteq\mathbb R$, a nondegenerate open interval $(a,b)$ with
$-\infty\le a<b\le+\infty$ and at least two points, read in seconds. Fix an
**inertial frame** of the model, that is the adapted chart
$(o,u,(e_1,e_2,e_3))$ with coordinates $(t,x)$ of [[post-cm01-frames]]. A
**motion** of the model in this frame is a map
$x:I_0\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ for which there exist a map
$c:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ and a map $R:I_0\to SO(3)$, both of class $C^2$
(componentwise derivatives, [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] for the coordinates
and [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]] for the target), such that
$$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho\qquad(t\in I_0,\ \rho\in\mathbb R^3).$$
Adopt: the motions of the model are the maps of this form, and the pair
$(c,R)$ is the **configuration path** of the motion. The map
$x(t,\cdot):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is the **placement** at time $t$ and is
the rigid placement of [[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]]
with translation $c$ and rotation $R$; its material velocity is
$\partial_tx(t,\rho)=c'(t)+R'(t)\rho$, defined by differentiability of $c$ and
of the entries of $R$. The time window $I_0$ is the interval on which the
model's configuration path is considered; the model's time coordinate is
the frame time $t$.

**(iii) Rigidity idealization.** The idealization adopted is that the model
describes a body that does not deform, and its content is the representation
(ii): a placement of the form $x=c+R\rho$ with $R\in SO(3)$ preserves every
mutual distance, since $R(t)$ preserves the Euclidean norm
([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]), so for all $\rho,\rho'\in\mathbb R^3$
the number $\lVert x(t,\rho)-x(t,\rho')\rVert_2=\lVert\rho-\rho'\rVert_2$ is
independent of $t$. The model class (ii) is *adopted* as the definition of a
rigid-material placement; a motion of material points that preserves all
mutual distances but whose label set fails to determine a rotation is not
claimed to be of this form, and the general characterization of
distance-preserving placements is neither asserted nor used on this page.
For a **nondegenerate labeling** — a label set containing the origin and two
linearly independent material vectors — distinct configurations $(c,R)$ and
$(\bar c,\bar R)$ give distinct placements, by [[lem-cm-rigid-labeling-stabilizer]];
the configuration data of (ii) therefore do not overcount for such a body.
Degenerate labelings and degenerate mass distributions are not excluded by
this postulate; the later items of the pair state where invertibility of the
inertial data must be assumed.

**(iv) Centre of mass and orientation.** Because the reference coordinates are
centred, the identity
$$\int x(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho)=mc(t)$$
holds for every motion, by linearity of the integral and
$\int\rho\,d\nu=0$; the physical reading is that $c(t)$ is the position of the
centre of mass of the model in the placement at time $t$. The rotation
$R(t)$ is the model's **orientation**: it carries reference coordinates into
the frame's spatial coordinates, and the **body-fixed frame** at time $t$ is
the ordered orthonormal basis $(R(t)e_1,R(t)e_2,R(t)e_3)$ of the spatial
space. The reading of $R(t)$ as the orientation of the placement uses the
nondegeneracy of (iii): for a nondegenerate labeling the material points
determine $R(t)$ uniquely, so the orientation is an attribute of the body's
placement and not of the choice of label coordinates.

**(v) Frame changes.** The description of a motion in a second inertial frame
is obtained by the change of coordinates $t'=t+b$, $x'=Qx+ut+a$ of
[[post-cm01-frames]] clause (iv), applied to every event of the motion; here
$Q\in SO(3)$ and $u\in\mathbb R^3$ are the rotation and the boost velocity of
that clause, written $R$ and $v$ there and renamed here to avoid a clash with
the orientation path $R(t)$ of clause (ii) and with the material velocity
field of the pair's definition. With the same $\rho$ labelling a material
point, the description in the second frame is
$$\tilde x(t',\rho):=Q\,x(t'-b,\rho)+u\,(t'-b)+a .$$
This description is again a motion of the model, with configuration path
$$\tilde c(t')=Qc(t'-b)+u\,(t'-b)+a,\qquad \tilde R(t')=Q\,R(t'-b),$$
because $SO(3)$ is closed under multiplication
([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]); this is a consistency requirement of
the model's frame language, exactly as for the particle worldlines of
[[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (ii). The derived transformation laws of the
angular velocity, of the inertia data and of the kinetic splitting are
theorems of this pair's page, not part of this postulate.

**(vi) No dynamics.** This postulate fixes the kinematic class of the model
and its mass data only. It asserts no force law, no torque law, no equation of
motion for the pair $(c,R)$, and no balance or conservation law; in
particular the model does not by itself constrain the configuration path,
and the effect of forces and torques on a body is a separate model
assumption. It also asserts no measured value of any mass, length, duration
or orientation.

**(vii) Scope and exclusions.** The branch excludes deformation, internal
degrees of freedom such as temperature, chemical state or an independent spin
variable, variable mass, ablation and impact events, contact, friction and
dissipative constitutive laws, and any relativistic or quantum description.
It excludes bodies whose mass distribution is not a bounded finite Borel
measure of the stated kind. A rigid-material model is not a system of
finitely many particle labels: the continuum measure $\nu$ carries the mass
data of the model, and the situations of point masses are the special cases
of measures supported on finitely many points. All physical statements about
the model weight material points by $\nu$; properties of $\nu$-null sets of
labels are not physical properties of the body.

**Numerical SI convention.** Let $T$ denote physical elapsed time and fix
$T_*=1\,\mathrm s$, $M_*=1\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $D_*=1\,\mathrm m$.
Below $t:=T/T_*$ is dimensionless and all quantities are numerical SI
values: inertia is divided by $M_*D_*^2$, angular velocity and its
perturbations by $T_*^{-1}$, angular momentum by $M_*D_*^2/T_*$,
and energy by $M_*D_*^2/T_*^2$. Primes differentiate with respect to $t$.
Restore physical angular velocity by
$\omega_{\rm phys}(T)=\omega(T/T_*)/T_*$ and angular momentum by
$l_{\rm phys}(T)=(M_*D_*^2/T_*)l(T/T_*)$.
The displayed numerical rates $1$, $2$, $1/\sqrt3$ mean physical rates
$1/T_*$, $2/T_*$, $1/(\sqrt3 T_*)$; $\lambda_j$ is restored by
$\lambda_{j,\rm phys}=\lambda_j/T_*^2$.
Thus $\cos t$, $\sin t$, $\cos(t/\sqrt3)$ and the hyperbolic functions
have dimensionless arguments; $t=\pi/2$ means $T=\pi T_*/2$.
For the reconstructed motion use
$x_{\rm phys}(T,\rho_{\rm phys})=D_*x(T/T_*,\rho_{\rm phys}/D_*)$;
the chain rule restores $R_{\rm phys}^{\mathsf T}dR_{\rm phys}/dT
=[\omega_{\rm phys}]_\times$ and the dimensioned torque-free equation.
This convention uses [[def-cm01-units]] and reports no measurement.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), inherited for finite mass moments and inertial
integrals through the rigid-material and torque-balance suppliers, and for
the double-cover surjectivity used in the quaternion constructions below. Consider two **declared** models of the rigid-material branch
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]], each with body inertia matrix diagonal in the
declared positively oriented orthonormal basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ and no other inertia data,
each with time window $I_0=\mathbb R$ (equivalently all physical times $T\in\mathbb R$),
each used in the torque-free branch of [[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause
(iv):

- **Model S** (symmetric): $I=\mathrm{diag}(1,1,2)$ in kilogram metres
  squared in the declared units ([[def-cm01-units]]); the principal moments
  are $I_{1}=I_{2}=1$, $I_{3}=2$.
- **Model A** (asymmetric): $I=\mathrm{diag}(1,2,3)$; the principal moments
  are $I_{1}=1<I_{2}=2<I_{3}=3$.

Verify the following.

1. **Principal-axis spins.** For each model, each $j$ and each $\Omega\in\mathbb R$,
   the constant path $\omega\equiv\Omega e_{j}$ is the body angular velocity
   of a torque-free motion; along it $l=\Omega I_{j}e_{j}$ is constant,
   $C=\Omega^{2}I_{j}^{2}$ and $E=\tfrac12\Omega^{2}I_{j}$. In Model S with
   $j=3$ and $\Omega=2$ this gives $l=4e_{3}$, $C=16$, $E=4$; in Model A with
   $j=1$ and $\Omega=1$ it gives $l=e_{1}$, $C=1$, $E=\tfrac12$.
2. **A non-uniform symmetric-top motion.** For Model S the path
   $$\omega(t)=\bigl(\tfrac12\cos t,\ \tfrac12\sin t,\ 1\bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R)$$
   satisfies the torque-free Euler equations
   $l'=l\times(I^{-1}l)$ and is the body angular velocity of a torque-free
   motion of Model S; along it
   $$l(t)=\bigl(\tfrac12\cos t,\ \tfrac12\sin t,\ 2\bigr),\qquad C=\frac{17}{4},\qquad E=\frac98,\qquad\lVert\omega(t)\rVert_2^{2}=\frac54,$$
   and $\omega$ is not constant: $\omega(\tfrac\pi2)-\omega(0)=(-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,0)$.
3. **Linearization of Model A at its principal-axis spins.** At the spin
   $\Omega e_{1}$ with $\Omega=1$ the linearized system of
   [[pthm-cm11-linearized-spin]] has $\lambda_{1}=-\tfrac13$, $\kappa_{1}=1/\sqrt3$, and the
   pair $(\delta_{2},\delta_{3})=(\cos(t/\sqrt3),\ -\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\sin(t/\sqrt3))$
   solves the transverse equations; at the intermediate spin $e_{2}$ with
   $\Omega=1$ the linearized system has $\lambda_{2}=\tfrac13>0$ and the
   solution with $\delta_{1}(0)=1$, $\delta_{3}(0)=0$ has $\delta_{1}(t)=\cosh(t/\sqrt3)$,
   which is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$; at the extreme spin $e_{3}$ with
   $\Omega=1$ one has $\kappa_{3}=1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), carried through [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]
clause (i) and [[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] for finite mass moments, through
[[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (i) and the inertial-integral suppliers
of [[pthm-cm11-euler-equations]] and [[pthm-cm11-torque-free-invariants]],
and through the double-cover supplier of
[[def-cm-quaternion-rotation-map-and-cover]] for the surjectivity used to
choose initial unit quaternions. The stability and escape calculations
for a given positive diagonal $I$ introduce no additional choice principle.
Adopt a **nondegenerate** model of the rigid-material branch
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] with pairwise distinct principal moments, and
label a positively oriented principal basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$, $Ie_{j}=I_{j}e_{j}$, so that
$$I_{1}<I_{2}<I_{3}.$$
Use the model in the **torque-free** branch of [[post-cm11-torque-balance]]
clause (iv). Along any motion write $l:=I\omega$; the torque-free $l$-path
solves $l'=l\times(I^{-1}l)$ and is the restriction of a solution defined on
all of $\mathbb R$ ([[pthm-cm11-torque-free-invariants]] clauses 2 and 4).
Write $I_0$ for the model's time window. All physical realizations below
use paths restricted to $I_0$; clause 3's forward-time realization assumes
$[0,\infty)\subseteq I_0$. Let $L\neq0$. Then:

1. **Stability of the extreme-axis spins.** For $j=1$ and $j=3$ the constant
   path $t\mapsto Le_{j}$ is Lyapunov stable for the $l$-system
   ([[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]): for every $\varepsilon>0$
   there is $\delta\in(0,\varepsilon]$ such that every maximal solution $l$ with
   $\lVert l(0)-Le_{j}\rVert_2<\delta$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and
   satisfies $\lVert l(t)-Le_{j}\rVert_2<\varepsilon$ for all $t\ge0$.
   Consequently every torque-free motion of a model of the branch whose time
   window contains $[0,\infty)$ and whose datum satisfies
   $\lVert l(0)-Le_{j}\rVert_2<\delta$ has, with $\Omega:=L/I_{j}$,
   $$\lVert l(t)-Le_{j}\rVert_2<\varepsilon,\qquad \lVert\omega(t)-\Omega e_{j}\rVert_2<\frac{\varepsilon}{I_{\min}}\qquad(t\ge0),$$
   where $I_{\min}=I_{1}$.
2. **Explicit deviation bound.** For $j=1$ define on $\mathbb R^{3}$
   $$c_{1}:=\tfrac12\Bigl(\frac1{I_{1}}-\frac1{I_{2}}\Bigr)>0,\qquad D_{1}(l):=\tfrac12\Bigl(\frac{\langle l,l\rangle}{I_{1}}-\langle l,I^{-1}l\rangle\Bigr)\ \ge0,$$
   and for $j=3$
   $$c_{3}:=\tfrac12\Bigl(\frac1{I_{2}}-\frac1{I_{3}}\Bigr)>0,\qquad D_{3}(l):=\tfrac12\Bigl(\langle l,I^{-1}l\rangle-\frac{\langle l,l\rangle}{I_{3}}\Bigr)\ \ge0.$$
   Along every solution of $l'=l\times(I^{-1}l)$ one has, for all $t$ in its
   interval, with $l(0)$ evaluated on its unique global extension if
   the original interval does not contain $0$,
   $$l_{2}(t)^{2}+l_{3}(t)^{2}\le\frac{D_{1}(l(0))}{c_{1}},\qquad l_{1}(t)^{2}+l_{2}(t)^{2}\le\frac{D_{3}(l(0))}{c_{3}}.$$
3. **Instability of the intermediate-axis spin.** The spin $l_{0}:=Le_{2}$ is
   not Lyapunov stable. More precisely, with
   $$a:=\sqrt{\frac{1/I_{1}-1/I_{2}}{1/I_{2}-1/I_{3}}}>0,\qquad c_{0}:=a\Bigl(\frac1{I_{2}}-\frac1{I_{3}}\Bigr)\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\,\lvert L\rvert>0,\qquad \delta_{0}:=\frac{\lvert L\rvert}{2\sqrt{1+a^{2}}},\qquad \varepsilon_{0}:=\frac{\lvert L\rvert}{2},$$
   if $[0,\infty)\subseteq I_0$, then for every $\delta>0$ there are a
   torque-free **motion** of this model on $I_0$, with body angular velocity $\omega$,
   and a time $t\ge0$ such that
   $$\lVert l(0)-Le_{2}\rVert_2<\delta,\qquad \lVert l(t)-Le_{2}\rVert_2\ge\varepsilon_{0},$$
   and the escape can be arranged with $t\le c_{0}^{-1}\log(\delta_{0}/\eta)$
   for any prescribed $\eta\in(0,\min\{\delta_{0},\delta\})$ whose initial
   datum $l^{\eta}:=\bigl(\eta,\ \sigma\sqrt{L^{2}-(1+a^{2})\eta^{2}},\ -\sigma a\eta\bigr)$,
   $\sigma:=L/\lvert L\rvert$, satisfies $\lVert l^{\eta}-Le_{2}\rVert_2<\delta$. Such $\eta$ exist arbitrarily close to zero, and the datum belongs to the $l$-system.
4. **Orientation caveat.** For $j=1$ or $j=3$ and every $\Omega\neq0$ there
   are two torque-free motions of the model, with $c\equiv0$, whose body
   angular velocities are both constantly equal to $\Omega e_{j}$ and whose
   orientation paths $R_{1},R_{2}$ satisfy $R_{2}(t)=R_{1}(t)S$ for every $t$
   and a fixed rotation $S\neq I_{3}$. Consequently clause 1 asserts nothing
   about the closeness of the orientations of two motions.

The statement is conditional on the adopted model and zero-torque balance; it
asserts no force, no damping, no measurement and no empirical law.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only through the integrals of
[[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]]. Adopt a model of the rigid-material branch
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] that is **nondegenerate** in the sense of
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] clause (a) (no line through the origin carries
the whole mass), and use it in the **torque-free** external-torque branch of
[[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iv): the datum vanishes, so along every
motion of the resulting model the adopted balance reads $L_c'=0$ on the time
window $I_0$. Let $\omega$ be the body angular velocity, $I$ the body inertia
matrix and $l:=I\omega$ ([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]],
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]). Then:

1. **Conservation of angular momentum.** The angular momentum about the
   centre of mass $L_c(t)=R(t)l(t)$ of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]] clause
   4 is constant on $I_0$; in particular $\lVert L_c\rVert_2$ is constant.
2. **Energy-momentum invariants and principal components.** The scalars
   $$C:=\langle l,l\rangle=\lVert L_c\rVert_2^{2},\qquad E:=\tfrac12\,\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\tfrac12\,\langle l,I^{-1}l\rangle$$
   are constant on $I_0$, and $l$ satisfies the torque-free equation
   $$l'=l\times(I^{-1}l).$$
   If $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ is a positively oriented orthonormal eigenbasis of $I$ with
   $Ie_{j}=I_{j}e_{j}$ and $l=\sum_{j}l_{j}e_{j}$
   ([[pthm-cm10-principal-axes]] clauses (a)-(b)), then
   $$C=\sum_{j}l_{j}^{2},\qquad E=\sum_{j}\frac{l_{j}^{2}}{2I_{j}},$$
   and the component equations are
   $$l_{1}'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_{3}}-\frac1{I_{2}}\Bigr)l_{2}l_{3},\qquad l_{2}'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_{1}}-\frac1{I_{3}}\Bigr)l_{1}l_{3},\qquad l_{3}'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_{2}}-\frac1{I_{1}}\Bigr)l_{1}l_{2}.$$
3. **The energy invariant is the rotational kinetic energy.** $E$ equals the
   rotational term $\tfrac12\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega$ of the model's kinetic
   energy in clause 3 of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]]; and with
   $I_{\min}:=\min_{j}I_{j}>0$ one has
   $$\lVert\omega(t)\rVert_2^{2}\le\frac{2E}{I_{\min}}\qquad(t\in I_0).$$
   In particular both $l$ and $\omega$ are bounded on $I_0$.
4. **The spin field is globally solvable.** The autonomous field
   $F(l)=l\times(I^{-1}l)$ on $\mathbb R^{3}$ is locally Lipschitz in the
   state variable ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]), and
   every solution of $l'=F(l)$ has a unique maximal extension defined
   on all of $\mathbb R$, and that extension satisfies $\lVert l(t)\rVert_2=\lVert l(0)\rVert_2$
   for every $t$. Consequently the $l$-path of a torque-free motion is the
   restriction to $I_0$ of a solution defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and its
   path is contained in the compact level set
   $$\Lambda(C,E):=\bigl\{z\in\mathbb R^{3}:\langle z,z\rangle=C,\ \tfrac12\langle z,I^{-1}z\rangle=E\bigr\},$$
   which is nonempty because it contains the datum at any chosen time of the motion.

The statement is conditional on the adopted model, its nondegeneracy and the
zero-torque balance; it asserts no orientation of the body in space, no
measured value and no empirical law.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$ for the three independent *dimension symbols* of length, duration and mass. A **dimension** is an element of the free abelian group generated by $\ell,\tau,\mu$, that is, a triple $(a,b,c)\in\mathbb Z^3$ written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$; **products and inverses** of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, so that $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\cdot\ell^{a'}\tau^{b'}\mu^{c'}=\ell^{a+a'}\tau^{b+b'}\mu^{c+c'}$ and $(\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c})^{-1}=\ell^{-a}\tau^{-b}\mu^{-c}$. The **dimensionless** dimension is $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}$, abbreviated $1$.

**(b) The dimension map.** The conventions assign to the quantities of the framework a **dimension** $[X]$, subject to the rules

$$[XY]=[X][Y],\qquad [X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1},\qquad \left[\frac{dX}{du}\right]=[X][u]^{-1},$$

and to the requirement that a sum $X+Y$ is meaningful only when $[X]=[Y]$, in which case $[X+Y]=[X]$. The third rule applies to a differentiable dependence of a quantity $X$ on a quantity $u$ and covers iterated differentiation, so that $[d^{2}X/du^{2}]=[X][u]^{-2}$. The assignment is part of the conventions: the rules above are consistency requirements on it, not physical laws and not theorems.

**(c) Reference units.** The **metre** is the reference unit of length, the **second** the reference unit of duration and the **kilogram** the reference unit of mass. A quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\,\mathrm s^{b}\,\mathrm{kg}^{c}$: its value is a real multiple of that unit, and the conventions fix how the numerical value of a quantity is read (a coordinate value alone is a real number, and the unit declaration attaches its dimension). The coordinates of an adapted chart of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinate components $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; the slice distance $d_{g}$ of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] between simultaneous events is read in metres.

**(d) Typed quantity conventions.** The following constructions specify the quantities whose dimensions are recorded here, without adopting their dynamics. Fix a positive integer $N$, a nondegenerate open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with time parameter $t$ in seconds, position curves $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ with components in metres, and constant parameters $m_i>0$ in kilograms, for $1\le i\le N$. Derivatives and integrals have the meanings of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. These are conditional numerical constructions in a fixed spatial coordinate system; whether they represent a particular system is a separate model assumption.

1. **Velocity and acceleration** are the maps $w_i=x_i':I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $a_i=x_i'':I\to\mathbb R^3$, of dimensions $\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ componentwise.
2. The **mass operator** is the linear map $\mathsf M:(\mathbb R^3)^N\to(\mathbb R^3)^N$, $\mathsf M(z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(m_1z_1,\ldots,m_Nz_N)$, with dimension $\mu$; the **momentum** of label $i$ is $p_i=m_iw_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$, with component dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$.
3. A **force input** is a specified map $F:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, where $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open, its arguments are time, positions and velocities, and each output component has dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. No regularity or equation equating $F$ with $\mathsf M x''$ is adopted here. A later model must state both if needed.
4. For a specified scalar **potential energy** map $U:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$ and a tuple $x(t)\in O$, the **kinetic energy** is $T(t)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^N m_i\sum_{j=1}^3(w_i(t))_j^2$, and the **mechanical energy** is $E(t)=T(t)+U(t,x(t))$. 5. Given a scalar map $L:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R$ of the energy dimension and $t_0<t_1$ in $I$, assume $t\mapsto L(t,x(t),w(t))$ is integrable on $[t_0,t_1]$. Its **action on this curve segment** is the real number $S[x;t_0,t_1]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(t,x(t),w(t))\,dt$, with dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$ (the integration convention multiplies the integrand's dimension by duration). No variational principle is imposed.
6. Relative to the chosen spatial origin, define the **angular momentum** $J_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ by $J_i(t)=x_i(t)\times p_i(t)$, where for $r,s\in\mathbb R^3$ the operation is explicitly $r\times s=(r_2s_3-r_3s_2,r_3s_1-r_1s_3,r_1s_2-r_2s_1)$. 7. A **rotation matrix** here means a real $3\times3$ matrix $R$ satisfying $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$; its entries are dimensionless. A radian angle is an arc length divided by its positive radius, hence dimensionless. A generalized coordinate means a component of a specified local coordinate chart on a configuration space; each such component has its own declared dimension, and only quantities of equal dimension are added.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any constant or parameter of a model is fixed by this item: in particular no mass, length or duration of any concrete system is asserted, and no measured value is recorded. Two numerical values that are equal but carry different dimensions are not thereby the same quantity. Where a treatment or a later item suppresses a dimensionful constant by a natural-unit convention, that convention is read as shorthand for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored, and it changes no dimension fixed here.

derivations.claim: With $I_{1}=1$, $I_{2}=2$, $I_{3}=3$ and $L=1$: $1/I_{1}-1/I_{2}=\tfrac12$, $1/I_{2}-1/I_{3}=\tfrac16$, so $a^{2}=\tfrac{1/2}{1/6}=3$ and $a=\sqrt3>0$ by [L4]; then $c_{0}=a\,(1/I_{2}-1/I_{3})\,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\lvert L\rvert=\sqrt3\cdot\tfrac16\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}=\tfrac{3}{12}=\tfrac14$ by [L4]. Further $1+a^{2}=1+3=4$, so $\delta_{0}=\tfrac{\lvert L\rvert}{2\sqrt{1+a^{2}}}=\tfrac1{2\cdot2}=\tfrac14$ by [L4] and $\varepsilon_{0}=\tfrac{\lvert L\rvert}{2}=\tfrac12$, which is claim 1.

Writing $s=\sqrt{1-4q^{2}}$, one has $s^{2}=1-4q^{2}$; hence $C(l^{q})=q^{2}+s^{2}+3q^{2}=4q^{2}+1-4q^{2}=1$ and $E(l^{q})=\tfrac12\bigl(q^{2}+\tfrac{s^{2}}{2}+\tfrac{3q^{2}}{3}\bigr)=\tfrac12\bigl(q^{2}+\tfrac{1-4q^{2}}{2}+q^{2}\bigr)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac14$ by [L4]. For $l_{0}=e_{2}$: $C(l_{0})=1$ and $E(l_{0})=\tfrac12\langle e_{2},I^{-1}e_{2}\rangle=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac14$. This is claim 2, and by [L3] the perturbed datum and the spin datum lie on the same invariant level.

For the proximity bound: $\lVert l^{q}-l_{0}\rVert_2^{2}=q^{2}+(s-1)^{2}+3q^{2}=4q^{2}+(1-s)^{2}$, and $1-s=\tfrac{1-s^{2}}{1+s}=\tfrac{4q^{2}}{1+s}\le4q^{2}$ because $s\ge0$; with $q=\tfrac1{400}$, $4q^{2}=\tfrac{4}{160000}=\tfrac1{40000}$ and $(1-s)^{2}\le(4q^{2})^{2}=\tfrac{16}{400^{4}}=\tfrac{1}{16\cdot10^{8}}<\tfrac{1}{10^{9}}$, so $\lVert l^{q}-l_{0}\rVert_2^{2}\le\tfrac1{40000}+\tfrac1{10^{9}}<\tfrac1{10000}$, whence $\lVert l^{q}-l_{0}\rVert_2<\tfrac1{100}$ by [L4] applied to the nonnegative squares. Moreover $q=\tfrac1{400}<\tfrac1{100}=\min\{\delta_{0},\tfrac1{100}\}$ by step 1.1. This is claim 3.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only for the finiteness of the defining
integrals of the model's inertial quantities. Adopt the heavy symmetric top
branch [[post-cm11-heavy-top]] with parameters $A_{c}>0$, $C_{c}>0$, $d>0$,
$g>0$ and total mass $m>0$; use the notation of that postulate: the pivot
material point $\rho_{p}=-d\,e_{3}$ is held at the origin, so
$c(t)=d\,R(t)e_{3}$; the pivot reaction contributes no torque about the
origin; and the external gravitational field is $G=-g e_{3}$ with total
torque about the origin $\tau_{p}(t)=-mgd\,(R(t)e_{3})\times e_{3}$. Put
$$A:=A_{c}+md^{2}>0,\qquad C:=C_{c}>0,$$
the transverse moment of the model about the pivot and its axial moment. Let
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ be a motion of the branch with time window $I_0$,
and suppose that there are functions $\varphi,\theta,\psi:I_0\to\mathbb R$
of class $C^{2}$ with $\theta(I_0)\subseteq(0,\pi)$ and
$$R(t)=\Theta\bigl(\varphi(t),\theta(t),\psi(t)\bigr)=R_{z}\bigl(\varphi(t)\bigr)R_{y}\bigl(\theta(t)\bigr)R_{z}\bigl(\psi(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in I_0),$$
the Euler-angle description of [[def-cm-euler-angle-parametrization-and-heavy-top-system]].
Then:

1. **Angular momentum about the pivot.** With $\omega$ the body angular
   velocity of the motion and
   $\tilde I:=A\,(e_{1}e_{1}^{\mathsf T}+e_{2}e_{2}^{\mathsf T})+C\,e_{3}e_{3}^{\mathsf T}$
   (the diagonal matrix $\mathrm{diag}(A,A,C)$ in the principal basis) one has
   $$J_{p}(t):=\int x(t,\rho)\times\partial_{t}x(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho)=R(t)\,\tilde I\,\omega(t),$$
   and the balance of [[post-cm11-heavy-top]] clause (v) reads
   $J_{p}'=\tau_{p}$ with
   $$\tau_{p}(t)=-mgd\,\bigl(R(t)e_{3}\bigr)\times e_{3},\qquad \tau_{p}(t)\cdot e_{3}=0 .$$
2. **Body-frame pivot equations.** With $\gamma(t):=R(t)^{\mathsf T}e_{3}$,
   $$\tilde I\,\omega'+\omega\times\tilde I\,\omega=-mgd\,\bigl(e_{3}\times\gamma\bigr)\qquad\text{on }I_0,$$
   that is, componentwise in the principal basis,
   $$A\omega_{1}'=(A-C)\omega_{2}\omega_{3}+mgd\,\gamma_{2},\qquad A\omega_{2}'=(C-A)\omega_{1}\omega_{3}-mgd\,\gamma_{1},\qquad C\omega_{3}'=0 .$$
   Under the Euler-angle description of the statement,
   $$\gamma=\bigl(-\sin\theta\cos\psi,\ \sin\theta\sin\psi,\ \cos\theta\bigr),\qquad \omega_{3}=\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta .$$
3. **Reduction to one dimension.** Define on $I_0$
   $$b:=C\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr),\qquad a:=A\,\varphi'\sin^{2}\theta+b\cos\theta .$$
   Then $b$ and $a$ are constant on $I_0$; consequently
   $$\varphi'=\frac{a-b\cos\theta}{A\sin^{2}\theta},\qquad \psi'=\frac{b}{C}-\frac{(a-b\cos\theta)\cos\theta}{A\sin^{2}\theta};$$
   the **reduced energy**
   $$E:=\tfrac12 A\,\theta'^{2}+\frac{(a-b\cos\theta)^{2}}{2A\sin^{2}\theta}+\frac{b^{2}}{2C}+mgd\cos\theta$$
   is constant on $I_0$; and with the **effective potential**
   $$U(\theta):=\frac{(a-b\cos\theta)^{2}}{2A\sin^{2}\theta}+\frac{b^{2}}{2C}+mgd\cos\theta$$
   one has $A\,\theta''=-U'(\theta)$ on $I_0$.
4. **The heavy-top system.** Equivalently, $(\varphi,\theta,\psi)$ is a
   heavy-top trajectory of [[def-cm-euler-angle-parametrization-and-heavy-top-system]]
   with parameters $(A,C,m,d,g)$, and clauses 1-4 of
   [[thm-cm-heavy-top-reduction]] hold for it.

interval: no claim is made that every motion of the branch admits such a
description, that a description extends across the poles $\theta\in\{0,\pi\}$
(where the sleeping-top and hanging configurations lie), or that the
description is unique. On every subinterval on which a description with
$\theta\in(0,\pi)$ exists, the conclusions hold there. The statement asserts
no friction or driving torque at the pivot, no measurement and no empirical
