Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following **heavy symmetric
top branch** of the rigid-material model, in the setting of
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]].

**(i) Setting.** A model of the branch carries the data of
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: a reference mass distribution $\nu$ with total
mass $m>0$ and centred reference coordinates, a time window $I_0$, an
inertial frame with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]),
whose origin is chosen at the pivot point of clause (iii), and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^{2}$
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]). Assume the Axiom of Countable
Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), used only through the
integrals of the model's inertial quantities. Fix once and for all an
orthonormal basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ of the reference coordinates.

**(ii) Axisymmetry and the declared parameters.** The body inertia matrix of
the model ([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] clause (a)) is
$$I=A_{c}\,(e_{1}e_{1}^{\mathsf T}+e_{2}e_{2}^{\mathsf T})+C_{c}\,e_{3}e_{3}^{\mathsf T},\qquad A_{c}>0,\ C_{c}>0,$$
so that $e_{3}$ is the **symmetry axis**; the numbers $A_{c}$, $C_{c}$ are
declared model parameters of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}$, read in kilogram metres
squared, and are not measured within the framework. The branch also declares
a **pivot distance** $d>0$ of dimension $\ell$ and a **field strength**
$g>0$ of dimension $\ell\tau^{-2}$, read in metres per second squared
([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(iii) The pivot constraint.** The material point of reference coordinate
$\rho_{p}:=-d\,e_{3}$ is the **pivot material point**; it lies on the
symmetry axis at distance $d$ from the centre of mass. The motions of the
branch are those satisfying
$$c(t)+R(t)\rho_{p}=0\qquad(t\in I_{0}),$$
    that is $c(t)=d\,R(t)e_{3}$: the pivot material point is held fixed at the
    origin of the inertial frame for the whole time window, and the centre of
    mass lies on the sphere of radius $d$ about the origin. The
constraint is maintained by a mechanism (a bearing, a hinge or a fine
support) whose force system is **ideal** in the sense adopted for
frictionless hinges in [[post-cm06-ideal-reaction-law]] clause (iii) together
with the virtual-work law of its clause (i): the mechanism exerts on the body
a force system equivalent to a single force applied at the pivot point, so
that its total torque about the origin **vanishes**. The holonomic-constraint
vocabulary of [[def-cm06-holonomic-constraint-model]] — constrained curve
families, reaction fields and the declaration that the constraint is
maintained by an additional force contribution — is the framework's account
for finitely many particle labels; the present model is a continuum, and this
clause adopts the analogous idealisation for it. No friction, damping or
driving torque at the pivot is asserted; such torques are excluded and would
have to be declared as part of a torque datum with their own model.

**(iv) The uniform gravitational field.** The model declares a **uniform
gravitational acceleration** $G:=-g\,e_{3}$ of dimension $\ell\tau^{-2}$:
every material point of the body is subject to the external force
$G\,d\nu$, that is, the force per unit mass is the constant vector $-g e_{3}$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] for the
spatial vectors). The field is a model idealisation: it asserts neither a
particular direction in any absolute sense (the direction $e_{3}$ is a
declared frame direction) nor a measured value of $g$, and it is not
asserted to represent the Earth's or any planet's field. The resultant of
this force system and its total torque about a point are computed in
the reduction theorem of this page; in particular the resultant is the total weight
$-mg e_{3}$ applied at the centre of mass.

**(v) The adopted dynamics.** Along every motion of the branch adopt the
**balance of angular momentum about the pivot**: with
$$J_{p}(t):=\int\bigl(x(t,\rho)-0\bigr)\times\partial_{t}x(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho)$$
the angular momentum of the model about the origin, and with $\tau_{p}(t)$
the total external torque about the origin — the sum of the gravitational
torque and of the pivot reaction torque, the latter vanishing by clause
(iii) — adopt
$$J_{p}'(t)=\tau_{p}(t)\qquad(t\in I_{0}).$$
This is an adopted dynamical law of the branch, analogous to but distinct
from the balance of [[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iii) about the
centre of mass; it acquires content only together with the kinematic
constraint of clause (iii) and the external force system of clause (iv). No
equation of motion for the pivot reaction is asserted: the reaction is
whatever force the ideal mechanism supplies, and its torque about the origin
is zero by clause (iii).

**(vi) Scope and exclusions.** The branch excludes non-axisymmetric bodies
($A_{c}$ and $C_{c}$ are the two transverse and the axial moment and no other
inertia data are used), bodies whose mass distribution fails to produce this
inertia matrix, non-uniform gravitational fields, friction and driving
torques at the pivot, rolling or sliding contacts, impacts, deformable
bodies and variable mass, and every relativistic or quantum description. It
asserts no force law for the pivot reaction, no conservation law and no
measured value of $A_{c}$, $C_{c}$, $m$, $d$ or $g$. Whether the branch is
adequate for a given apparatus — a top on a bearing, a gyroscope in a gimbal,
a spinning shell — is decided by comparing the model's conditional
predictions with reported observations of that apparatus under its stated
regime, and agreement is evidence about the combined model and apparatus, not
a proof of the idealisation.

**(vii) Relation to the other balances.** The balance of clause (v) is not
claimed to be a consequence of the centre-of-mass balance of
[[post-cm11-torque-balance]] clause (iii), nor conversely; the two are
separate adopted laws about different points, and neither is deduced from the
framework's particle balances. A model may use both simultaneously, and the
reduction theorem of this page uses only clause (v) together with clauses
(ii)-(iv).

For $a\in\mathbb R$ define, in the standard basis of $\mathbb R^3$,
$$R_z(a):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos a&-\sin a&0\\ \sin a&\cos a&0\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad R_y(a):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos a&0&\sin a\\ 0&1&0\\ -\sin a&0&\cos a\end{pmatrix}\in M_3(\mathbb R).$$
Then:

1. $R_z(a)\in SO(3)$ and $R_y(a)\in SO(3)$ for every $a$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]), $R_z(a)e_3=e_3$ and $R_y(a)e_2=e_2$, and $R_z(0)=R_y(0)=I_3$.
2. $R_z(a)R_z(b)=R_z(a+b)$ and $R_y(a)R_y(b)=R_y(a+b)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$.
3. For every differentiable $a:I\to\mathbb R$ on an interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-derivative]], [[def-interval]]), the matrix-valued curves $t\mapsto R_z(a(t))$ and $t\mapsto R_y(a(t))$ are differentiable with $$(R_z\circ a)'=a'\,R_z(a)\,[e_3]_\times=a'\,[e_3]_\times R_z(a),\qquad (R_y\circ a)'=a'\,R_y(a)\,[e_2]_\times=a'\,[e_2]_\times R_y(a),$$ where $[e_3]_\times,[e_2]_\times$ are the cross-product matrices of [[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]].

**Euler-angle parametrization.** Let $R_z,R_y$ be the coordinate rotation matrices of [[lem-cm-coordinate-rotation-matrices]]. The **Euler-angle parametrization** is the map
$$\Theta:\mathbb R\times(0,\pi)\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow SO(3),\qquad \Theta(\varphi,\theta,\psi):=R_z(\varphi)\,R_y(\theta)\,R_z(\psi),$$
which is $SO(3)$-valued by [[lem-cm-coordinate-rotation-matrices]] and [[lem-cm-so3-is-a-matrix-group]]. The numbers $(\varphi,\theta,\psi)$ are the **Euler angles** and the open set $\mathbb R\times(0,\pi)\times\mathbb R$ is its **domain**; $\theta$ is restricted to the open interval $(0,\pi)$ so that $\sin\theta>0$, with $\pi$ defined as twice the smallest positive cosine zero ([[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]]) and positivity supplied by [[cor-pi-is-the-first-positive-sine-zero]]. No injectivity and no chart or diffeomorphism property of $\Theta$ is asserted or used here, and no periodicity of the angles is imposed — the real parameters stand for themselves.

**Parameters.** Fix reals $A>0$, $C>0$, $m>0$, $d>0$ and $g>0$; they are mathematical parameters, not identified with any physical quantity in this item.

**The heavy-top function.** Write $q=(\varphi,\theta,\psi)$ for a point of the domain and $v=(\varphi',\theta',\psi')$ for a triple of reals. The **heavy-top function** is
$$L(q,v):=\tfrac12A\bigl(\theta'^2+\varphi'^2\sin^2\theta\bigr)+\tfrac12C\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)^2-mgd\cos\theta,$$
using the sine and cosine of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]. Repeated application of the sine/cosine derivative identities ([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]]) and the finite sum, product and chain rules ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule]]) gives continuous partial derivatives of every order, so it is $C^\infty$ on the domain times $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); its relevant partial derivatives are, explicitly,
$$\partial_{\varphi'}L=A\varphi'\sin^2\theta+C\cos\theta\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr),\qquad \partial_\varphi L=0,$$
$$\partial_{\theta'}L=A\theta',\qquad \partial_\theta L=A\varphi'^2\sin\theta\cos\theta-C\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)\varphi'\sin\theta+mgd\sin\theta,$$
$$\partial_{\psi'}L=C\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr),\qquad \partial_\psi L=0.$$

**The heavy-top system.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points. A **heavy-top trajectory** for these parameters is a twice-differentiable curve $q=(\varphi,\theta,\psi):I\to\mathbb R\times(0,\pi)\times\mathbb R$ such that, with $q'=(\varphi',\theta',\psi')$ its derivative, the three second-order equations
$$\frac{d}{dt}\Bigl(A\varphi'\sin^2\theta+C\cos\theta\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)\Bigr)=0,\qquad \frac{d}{dt}\bigl(A\theta'\bigr)=A\varphi'^2\sin\theta\cos\theta-C\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)\varphi'\sin\theta+mgd\sin\theta,$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}\Bigl(C\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)\Bigr)=0$$
hold on $I$, all functions being evaluated at $t$. These displayed equations are the definition of the system; they are written out so that no separate definition of a variational principle is needed. The first and third are the statements that $\partial_{\varphi'}L$ and $\partial_{\psi'}L$ are constant along the trajectory.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $\gamma$ be the unique smallest positive zero of cosine supplied by [[thm-cosine-has-a-smallest-positive-zero]]. Define
$$\pi:=2\gamma.$$

Thus $\pi>0$ and $\pi/2=\gamma$.
There is a unique $\gamma\in(0,2)$ with $\cos\gamma=0$. It is the smallest positive zero of cosine.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

derivations.claim: Put $\theta=\pi/3$, $c=\cos\theta$ and $s=\sin\theta$. Since $0<\theta<\pi/2$, [L5] gives $0<c<1$ and $s>0$. The addition formulas [L5] and Pythagorean identity [L4] give $\cos\pi=\cos(3\theta)=4c^{3}-3c$; as $\cos\pi=-1$, $(c+1)(2c-1)^{2}=0$. Because $c>0$, $c=1/2$. Then $s^{2}=1-c^{2}=3/4$ and $s>0$, so the uniqueness of the nonnegative square root [L5] gives $s=\sqrt3/2$.

By [L2] with $\varphi'=1$, $\theta'=0$, $\psi'=2$, $\theta_{0}=\pi/3$ and $\psi(t)=2t$: $\omega(t)=\bigl(-\sin\theta_{0}\cos(2t),\ \sin\theta_{0}\sin(2t),\ 2+\cos\theta_{0}\bigr)=\bigl(-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\cos(2t),\ \tfrac{\sqrt3}2\sin(2t),\ \tfrac52\bigr)$ and $\gamma(t)=\bigl(-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\cos(2t),\ \tfrac{\sqrt3}2\sin(2t),\ \tfrac12\bigr)$ by step 1.1 and [L2].

With $\varphi'=1$, $\theta'=0$, $\psi'=2$, $\sin^{2}\theta_{0}=\tfrac34$ and $\cos\theta_{0}=\tfrac12$ by [L4]: $b=C(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta_{0})=1\cdot(2+\tfrac12)=\tfrac52$ and $a=A\varphi'\sin^{2}\theta_{0}+b\cos\theta_{0}=3\cdot\tfrac34+\tfrac52\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac94+\tfrac54=\tfrac72$.

Compute both sides of the balance with $\tilde I=\mathrm{diag}(3,3,1)$: by [L4], $\omega'=\bigl(\sqrt3\sin(2t),\ \sqrt3\cos(2t),\ 0\bigr)$, so $\tilde I\omega'=\bigl(3\sqrt3\sin(2t),\ 3\sqrt3\cos(2t),\ 0\bigr)$, and with $\tilde I\omega=\bigl(-\tfrac{3\sqrt3}2\cos(2t),\ \tfrac{3\sqrt3}2\sin(2t),\ \tfrac52\bigr)$, the coordinate formula for the cross product gives $(\omega\times\tilde I\omega)_{1}=\tfrac{5\sqrt3}4\sin(2t)-\tfrac{15\sqrt3}4\sin(2t)=-\tfrac{5\sqrt3}2\sin(2t)$, $(\omega\times\tilde I\omega)_{2}=-\tfrac{15\sqrt3}4\cos(2t)+\tfrac{5\sqrt3}4\cos(2t)=-\tfrac{5\sqrt3}2\cos(2t)$ and $(\omega\times\tilde I\omega)_{3}=0$. Hence the left side is $\bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\sin(2t),\ \tfrac{\sqrt3}2\cos(2t),\ 0\bigr)$. On the right, $e_{3}\times\gamma=(-\gamma_{2},\gamma_{1},0)=\bigl(-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\sin(2t),\ -\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\cos(2t),\ 0\bigr)$ and $mgd=1$, so the right side is the same vector; the balance holds for every $t$.

The reduced energy: $E=\tfrac12A\theta'^{2}+\tfrac{(a-b\cos\theta_{0})^{2}}{2A\sin^{2}\theta_{0}}+\tfrac{b^{2}}{2C}+mgd\cos\theta_{0}=\tfrac{(9/4)^{2}}{2\cdot3\cdot(3/4)}+\tfrac{25/4}{2}+\tfrac12=\tfrac{9}{8}+\tfrac{25}{8}+\tfrac48=\tfrac{38}{8}=\tfrac{19}{4}$, where $a-b\cos\theta_{0}=\tfrac72-\tfrac54=\tfrac94$ by step 2.2.

The constraint $c(t)+R(t)(-de_{3})=dR(t)e_{3}-dR(t)e_{3}=0$ holds by the definition of $c$; hence with step 3.1 the data constitute a motion of the branch satisfying the adopted pivot balance, and clauses 1-2 of [[pthm-cm11-top-reduction]] apply.

The three equations of the heavy-top system of [L3] hold for the triple: the first and third are the statements that $a$ and $b$ of step 2.2 are constant, and the second is $0=A\varphi'^{2}\sin\theta_{0}\cos\theta_{0}-C(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta_{0})\varphi'\sin\theta_{0}+mgd\sin\theta_{0}=3\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}4-\tfrac{5\sqrt3}4+\tfrac{2\sqrt3}4$ with $\varphi'=1$, which vanishes by [L4]. Hence $(\varphi,\theta,\psi)$ is a heavy-top trajectory with parameters $(A,C,m,d,g)=(3,1,1,1,1)$, and $A\theta''=-U'(\theta_{0})=0$; the conservation of $a$ and $b$ and the formulas $\varphi'=(a-b\cos\theta_{0})/(A\sin^{2}\theta_{0})=\tfrac{9/4}{9/4}=1$ and $\psi'=b/C-(a-b\cos\theta_{0})\cos\theta_{0}/(A\sin^{2}\theta_{0})=\tfrac52-\tfrac{9/4\cdot1/2}{9/4}=\tfrac52-\tfrac12=2$ of [L3] are consistent with the data, so the motion is a steady precession with constant nutation angle $\pi/3$.

The reverse direction (constructing the motion from the system alone) is not needed: the motion is displayed, and the example verifies the balance directly rather than by a converse theorem.
